Kendall's tau serves as a nonparametric metric for correlation, offering robustness against outliers and applicability to arbitrary data types. However, for large datasets, calculating the exact value of Kendall's tau becomes computationally prohibitive due to the $O(n^2)$ complexity of the naive algorithm. Although recent advances have introduced efficient linear-time methods, these often rely on approximations that may sacrifice accuracy. This study demonstrates that highly accurate confidence intervals for Kendall's tau can be derived without approximating the statistic itself. Specifically, we propose linear-time confidence intervals grounded in the asymptotic normality of Kendall's tau and derive finite-sample corrections to enhance accuracy. Furthermore, we develop linear-time confidence intervals applicable to both in- and out-of-sample data using leverage scores. Our approach maintains the accuracy of exact inference while achieving linear computational complexity, representing the first method to guarantee exact type-I error control with $O(n)$ runtime. Additionally, our tight theoretical analysis reveals that the variance of Kendall's tau is significantly smaller than previously estimated, enabling the construction of valid linear-time confidence intervals. We validate our method's accuracy and efficiency through simulations and a real-world case study involving Twitter activity. We introduce a technique for constructing closed manifolds by utilizing a random Euler characteristic function defined on a semi-open manifold. The level sets of this function serve as the target manifolds. By defining a specific collection of coordinate charts and applying a limit process, we ensure that the manifold expands to enclose the target manifold as the colimit. We further extend this method to produce higher-dimensional manifolds. Initially, the weighting of the random Euler characteristic function determines the topology of the resulting manifold; however, in the subsequent level, specific weights are required to achieve manifolds with non-constant Euler characteristics. Ultimately, this process generates closed manifolds featuring non-constant Euler characteristics, alongside a level of weighting that can be interpreted as the "distance" between two points on these manifolds. This construction has potential applications in training neural networks, as the identified target manifolds can function as training sets, thereby introducing geometric information into the training procedure. Additionally, the method offers a means to represent data with non-constant Euler characteristics. To validate these claims, we provide examples of trained neural networks and data sets modeled after the resulting manifolds. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/DeepGeometries/EulerCharManifolds. Our findings were presented at the NeurIPS 2021 Datasets and Applications Track. This work assesses the sensitivity of the top quark mass measurement using a topological amplitude method within the LHCtt experiment, which analyzes $t\overline{t}$+jet events. We conducted a 21 cm neutral hydrogen survey targeting the high-mass star-forming region G176.51+00.20, utilizing the NRO 45 m telescope. This survey successfully detected 11 neutral hydrogen (HI) narrow-line self-absorption features. By combining HI velocity channels with 12CO J=1-0 data, we identified 6 of these features as self-absorbed lines, indicating the presence of HI cold clumps. We calculated the HI masses of these cold clumps to be (0.001–0.003) M☉. These clumps are situated approximately 0.1–0.2 pc from the star-forming region, which aligns with the typical scale of star-forming clouds. Additionally, we detected 5 HI self-absorbed lines in the velocity range of 47.5–52.5 km s⁻¹, attributed to HI cold clumps with masses of (0.002–0.005) M☉ located about 0.2 pc away. These clumps exhibit low excitation temperatures and high densities, suggesting they may be in the process of forming. This study represents the first detection of HI narrow-line self-absorptions toward G176.51+00.20, offering valuable insights into the HI structure of this region. The detected HI cold clumps demonstrate that the NRO 45 m telescope is highly effective for observing HI narrow-line self-absorptions in star-forming regions. Furthermore, the findings suggest that HI narrow-line self-absorptions can be utilized to investigate the HI structure of star-forming regions. Future investigations should employ higher resolution and sensitivity to detect more HI self-absorptions in star-forming regions. This report assesses various deep neural network domain adaptation methods for image recognition. This paper investigates the number of arcs with cardinality $k$, denoted by $N_k(\mathbb F_q^2)$, demonstrating that this count can be expressed through the number of convex $k$-gons inscribed in the unit circle. The findings generalize existing results, specifically the formula for $N_4(\mathbb F_q^2)$. Our proofs rely on analyzing the associated incidence matrix and applying linear algebra techniques. Furthermore, we provide computational data for $N_k(\mathbb F_p^2)$ where $p \leq 1000$. ParGNE offers modular components for modeling graphs, GNNs, and explanations, alongside a set of configurable parameters that define how these elements interact. This extensive evaluation provides the first broad characterization of current techniques, revealing that no single method excels across all scenarios. Instead, we identify consistent trends and trade-offs regarding performance, scalability, and computational efficiency, which can guide practitioners in selecting appropriate methods for specific applications. We conducted a substructure analysis of the galaxy cluster RXCJ0232.2-4420 using a combined sample of 1.2 million galaxies from the Sloan Digital Sky Survey. By applying the biweight estimator, we determined the cluster's redshift to be $z=0.4422 \pm 0.0001$. Utilizing the Slutzky transform, we identified two distinct substructures: a northern group at $z=0.4442 \pm 0.0001$ and a southern group at $z=0.4457 \pm 0.0001$. Additionally, we performed substructure analysis on Chandra X-ray data, which revealed two substructures aligning with the redshift findings. We estimated the physical properties of the cluster, including a mass of $M_{500}=1.10^{+0.35}_{-0.29} \times 10^{14} M_{\odot}$ derived from galaxy counts, and the same mass value obtained from both X-ray data and the Slutzky transform. Furthermore, we determined the cluster's dynamical state using the Biweight estimator. Finally, we conducted a spectroscopic study of the cluster's brightest galaxies. The Legendre memory unit (LMU) represents a newly introduced recurrent neural network (RNN) architecture that leverages Legendre polynomials to enhance memory capabilities. While the application of Legendre polynomials to memory-enhanced networks is a novel concept, the technique itself is well-established and has been successfully applied across diverse fields such as machine learning, physics simulations, and computational fluid dynamics. These parallelized LMU training methods are anticipated to be adaptable for other domains. Although the computational demands of training data-driven models with enhanced memory are expected to grow, the implementation of parallel training strategies is not inherently complex. Specifically, data parallelization can be achieved by distributing data batches across multiple GPUs, whereas model parallelization involves dividing the network into sub-layers trained concurrently. The current implementation was developed using PyTorch and is publicly accessible on GitHub. Additionally, the codebase includes a data augmentation module for generating training samples from the MNIST and Fashion-MNIST datasets. This work demonstrates a straightforward approach to training enhanced neural networks using a single GPU. However, as these models are more computationally intensive than standard RNNs, utilizing multiple GPUs is necessary for efficient training. The presented code outlines a basic data parallelization strategy for GPUs. Furthermore, the current implementation does not address mixed data and model parallelization. Future research is required to explore both model parallelization and advanced data parallelization schemes, such as distributed data-parallel training combined with model parallelization. Ultimately, the primary objective is to enable the training of large-scale enhanced neural networks on high-performance computing systems. This work is expected to facilitate such training in the future. Additionally, the code does not currently support distributed training environments like MPI. Incorporating such features is a direction for future research. Finally, while this paper demonstrates parallelization using a single node with multiple GPUs, future studies should extend these methods to multi-node GPU clusters. Although the Standard Model of particle physics has endured numerous experimental tests, it is widely believed to be an incomplete low-energy approximation of a deeper, wider theory. Consequently, numerous experiments are investigating new physics beyond the Standard Model, with a specific focus on feeblely-interacting particles. This review, which is based on an invited talk, details the most recent experimental initiatives in this field, including their theoretical foundations, rationale, and experimental strategies. It highlights the Axion-Haloscope, LABSearch, SHiP, and COHERENT as key facilities for detecting axions, dark matter, and other new, weakly-interacting particles. Furthermore, the text underscores the significance of accelerator-based experiments and their contributions to understanding new physics. Finally, the review concludes with an analysis of future prospects for axion searches and their potential to address the discrepancy in the measured values of the Standard Model parameters $\theta_q$ and $g_A^f$. Ultimately, these feeblely-interacting particles represent a promising avenue for discovering new physics. While numerous studies have examined how social structures influence language development, fewer have addressed the impact of social structure changes on such systems. This research investigates the evolution of social structure and its effect on language within a social network framework using a naming game model driven by individual agents seeking to maximize personal utility. Our findings indicate that, despite a predisposition toward efficiency, this model naturally generates diverse, complex, and robust languages characterized by a power-law distribution of vocabulary sizes. Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) represent a growing method for integrating prior physical knowledge, typically in the form of differential equations, to address inverse problems. However, current optimization techniques used to train PINNs often struggle, frequently failing to converge or producing highly inaccurate results. This study demonstrates that adding a small momentum term during the training process can substantially enhance both convergence and accuracy. Specifically, we find that momentum helps overcome PINNs' inherent spectral limitations by mitigating the excessive bias toward low-frequency modes. Our analysis reveals that momentum allows for more effective updates in high-frequency modes, thereby reducing their training loss. We validate these findings across various inverse problems involving the heat equation, wave equation, and advection-diffusion equation. Furthermore, we introduce a theoretical framework to explain this phenomenon and apply it to simple one-dimensional cases. Finally, we illustrate the utility of momentum-based PINNs in reconstructing time-varying coefficients from noisy data. Overall, this research offers a straightforward yet effective strategy for improving PINN performance. The accompanying code can be found at https://github.com/taehyung-lee1234/Momentum-PINNs. This study examines a coupled wave system featuring one Neumann boundary condition and one locally perturbed Dirichlet condition, incorporating Kelvin-Voigt damping. We demonstrate that energy dissipation occurs at an algebraic rate proportional to the decay of the perturbation, thereby ensuring the asymptotic stability of the system. This result contrasts sharply with undamped coupled wave systems, where internal local disturbances typically prevent stability. The proof relies on applying an energy identity to a suitable modified energy functional. Furthermore, we establish that the modified energy remains equivalent to the original energy, up to constants that are independent of the system's parameters. We also analyze the impact of extending these local disturbances to the entire boundary. Additionally, we confirm that internal time-dependent disturbances, which vanish asymptotically, do not disrupt stability. However, we note that boundary disturbances are not addressed in this work, as they would necessitate additional assumptions regarding the compatibility of Dirichlet and Neumann data, thereby complicating the proof. Finally, although the system exhibits stability, it does not possess a standard exponential decay rate. Instead, the asymptotic behavior is characterized by a logarithmic decay rate, which is demonstrated through an energy differential inequality. The validity of this inequality is shown to hold for various choices of modified energy functionals. To illustrate the practical implications of this logarithmic decay rate, we conduct numerical simulations. These simulations indicate that the decay rate is highly sensitive to the size of the disturbed domain; specifically, shrinking the disturbed domain enhances decay, whereas expanding it diminishes the decay rate. This observation is particularly pronounced when the disturbed domain covers the entire boundary. Our findings suggest that exponential decay rates can be recovered when the disturbed domain encompasses the whole boundary, though this specific case is omitted from the current analysis. Instead, we focus on a simplified model where the disturbed domain is the entire boundary, utilizing an alternative modified energy functional to derive an energy differential inequality. This approach yields a preliminary proof of exponential decay, thereby recovering the result for globally disturbed coupled wave systems with Kelvin-Voigt damping. The remainder of the paper is structured as follows: Section 2 presents the model and its associated assumptions; Section 3 reviews relevant preliminary results; Section 4 addresses energy equivalence; Section 5 details the stability analysis; and Section 6 presents numerical simulations. We introduce a new method for detecting spin-dependent (SD) dark matter interactions using $\mathrm^6$Li within nuclear emulsions. Leveraging recent findings on the nucleon-decoupled tensor matrix element of $\mathrm^6$Li, we demonstrate that SD interactions with this isotope can yield significantly stronger nuclear effective cross sections compared to standard spin-dependent $\mathrm^3$He-nucleon SDDM interactions. Furthermore, we show that SDDM cross sections can be constrained using existing dark matter direct detection data derived from $\mathrm^6$Li content in natural germanium and copper. Finally, we explore the potential of future direct detection experiments utilizing $\mathrm^6$Li to establish nuclear sensitivity to sub-GeV scale SDDM. This approach offers an alternative to current direct detection methods for identifying light spin-dependent dark matter candidates. Additionally, we provide constraints on SDDM couplings to tensor charges, revealing a notable discrepancy between our results and those derived from $\mathrm^3$He. This inconsistency suggests the need for further $\mathrm^6$Li and $\mathrm^3$He tensor charge measurements to resolve the issue. Our findings also highlight the necessity of incorporating $\mathrm^6$Li contributions into future direct detection analyses to avoid misinterpreting dark matter signals. Specifically, we find that nuclear sensitivity to sub-GeV scale SDDM can be achieved with $\sim 100$ kg of highly enriched $\mathrm^6$Li, reaching spin-dependent cross sections as low as $\sigma_{SD} \sim 10^{-39} \mathrm{cm}^2$. This sensitivity is attainable with a next-generation $\sim 10$ year exposure of approximately $10^{11}$ $\mathrm^6$Li atoms per kilogram. Such an exposure could be realized through a novel $\sim 100$ kg of highly enriched $\mathrm^6$Li gas or via existing dark matter direct detection experiments employing $\sim 100$ kg of germanium or copper. We conclude that achieving this level of sensitivity is feasible within the next decade. Blind image deblurring seeks to simultaneously estimate the blur kernel and recover the latent sharp image from a blurred input. This task is inherently ill-posed, necessitating the use of deep learning approaches that leverage deep neural networks to reconstruct image details. However, existing methods often suffer from either excessive computational costs or inadequate exploitation of image priors. To address these issues, we introduce a novel blind deblurring framework grounded in kernel mixture. We hypothesize that a sharp image comprises multiple latent images with distinct image-level kernels. This prior is encoded into a network module that iteratively generates sharp images and aggregates their kernels to enhance the network's representation of image priors. By employing a joint training strategy, we enhance the model's robustness. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our method achieves superior performance compared to current state-of-the-art techniques. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/Chenchenchenchenchen/BlindDeblurWithKernelMix. Additionally, our trained models are available at https://drive.google.

We demonstrate the equivalence between the curved Rota-Baxter (BiHom-)system and the double curved Rota-Baxter (BiHom-)system. Furthermore, we establish an operad isomorphism linking the curved associative (BiHom-)Yang-Baxter equation to the double curved Rota-Baxter (BiHom-)system. Finally, we define an associative post-Yang-Baxter equation, whose solutions generate examples of left (right) $(\phi,q)$-pre-Lie (BiHom-)algebras, extending the work of Zhang and Zhang. Additionally, we illustrate how to construct curved Rota-Baxter (BiHom-)systems using solutions to the associative post-Yang-Baxter equation, thereby providing examples of double curved Rota-Baxter (BiHom-)systems. Specifically, we examine the classical case where no twisting maps are involved, demonstrating how the double curved Rota-Baxter (BiHom-)system generalizes the curved associative Yang-Baxter equation. Blockchain technology is fundamental for creating decentralized applications (DApps) that facilitate the exchange of value. However, existing solutions often suffer from performance bottlenecks, scalability issues, and reliance on trusted hardware. Canopus is a high-performance, scalable, and decentralized DApp designed to enable secure value transfers. Despite its advantages, Canopus currently lacks resilience against Byzantine failures. This paper introduces RCanopus, an enhanced version of Canopus that incorporates robust mechanisms to handle such failures. By utilizing a novel approach, RCanopus achieves the same safety and liveness guarantees as Canopus while maintaining identical performance levels. Furthermore, RCanopus outperforms other Byzantine fault-tolerant protocols, such as PBFT, in various benchmark tests. Experimental results demonstrate that RCanopus is 1.5 times faster than PBFT. Given these benefits, RCanopus is well-suited for real-world deployment, offering a more secure and resilient solution for decentralized value exchange. The modulus of lipid bilayer curvature is essential for understanding membrane deformations induced by embedded proteins. This study examines the impact of varying cholesterol concentrations on water bilayer curvature. Our findings indicate that cholesterol significantly alters the response of excess area to curvature, thereby modifying the effective bending modulus of the bilayer. We demonstrate, through the framework of the averaged bilayer response model, that this effect stems from the distinct area-composition relationships of the monolayers adjacent to the midplane and the interface between the two leaflets. These results hold critical significance for interpreting nanoscale membrane deformations caused by surface-bound proteins. Finally, we explore the implications of these findings regarding lipid bilayer mechanics. Specifically, our analysis reveals an optimal cholesterol concentration that minimizes the bending modulus, potentially facilitating membrane fusion. Additionally, we identify a phase transition in the effective bending modulus at approximately 25 mol% cholesterol, which may be associated with the liquid-ordered/liquid-disordered phase separation observed near 30 mol% cholesterol. This suggests the existence of a narrow two-phase region at nanoscale dimensions. These effects are not accounted for in current experimental data. Furthermore, we show that cholesterol can increase the bending modulus under specific conditions, such as when replacing unsaturated lipids with saturated ones or when high concentrations of polyunsaturated lipids are present. These observations are consistent with existing experimental evidence. Finally, we discuss the implications of these results for membrane biology. In conclusion, our findings suggest that cholesterol can modulate bending modulus across a wide range, from 10 to $50 k_B T$. This wide spectrum of bending moduli is crucial for understanding how membranes interact with various cellular processes. Additionally, our findings suggest that cholesterol may play a role in regulating membrane curvature during cellular events such as endocytosis and membrane fusion. Overall, our findings provide a comprehensive understanding of how cholesterol affects the bending modulus of lipid bilayers, with significant implications for both theoretical and experimental membrane biology. By elucidating the mechanisms by which cholesterol modulates the bending modulus, this work paves the way for further research into the role of cholesterol in cellular processes such as membrane trafficking and signal transduction. Furthermore, our findings may have implications for understanding the mechanisms of cholesterol-related diseases, such as atherosclerosis and Alzheimer's disease, and may inform the development of new therapeutic strategies targeting cholesterol metabolism. This paper presents a catalog of the most energetic cosmic rays identified during the first year of Phase I at the Pierre Auger Observatory. The analysis details the data quality and reduction procedures, including the methods employed to reject spurious events. Additionally, the paper discusses the potential energy evolution of ultra-high-energy (UHE) particles, as well as the observed composition and anisotropy of the sky distribution for energies above 10^{19.5} eV. Deep object detectors are widely used across numerous computer vision applications, yet previous research indicates that their predictions often lack reliability. This issue is particularly critical in safety-sensitive domains like autonomous driving, where undetected objects can lead to fatal outcomes. To address this, we propose BayesOD, the first method capable of generating uncertainty estimates for individual predictions from object detectors. By employing Monte Carlo (MC) dropout, BayesOD can be applied to any existing detector without the need for retraining or architectural changes. We evaluated the method using various deep learning-based detectors on two standard datasets, COCO and VisDrone. Our results demonstrate that BayesOD effectively produces uncertainty scores for single object detections. Furthermore, we show that these scores surpass state-of-the-art techniques in both calibration and discrimination metrics. Additionally, we explore how integrating these uncertainty scores can significantly enhance detector performance, especially in low-shot learning scenarios. This study introduces a novel traffic forecasting technique designed for traffic flow prediction, utilizing data collected from diverse sensors such as loop detectors and cameras. We break the traffic stream into short-duration segments, known as traffic moving snippets (TMS), which capture the dynamics of traffic flow. Each TMS is represented by a matrix composed of flow, speed, and density, alongside a temporal profile of the flow component. To predict a future TMS, we employ a deep learning approach utilizing Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks. For speed and density forecasting, we rely on the flow component, leveraging the strong correlations among all three flow variables. We developed a new segmentation method that maximizes the predictive accuracy of future TMS by effectively selecting relevant historical snippets. Additionally, we introduced a new evaluation metric to assess prediction quality across various time scales. Extensive experiments using real-world datasets from two cities in the United States demonstrate that our method achieves superior quality compared to baseline approaches. The code and data associated with this method are available at https://github.com/ahmedelshorbagy/TMS. However, the traditional reducing and rewriting methodologies have proven insufficient for the nuanced structures inherent in $\infty$-categories. To address this, we introduce a higher-dimensional, categorical variant of rewriting that maintains the established rules and coherences of rewriting theory while functioning coherently within an $\infty$-categorical environment. The construction of this rewriting machinery relies fundamentally on the theory of bicategories and bifunctors. Leveraging this approach, we establish a comprehensive coherence theorem for $\infty$-categories, thereby demonstrating the efficacy and applicability of our method. Additionally, we derive a full coherence theorem for strict $\infty$-categories as a specific instance. To facilitate these proofs, we also develop a novel, intrinsically categorical formulation of coherence that departs from the conventional set-theoretic approach. This new formulation is grounded in the axioms of a weak bihigher category, a structure that, to our knowledge, has not been previously defined in the literature. Accurate segmentation of the hippocampus is essential for diagnosing and monitoring various forms of Alzheimer's and epileptic diseases. This study introduces a two-stage Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) architecture designed to segment the hippocampus in 3D MRI scans. In the first stage, a U-Net model estimates a mask for the hippocampus and surrounding tissue. This predicted mask is then utilized in the second stage to train a 3D U-Net that segments the hippocampus into its left and right components. The model was evaluated using the Sun-IMW-SED 2018 dataset, which includes cases of Alzheimer's disease, hippocampal sclerosis, and no disease. Quantitative results demonstrate that the proposed two-stage network outperforms the single-stage approach in terms of accuracy. The code is accessible at: https://github.com/abhishekkumar1995/3D-UNet-and-3D-UNet-with-Mask. We examine the interference patterns produced by two independent particles confined in a two-dimensional box within the single-particle regime, focusing on their asymptotic behavior. By applying a multiplicative inverse power law to the Hamiltonian, we slow down the particles to analyze their dynamical interference interference. Our results demonstrate that particles with low kinetic energy exhibit a significant reduction in probability at certain locations, a phenomenon known as the transversal pigeonhole effect. This contrasts with conventional quantum mechanics, where the pigeonhole effect in spatially confined systems typically increases probability. Furthermore, we analyze the statistical properties of the interarrival times for transversal modes, revealing that these times are uncorrelated and follow a Poisson distribution. Finally, we explore potential experimental applications of this transversal pigeonhole effect using ultracold atoms. This study represents the first observation of the transversal pigeonhole effect. Additionally, it marks the initial investigation into multiple interference within the single-particle regime, alongside an examination of the statistical properties of interarrival times in a non-Hermitian quantum system. The interarrival times show no correlation and align with Poisson statistics. Our findings are expected to be testable in upcoming experiments utilizing ultracold atoms. The Cosmic Ray Albedo Neutron Decay (CRAND) mechanism is widely regarded as the primary driver for generating the inner trapped proton population in Earth's radiation belts. Once cosmic ray protons collide with the Moon, they produce neutrons that propagate to Earth and become trapped within the geomagnetic field. This study presents a one-year Monte Carlo simulation tracking these trapped protons at low Earth orbits. The results indicate that, on average, the CRAND process produces approximately $10^9$ protons at an energy level of 10 MeV. This figure is roughly 100 times lower than the total count of trapped protons observed by the CRRES satellite in 1991, suggesting that additional physical processes are necessary to account for the full inner trapped proton population. Furthermore, the paper explores potential candidates for these supplementary processes. Additionally, we provide a detailed analysis of the spatial and temporal distributions of the simulated proton population, as well as their energy and magnetic local time dependencies. Finally, the study examines the proton phase space density (PSD) distribution, which the CRAND mechanism alone cannot produce. Consequently, we propose that radial transport processes, such as wave-particle interactions, are required to generate the high PSD levels characteristic of the inner trapped proton population. These processes are likely responsible for creating the so-called "slot region." Overall, the findings suggest that radial transport mechanisms are essential for forming the inner radiation belt, while the CRAND process is primarily responsible for generating the outer radiation belt. These conclusions are supported by the observation that the average outer trapped proton population (below 10,000 km altitude) is approximately $10^9$, which is about 10 times closer to the CRRES 1991 data than the population within 10,000 km. The MGP framework sequentially stacks multiple M-GNN layers, progressively expanding the graph's node count and connectivity to extract hierarchical information from diverse levels. Subsequently, M-GNN layers are embedded into the MGP framework's shrinkage skeleton to rewire local topology links, enabling the model to learn complex interactions between nodes and their neighbors. Extensive experiments across five real-world datasets demonstrate that the proposed framework outperforms state-of-the-art DGNN models and traditional machine learning algorithms in both accuracy and inference speed. We introduce a novel, unified model for the extinction, emission, and polarization of diffuse interstellar dust. This framework describes extinction via a collection of amorphous dust grains, classifying them by size and composition, while emission is represented by gas-phase astrophysical polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs). This approach is grounded in a comprehensive analysis of a vast database of extinction curves, polarization data, and infrared spectral observations. By employing a single set of physical parameters, the model successfully explains extinction across all wavelengths, accounts for infrared emission from PAHs, and generates synthetic polarization curves that align with observed data. Furthermore, the model establishes a direct link between infrared emission and extinction, indicating that this relationship remains stable regardless of environmental variations. We provide a parameter set for each galaxy, including the Milky Way, M31, M33, M32, M82, and NGC 4449, which can be utilized to generate synthetic extinction curves, infrared spectra, and polarization curves for these galaxies. Additionally, we provide the source code for the "Astrodust+PAH" model, which is available at https://github.com/astropartikellab/astrodust_plus_pah. This model is designed to be easily adapted for future studies of dust in galaxies. We conclude that the astrophysical PAH component is essential for accurately reproducing polarization data. Our findings demonstrate that the astromolecular+PAH model offers a unified description of dust properties in the diffuse interstellar medium, thereby simplifying the interpretation of observational data. This model holds significant potential for enhancing the accuracy of dust property estimates in cosmological simulations. The Astrodust+PAH extinction, polarization, and emission data can be accessed at https://www.researchgate.net/profile/Anders_Borregaard_Rasmussen2. Our model is also integrated into the Radiative Transfer in Three Dimensions (RTT3+), a radiative transfer code for dust and magnetic fields in the interstellar medium, which is available at https://github.com/astropartikellab/RTT3plus. RTT3+ is a standalone program that utilizes the Astrodust+PAH extinction, polarization, and emission data. We have also developed a new tool, "AstroDict," which allows users to easily access the Astrodust+PAH data and generate synthetic extinction, polarization, and emission curves. We report the discovery of a 1.5 Jupiter-mass planet orbiting the young, low-mass star CIDA 1, identified through high-contrast imaging. This system is notable because the planet resides within a protoplanetary disk, making it a critical addition to research on formation pathways for both massive and low-mass objects. By analyzing the system's architecture, we infer that the planet formed via core accretion and migrated inward from its birthplace. Our findings highlight the necessity of investigating the inner regions of protoplanetary disks around low-mass stars to uncover the previously unseen population of giant planets. Furthermore, the presence of this planet in the system offers valuable insights into the early stages of planet formation. Finally, we present the first constraints on the internal structure of CIDA 1, which will facilitate future studies of its evolution and atmospheric properties. This study is part of the Cores in Disks (CIDA) initiative, a survey of 100 young stars with ages between 1 and 10 million years. The selected targets are characterized by low-mass primaries ($\lesssim 1.5 M_{\odot}$) and are known to host protoplanetary disks. This paper focuses on the characterization of the CIDA 1 system, with a comprehensive analysis of the entire CIDA sample to be published in a subsequent paper. The remaining CIDA sample will be detailed in Paper II. Image segmentation and restoration are two fundamental tasks in computer vision. While image restoration techniques can provide valuable insights for segmentation models, current state-of-the-art approaches typically apply these methods only as post-processing steps. This paper introduces a novel variational segmentation model that integrates restoration mechanisms as a core component. We investigate two types of restored image generation methods: one that incorporates structural information and another that enhances color and texture details. To evaluate our approach, we tested it on both synthetic and real-world datasets. Our results demonstrate that this model outperforms state-of-the-art methods, achieving an F1 score of 0.801 on synthetic data and 0.734 on real data. Additionally, we provide an in-depth analysis of the model's behavior across various input images. The source code and models are accessible at https://github.com/ChenchenZhang1998/SegRestoration.

Abstract Interpretation (AI) relies on a mathematical framework that links the concrete and abstract domains through four fundamental operations: the concrete semantics ($\gamma$), the abstract semantics ($\alpha$), the $\beta$-transform, and the $\sigma$-transform. This paper demonstrates that the $\beta$-transform can be decomposed into two distinct components: an ascending transform and a descending transform. The ascending phase initiates with a least fixed point computation within the AI lattice, followed by a $\beta$-transform application to obtain a precise post-fixpoint. Subsequently, a descending transform is applied to map these post-fixpoints to the abstract domain, yielding a more accurate approximation than the standard $\beta$-transform. We illustrate the benefits of this approach through an example involving loop invariant computation, showing how the descending post-fixpoint surpasses the traditional $\beta$-transform in accuracy. Furthermore, we establish the relationship between these novel post-fixpoints and the traditional $\sigma$-transform, proving they are more precise. Finally, we outline a general methodology for constructing descending transforms, which holds significant potential for enhancing existing AI techniques. Our experimental findings indicate that this improvement is compatible with various AI frameworks, including interval analysis, abstract interpretation using abstract domains, and octagon analysis. Additionally, we highlight that the proposed technique is computationally efficient, as the additional cost involves only a single fixed-point computation and the application of a descending transform. To the best of our knowledge, this contribution represents the first instance of such an enhancement in AI. We have implemented this method in the AI platform APIN and released the source code under an open-source license. We anticipate that this contribution will foster new research directions aimed at further improving AI accuracy. The paper concludes by discussing several open questions regarding this approach. Finally, we acknowledge the contributions of our colleagues, who provided valuable feedback and suggestions. We extend our sincere gratitude to them. We hope this work inspires new research avenues aimed at further advancing the field of AI. Topological materials have recently garnered significant attention due to their unique properties, including the presence of protected states and the quantum Hall effect at zero magnetic field. Inspired by advances in ultrafast laser technology, this study explores the possibility of inducing topological phases in oxide perovskites through illumination. Using first-principles calculations, we examine how light influences topology in specific oxides, such as SrTiO$_3$ and BaTiO$_3$. Our results demonstrate that optical excitation can shift phonon frequencies and modify the topological characteristics of these materials. These findings offer a pathway for manipulating topological states via external stimuli and hold promise for developing novel photonic and optoelectronic devices.

Although many efficient outlier detection algorithms exist for Euclidean spaces, metric space methods often suffer from reduced accuracy due to distance computation errors. This paper introduces a novel outlier detection algorithm leveraging proximity graphs, which accurately and rapidly computes nearest neighbor distances within metric spaces by mapping them onto graphs. Our method constructs a proximity graph based on the triangle inequality and performs outlier detection by querying this graph. We evaluated our approach against multiple state-of-the-art methods using real-world datasets. The results demonstrate that our method achieves performance comparable to or exceeding that of existing solutions, while also offering superior scalability for large datasets. Furthermore, experimental findings indicate that the performance of the proposed method is more robust across different parameters than most competing approaches. This work shifts the focus to fairness in neural networks operating on graph data. We introduce a fair learning algorithm designed to mitigate bias in local node representations generated by neural networks on graphs. Our method employs a deep neural network to learn a metricization function that adjusts the graph structure to ensure fairness across sensitive attributes. This adjustment is applied exclusively to the neighborhood information feeding into each node, leaving the rest of the graph structure and the primary learning algorithm untouched. Empirical evaluations demonstrate that our proposed algorithm effectively reduces bias while maintaining predictive performance comparable to that of baseline models. This study examines kinetic models of reversible enzyme reactions, comparing two methods for deriving analytic approximate solutions. Specifically, the Homotopy Perturbation Method (HPM) and the Simple Iteration Method (SIM) are employed to solve non-linear reaction equations. The validity and accuracy of these approximations are assessed by contrasting them with the exact solutions. The findings indicate that for small parameters, both methods yield results with high accuracy. However, when the parameters are large, the HPM remains a good approximation, whereas the SIM produces significant errors. Additionally, a comparison between direct and indirect HPM approximations reveals that the direct approach provides a more accurate approximation. These conclusions are supported by numerical examples. Ultimately, the study demonstrates that HPM is a highly effective technique for obtaining accurate and reliable approximations of the solutions to non-linear reversible enzyme reaction equations. All computations were performed using Maple software. This study introduces a new rational expectation framework for asset price bubbles that accounts for their mean-reverting nature and the randomness of their bursting. Within this model, the mean of the log-time-to-bursting process follows an Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process, causing the time-to-bursting to revert to a long-run equilibrium value. Consequently, the expected time-to-bursting and the time-to-bursting variance both return to their long-run means. The model's parameters can be estimated using an extended version of the Phillips-Saulles (2011) method, and the resulting moments serve as tests for the presence of financial bubbles. Applying this methodology to historical data reveals evidence of financial bubbles in the S&P 500 and gold prices. Furthermore, a simulation study demonstrates that these empirical findings cannot be attributed to the common trends shared by both assets. Finally, a simulation analysis of the data's properties indicates that a random-walk model with a stochastic trend fails to replicate the observed evidence. Overall, this paper offers fresh insights into financial bubbles and proposes novel testing procedures for detecting them. Notably, these new bubble-detection methods are distinct from conventional financial-bubble diagnostics. Additionally, the findings suggest that the traditional concept of a "crash" is inaccurate, as the bursting of a financial bubble is primarily governed by the characteristics of the underlying bubble. Specifically, when a bubble bursts, the price drops to its long-run mean, and the time-to-bursting also mean-reverts to its long-run equilibrium. These results underscore the need to refine the traditional understanding of financial bubbles and the bursting mechanisms. The code used to implement this new rational-expectation bubble model is available at https://github.com/ChenYi1992/Financial-Bubbles. We simulated the ground state of a quantum harmonic oscillator subjected to a $Z_2$ drive utilizing path integral formulations. Specifically, we employed path integral Monte Carlo techniques to evaluate the potential energy and the real part of the Wigner distribution for a single oscillator particle. These methods were also applied to a $Z_2$-dimer, a system comprising two quantum harmonic oscillators linked by a potential tunneling step. Our results demonstrate that the numerically computed ground state energies align with analytical predictions. Additionally, the Wigner distributions indicate that the simulated states correspond to the driven system's ground state, supported by the calculation of the Wigner distribution's second moment. Furthermore, the second moment of the Wigner distribution for the $Z_2$-dimer exhibits a cusp at the critical point, signaling a quantum phase transition. This behavior is further corroborated by the second derivative of the ground state energy with respect to the driving force, which also displays a cusp at the critical point where a quantum phase transition occurs. Ultimately, the Wigner distribution reveals that the $Z_2$-dimer ground state shifts from a localized to a delocalized state across the quantum phase transition. These findings suggest that Wigner distributions serve as a valuable tool for characterizing quantum systems within quantum chemistry and field theory simulations. Our work also highlights the potential of quantum computers to simulate quantum systems using quantum field theory formulations. Finally, we introduce a novel application of quantum machine learning to simulate quantum systems, where a quantum circuit was trained to model the driven quantum harmonic oscillator. This approach yielded computed ground state energies consistent with Monte Carlo simulations. The training process involved a quantum circuit featuring controlled Hadamard and controlled-Z gates, with the probability distribution of the controlled-Hadamard gate varying as the system approaches the critical point. Ultimately, the output of the quantum circuit exhibits a cusp at the critical point of the quantum phase transition. This indicates that the trained quantum circuit can be utilized to simulate the driven quantum harmonic oscillator, as the quantum circuit output displays a cusp at the critical point of the quantum phase transition. These findings suggest that quantum machine learning can effectively simulate quantum systems, potentially offering a new avenue for characterizing quantum systems in quantum chemistry and field theory simulations. Finally, we discuss the potential of quantum machine learning as a complementary tool for characterizing quantum systems. This study examines the feasibility of using lexical replacements to augment Arabic-English code-switching (CSWC) data. We introduce a novel data generation pipeline designed to produce gold-standard CSWC datasets from monolingual resources. Our approach involves replacing lexical items in Arabic-English code-switched sentences with words from a single source language, followed by either manual or automatic reconstruction of the original sentences. We employ a combination of automatically extracted monolingual parallel data and cross-lingual morphological replacements to create this gold-standard dataset. The resulting datasets contain around 100,000 sentences, enabling the training of a Transformer-based model for sentence-level CSWC. We assess the efficacy of our model through both quantitative and qualitative analyses. Our findings indicate that the generated CSWC datasets are of high quality and can serve as a valuable resource for expanding training data in low-resource environments. Furthermore, the model demonstrates a strong capacity for sentence-level reconstruction, surpassing both manual and automatic methods. Additionally, the model generalizes effectively to reconstruct sentences from a separate monolingual Arabic corpus, even though no Arabic sentences were included in its training data. This success is attributed to the code-switched nature of the CSWC corpus, which imparts a degree of cross-lingual transferability to the model. Finally, we explore the application of this model to augmentate out-of-vocabulary (OOV) words in cross-lingual machine translation tasks. Experiments on a parallel Arabic-English tweet corpus reveal that our model can reduce OOV rates by approximately 10% to 15%. Given the scarcity of code-switched data in low-resource settings, this research holds significant potential for future advancements in various NLP tasks. We demonstrate that no subgroup of the homeomorphism group of a compact surface, which fixes the boundary and acts with sufficient transitivity on the interior, can be Roelcke precompact when equipped with the topology inherited from the compact-open topology. Consequently, such groups cannot serve as universal minimal groups or Dixmier pairs. This result extends to groups acting on surfaces with non-trivial Euler characteristic that are Roelcke precompact only under the weaker condition of $\Gamma$-transitivity on the pair set. The proof relies on establishing the minimalness of the one-point compactification of an infinite set within the category of $T_0$-spaces. These findings have broad applications, yielding the aforementioned conclusions for groups with weaker action conditions and generating novel examples of non-$T_2$ spaces that are both minimal and Hausdorff. Furthermore, we characterize the Roelcke precompactness of subgroups within the group of all surface homeomorphisms and offer a partial positive solution to the problem of identifying which subgroups of the homeomorphism group of a compact manifold form Dixmier pairs. The latter result applies to manifolds where the dimension is not 3, 5, or 7, or where the group action is non-trivial on the boundary. The universal minimality of the one-point compactification is also utilized to prove that the homeomorphism group of the three-sphere, under the homeomorphism type of antipodal action, possesses a unique Roelcke precompactification and exhibits properties such as being minimal, Hausdorff, and extremally disconnected. The paper concludes with several open questions regarding the minimal spaces and universal minimal groups associated with surface homeomorphism groups. Notably, the universal minimal groups for the cases of a 2-sphere and a two-torus remain unidentified. This work represents a foundational step toward fully characterizing the minimal spaces and universal minimal groups for these groups by restricting the domain to one-point compactifications. To achieve this, we provide a comprehensive characterization of the homeomorphism groups of one-point compactifications and their actions, alongside the minimal and Hausdorff nature of certain such compactifications. Additionally, we present examples of minimal $T_0$-spaces homeomorphic to the one-point compactification of a discrete set and construct minimal Hausdorff spaces homeomorphic to the one-point compactification of a separable metric space of any dimension $n \geq 2$. Focusing on cases where the boundary simplifies to a Wess-Zumino-Witten model, we derive complete boundary algebras and identify two integrable branes: null-wrapping and supersymmetric. For supersymmetric branes, we explicitly construct all necessary fields. Finally, we examine the decoupling limit where the $\lambda$-deformation reduces to non-linear sigma models, identifying specific boundary algebras that retain integrability in this limit. Notably, our analysis reveals a novel class of integrable boundary conditions linked to holomorphic data. These findings are expected to facilitate the construction of new integrable quasi-exact systems. Notably, one of these solutions represents a magnetic wrapping brane, a concept previously unexplored in generalized $\lambda$-deformations. The effectiveness of computational physics simulations relies heavily on the quality of the underlying computational mesh. While various mesh generators exist, they often produce complex and irregular elements that can hinder simulation accuracy. This paper introduces a new meso-scale mesh generator designed to create high-quality hexahedral meshes. By employing our innovative Tets-to-Hex algorithm, we can efficiently convert existing meshes into hexahedral structures, significantly boosting performance. We validate the algorithm's efficacy across diverse scenarios, including mesh adaptation, the conversion of other element types to hexahedra, and large-scale mesh conversion. Furthermore, we demonstrate how to manage challenges associated with large deformations and inhomogeneous meshes. Finally, we apply our method to create hexahedral meshes for selected planets in the Universe. The source code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/ChenYan2018/TetsToHex.

Keywords: mesh generation, computational physics, hexahedralization, tetrahedral-to-hexahedral conversion, computational fluid dynamics.

Corresponding author: Chen Yan (cheny@tju.edu.cn)

## 1 Introduction

Tangible and practical results are paramount in computational physics. High-quality outcomes depend on two critical components: a well-designed numerical scheme and an optimal mesh. In many computational physics contexts, particularly in mesh-based simulations like computational fluid dynamics (CFD), the mesh serves as the foundation for these methods. Consequently, generating appropriate meshes is essential for achieving accurate solutions.

Numerous mesh generators have been developed to facilitate this process. However, the primary objective of this study is to produce hexahedral meshes. Tetrahedral meshes, though easier to generate, often result in inferior computational accuracy. Therefore, converting existing meshes into hexahedral structures is a vital step for enhancing performance and precision.

This work focuses on the automatic conversion of tetrahedral meshes into hexahedral ones. Our approach is termed "tets-to-hex" to reflect this function. The core of our strategy involves a sweeping algorithm that utilizes the connectivity information of the original tetrahedral mesh. This method has proven highly effective in converting large-scale and complex meshes.

Our primary algorithmic contribution lies in its ability to generate high-quality hexahedral meshes while maintaining strong computational efficiency. This capability is demonstrated through several applications: (1) converting large-scale and complex tetrahedral meshes; (2) converting large-scale triangular meshes; and (3) creating hexahedral meshes for the planets in the Universe.

Relation extraction (RE) focuses on identifying the relationship between a subject and an object within a sentence, serving as a critical task for knowledge base construction and semantic knowledge acquisition. While many state-of-the-art RE models utilize external knowledge to enhance performance, the knowledge they provide is often static and unchanging. In reality, knowledge graph links are inherently dynamic, as new facts are continuously discovered and new subjects or objects emerge. This dynamic nature of knowledge graph facts can significantly improve RE tasks by offering a vast amount of implicit information. To address this, we propose a knowledge graph link prediction mechanism to generate dynamic knowledge for RE. This approach involves two main steps: first, mapping words in sentences to entities in the knowledge graph to enrich contextual information; and second, leveraging the dynamic knowledge graph link prediction mechanism to infer dynamic facts for sentence-relevant entities, thereby enriching contextual knowledge. This study introduces a novel analytical propagation delay model tailored for deep submicron CMOS inverters. Utilizing Matlab's Curve Fitting Toolbox, the model is developed to depend on inverter supply voltage, input step voltage, and transistor width ratios. After parameter fitting, the model demonstrates exceptional accuracy, with all data points falling within a 2% error margin. Furthermore, the model's validity across different technology nodes is confirmed by successfully characterizing inverters from both 65nm and 45nm CMOS processes. Finally, the paper demonstrates how this compact model can be employed to predict the propagation delay of a ring oscillator.

**Keywords:** CMOS, Propagation Delay, Ring Oscillator, Curve Fitting Toolbox, Transistor Width Ratio.

In reinforcement learning, we often assume that rewards and transitions behave smoothly, meaning similar states yield similar rewards and next states. However, this approach fails when the state space lacks an intrinsic metric. This paper introduces a novel, metric-independent coarse-grained smoothness concept, which we demonstrate is both sufficient and necessary for deriving policies with provable guarantees. Our findings enable the application of this concept to topological spaces, provided they are embeddable into Euclidean space. We illustrate our theory with a policy optimization policy, showing that its performance can be guaranteed under the proposed framework. Furthermore, we extend this concept to Reinforcement Learning, decoupling it from gradient-based methods, and present an empirical policy supported by experimental evidence. Ultimately, this work offers a fresh perspective on smoothness in policy search, emphasizing its utility in topological and metric spaces. Additionally, we explore how this concept applies to other existing reinforcement learning algorithms. Empirical results confirm that algorithms grounded in coarse-grained smoothness outperform those that are not. Overall, this paper presents a new perspective on smoothness in policy search, highlighting its relevance across various mathematical settings.

The animacy category, which unites all objects regardless of their physical properties, is a fundamental concept in human ventral temporal cortex. While prior research has primarily relied on object-based psychophysics and functional MRI to investigate its organization, this study employed an image-by-image fMRI approach to directly map its structure. We utilized the seven-fieldria dataset, a large-scale visual object database containing 7,000 images across 1,000 categories, to present stimuli in a rapid event-related design. By applying representational similarity analysis, we examined the similarity structure of neural representations within the ventral temporal cortex. Our findings indicate that the animacy organization is highly graded rather than sharply segmented, contradicting earlier conclusions derived from region-of-interest analyses. Furthermore, the strength of this graded structure varies across the ventral temporal cortex, suggesting that the anatomical extent of this unique organization is more complex than previously believed. These results offer the first direct evidence for the fine-grained organization of the animacy category in this brain region. Collectively, our data support the hypothesis that the ventral temporal cortex contains a continuum of visual object representations, where the animacy category occupies a broader area than other distinct categories. Finally, we demonstrate that the organizational principles of the animacy category can be accurately modeled using deep neural networks trained on natural images. Our image-by-image methodology provides a means to probe neural selectivity for specific visual features, revealing that early regions encode low-level features like color and orientation, whereas more posterior regions represent higher-level features such as face-like or animal-like characteristics. This reveals a systematic, bottom-up organization of the animacy category within the ventral temporal cortex. Overall, our findings suggest that the unique organization of the animacy category is more prevalent and widespread than previously thought, and that ventral temporal cortex is not as homogeneously organized as earlier region-of-interest studies had indicated. These insights provide a foundation for future research aimed at elucidating the anatomical organization of visual object representations in the ventral temporal cortex. To facilitate further investigation, we have made the ventral temporal cortex fMRI data and our analysis code publicly available. This study introduces a structure-preserving filter designed for finite element simulations involving hyperelastic materials. The filter is formulated as a constrained convex optimization problem, with a corresponding efficient algorithm that leverages the problem's specific properties. The proposed method is robust and reliable, capable of eliminating noise and outliers while maintaining the original geometry. Additionally, the paper provides numerical results across various 1D and 2D simulation scenarios to demonstrate the filter's effectiveness. These examples illustrate how the filter can identify and remove outliers in both mesh size and element quality metrics, serving as a proof-of-concept for its application in adaptive mesh generation. Furthermore, several numerical cases demonstrate successful noise removal in simulated noisy data. All computations were performed using an open-source framework for hyperelasticity, and the source code is available at https://github.com/SebastianKluge/SPF. The filtering process is also implemented as a post-processing step within the simulation workflow to facilitate automated error detection and correction. Finally, the paper concludes by discussing potential future extensions of this approach. Notably, the structure-preserving filter is not restricted to hyperelasticity; it can be applied to any simulation where outliers or noise in mesh size or element quality must be addressed. The filtering process is expected to enhance the reliability of finite element computations, thereby improving the accuracy of the resulting solutions. This solution is accessible as a standalone structure-preserving filter, serving as a proof-of-concept for noise and outlier removal in finite element simulations. Furthermore, the work serves as a foundation for future research into adaptive mesh generation, as well as the detection and removal of mesh noise and outliers. Additionally, the framework is poised to enable feature extraction from noisy data, a capability currently under development. The proposed structure-preserving filter is expected to improve the quality of extracted features. All source code for the filter is available as a standalone package, decoupled from the specific framework used in this work. This allows researchers to apply the filter to their own simulation data. The required source code can be found at https://github.com/SebastianKluge/SPF. Users can access the filter either by running the simulation and filtering as a post-processing step or by downloading and implementing the standalone structure-preserving filter package. Furthermore, the feature extraction aspect is also treated as a standalone project, serving as a proof-of-concept for noise removal in simulations. This study introduces a method for reliably re-acting to partners' actions within multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) contexts. We propose Transfer Empowerment (TE), a social intrinsic motivation technique that identifies the most advantageous imitation policy for a given action by leveraging the agent's empirical data. By empirically comparing imitation policies, TE determines the set of actions that an agent can successfully replicate using its current knowledge. The goal is to encourage agents to reliably respond to their partners' moves, thereby enhancing coordination and joint performance. Our approach is evaluated in two MARL scenarios: a cooperative card game and a turn-based multi-agent pursuit-evasion task. The results demonstrate that TE effectively improves coordination, leading to superior performance when agents reliably react to their partners' actions. Furthermore, TE exhibits robustness in handling small to moderate variations in the training distribution, such as those caused by different Q-learning initializations or varying numbers of training steps. This indicates that TE can reliably improve coordination even when training data is limited. Additionally, TE achieves these performance gains without requiring any modifications to the existing MARL algorithm. We introduce MatSim, a fully unsupervised framework designed for material recognition. Given a single query image, MatSim identifies the material by matching it against a database of synthesized images representing various materials across diverse environmental conditions. Our approach leverages recent advances in contrastive self-supervised learning to train a simulator that generates images consistent with physical laws, thereby enabling a strong material descriptor for effective recognition. We validate our method using over 10,000 real-world images spanning more than 10,000 unique materials, demonstrating its ability to achieve near-perfect accuracy in a zero-shot setting. Furthermore, we demonstrate generalization capabilities beyond the training distribution, successfully recognizing materials in unseen images and real-world scenarios. Our code and datasets are publicly accessible at https://mat-sim.github.io. This work represents a significant advancement toward fully data-driven material simulation, achievable without the need for synthetic or annotated data. Additionally, we show that our material descriptors can enhance downstream tasks such as material segmentation and classification within a semi-supervised context. Finally, we illustrate that MatSim-generated descriptors facilitate accurate material recovery from low-quality images, like those captured by drone cameras. We begin by revisiting the definition of strict Lie 2-algebras, which are precisely equivalent to Lie categories, and rederive several established characterizations using categorical language. Subsequently, we examine the need to extend the concept of "strict" Lie 2-algebras to the weak variant, explicitly detailing weak Lie 2-algebras through axiomatic and categorical perspectives. After reviewing key properties of these weak structures, we conclude by briefly outlining the correspondence between Lie 2-algebras and specific types of Courant algebroids.

Keywords: Lie 2-algebra; Lie category; Lie groupoid; Lie algebroid; Courant algebroid.

We introduce a new approach for local image feature matching that bypasses the traditional sequential steps of detection, description, and matching. Instead, our method first establishes coarse, pixel-wise dense correspondences and subsequently refines them at a fine level. This is accomplished through a two-stage LoFTR model. In the first stage, a transformer-based cross-matching module generates dense features by leveraging low-resolution image patches to produce loose correspondences. The second stage operates in a multi-scale framework to refine these loose matches into precise matches within a transformer-based local feature module. We demonstrate that our method achieves state-of-the-art results across various datasets, including ORB-SEMAD, Pascal-LinEMD, and PolyU-EMD, for both indoor and outdoor scenes. Additionally, we have released an open-source implementation of LoFTR. Our method also facilitates feature matching for polarimetric synthetic aperture radar (SAR) imagery. We show that LoFTR can effectively match polarimetric SAR images by processing the four polarization channels as inputs to a multi-channel convolutional neural network. Experimental results confirm that LoFTR significantly outperforms existing techniques in matching polarimetric SAR images. Furthermore, we have released an open-source implementation of LoFTR for multi-channel SAR imagery. These advancements aim to facilitate key applications in optical and SAR image-based Inertial Navigation Systems. The source code is available at https://github.com/DepthAI/LoFTR. This study examines the bias inherent in the MDI/IPS algorithm, which generates the solar vector magnetic field dataset. The algorithm relies on inferences that are explicitly modeled but embedded in the methodology, potentially skewing results if specific conditions are not met. Consequently, magnetic field measurements may be systematically distorted if these model assumptions are omitted. We identify the specific characteristics of observations associated with these inferences and develop a method to identify and mitigate such biases. Our analysis reveals that both horizontal and line-of-sight magnetic field measurements are influenced by these biased inferences. We demonstrate that biases in horizontal fields arise from the IPS algorithm's inability to account for the finite size of MDI's full-disk images, whereas biases in line-of-sight fields stem from the vector field inferring algorithm's failure to handle limited angular resolution. We show that these biases can be corrected by substituting the original inferring models with modified versions that account for the finite size and limited angular resolution of MDI images. Finally, we discuss the impact of these biases on inferring measurements linked to solar features, including sunspots, active regions, and solar flares. Our findings indicate that uncorrected inferring models tend to overestimate magnetic field strengths in sunspots, active regions, and flares, while the proposed modified models provide more accurate measurements. This underscores the necessity of correcting for these inferring models to avoid underestimating magnetic field strengths in critical solar features. Furthermore, we demonstrate that these inferring models are accessible via the SolarSoft library, enabling users to apply these corrections. We conclude that the MDI/IPS inferring models are a significant source of bias in vector solar magnetic field datasets, and that this bias can be effectively mitigated by utilizing the provided modified inferring models. We propose that this correction should be adopted as a standard practice for all researchers utilizing MDI/IPS inferring magnetic field data. Our findings also hold relevance for future solar missions, such as the Solar Dynamics Observatory and the Solar Orbiter, which will produce vector magnetic field datasets. We recommend that researchers utilize the MDI/IPS inferring models provided in the SolarSoft library to correct for these biases in their respective datasets. By implementing these corrections, future missions will be able to produce more accurate and reliable solar vector magnetic field measurements. This will ultimately enhance our understanding of the Sun and its influence on the heliosphere. This study introduces a demand-side management (DSM) framework designed to foster cooperation among energy consumers. The system utilizes consumption scheduling, where the total energy consumed over a billing period by each group of consumers is predetermined. To further encourage collaboration, the framework implements instantaneous load billing, requiring users within the same schedule to share real-time electricity costs. To analyze these interactions, two aggregative games are developed: the Non-Strategic Interacting DSM Game (NSID) and the Strategic Interacting DSM Game (SID). In both games, consumers aim to minimize the sum of their instantaneous billing expenses and scheduling disutility. For the NSID game, we demonstrate the existence of at least one Nash equilibrium and propose two optimization techniques to efficiently calculate the equilibrium strategy profile. Simulation results confirm that the proposed methods outperform existing approaches in DSM implementations. Furthermore, we establish that the pure and proper potential properties hold for the SID game, guaranteeing the existence of a pure Nash equilibrium. Finally, numerical simulations are presented to illustrate how consumption scheduling can significantly lower strategic consumers' costs. Additionally, we investigate the impact of DSM on the price of anarchy in the proposed games. Our findings indicate that the price of anarchy in the SID game is substantially lower than that in the NSID game, suggesting that DSM is particularly beneficial for strategic consumers. This insight is supported by numerical results showing that strategic consumers achieve greater cost reductions under DSM compared to the NSID scenario. Ultimately, the proposed DSM scheme offers consumers cost savings ranging from 1% to 100% relative to the NSID case. These results underscore the critical role of DSM in achieving cost efficiency within interactive demand-side management. Furthermore, we establish that, assuming weak convergence and the absence of a mass point at $1$ for the spectral measure, the convergence rates in the ergodic theorem are essentially dictated by the decay rates of the spectral measure's Fourier transform. This indicates that the findings do not rely on any specific spectral type or orthogonality properties of the orbit. Additionally, these findings complement and extend the conclusions of Oelschläger and Roeder. Finally, we illustrate an explicit instance of irrational rotation on the circle where the optimal convergence rate for von Neumann's Ergodic Theorem is linked to Diophantine approximation. Moreover, we introduce a novel example of an irrational number on the circle for which the optimal convergence rate of von Neumann's Ergodic Theorem is precisely identified. Both of these specific results are derived using the recent $U$-process approach to ergodic averages. Finally, we explore the implications of these results for Birkhoff's Ergodic Theorem. Notably, the convergence rates in this context are governed by the fine-scale behavior of the spectral measure near $1$, which is characterized by local scaling dimensions. This represents a distinct and contrasting phenomenon compared to von Neumann's Ergodic Theorem. **Context.** The search for extremely metal-poor stars serves as a primary method for investigating the chemical evolution of the early Universe. However, accurately determining stellar metallicity is challenging because the three traditional indices—Fe/H, [α/Fe], and [Mg/Fe]—are difficult to measure in such rare stellar objects. **Aims.** This study aims to demonstrate that the Gaia Blue Photometer/Red Photometer (BP/RP) spectra can effectively identify metal-poor stars and determine their specific types. **Methods.** We developed a machine learning algorithm utilizing decision trees to classify stars based on BP/RP spectra. This algorithm was trained on a synthetic dataset of 100,000 stars, with spectral models generated via SMC and BACCHUS. Additionally, we created a method to classify stars according to their [Fe/H] values. **Results.** Our tests indicate that the proposed methods can identify metal-poor stars with [Fe/H] < -2.0 with approximately 90% accuracy. Furthermore, the classification of these stars by [Fe/H] < -2.0 yields an accuracy of about 80%. The distribution of the five decision tree features used to classify metal-poor stars reveals that BP/RP spectral energy distributions (SEDs) are the most critical factor in this classification. **Conclusions.** We demonstrate that Gaia BP/RP spectra are highly effective for identifying metal-poor stars, offering a valuable tool for the upcoming release of Gaia data. This approach will facilitate the creation of a catalogue of metal-poor stars, aiding astronomers in their search for these objects. Additionally, we show that the SEDs of metal-poor stars differ significantly from those of solar-metallicity stars, which can be utilized to distinguish between stellar types. This paper is based on the master's thesis of the first author.

Climate change is causing an increase in global wildfires, which pose significant threats to human life, property, and the environment. While numerous tools exist for predicting and monitoring these fires, there remains a lack of methods to assess fire seasons on a global scale. This study introduces a novel approach to define and measure global fire season severity using the Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer (MODIS) Active Fire Density (AFD) metric. We demonstrate that this definition aligns with human perceptions of varying fire seasons, exhibits distinct spatial and temporal characteristics, and maintains a strong linear relationship with AFD. Furthermore, we show that historical AFD data from the preceding 16 days can effectively forecast a year's entire active fire density pattern. Finally, we utilize these findings to evaluate and compare the impacts of different years' fire seasons on global forest cover. These findings offer valuable insights for both the monitoring and forecasting of global fire seasons. The datasets utilized in this study are accessible at https://github.com/ashwinbhat/Global-Fire-Season-Severity. The accompanying code is available at https://github.com/ashwinbhat/Global-Fire-Season-Severity. Specifically, the forecasting results suggest the potential for developing early warning systems for fire seasons. Finally, the study's results can inform the creation of new, more effective indices for studying global fire seasons. We investigate the correlations among corpus-derived metrics for the morphological complexity of natural languages. To achieve this, we calculate ten distinct complexity measures across a comprehensive typology consisting of 57 highly diverse languages, ranging from monomorphemic to agglutinative. These measures are derived from direct morphological analyses alongside morphosyntactic and morphological inventory data. Through correlational analyses, we establish a mapping between various information-theoretic and statistical approaches, identifying strong associations between the complexity of specific linguistic levels and Compressed Complexity, a recently proposed measure. Furthermore, cross-validation analyses demonstrate that these information-theoretic and statistical methods effectively predict morphological complexity levels, accounting for 75% to 90% of the variance observed in cross-linguistic complexity measures. Finally, we examine the implications of these findings for modeling complexity in natural language systems. Finally, our code and datasets are accessible at https://github.com/alexandervolk/Corpora-based-measures-of-Morphological-Complexity. Our analysis reveals that the probability distribution of small-scale lenses deviates from the predictions of the singular $\Lambda$CDM model. Specifically, we observe a significant suppression of lensing signals at angular scales smaller than $\theta \sim 10^{\prime\prime}$. This suppression aligns with the absence of dark matter subhalos expected from $\Lambda$CDM simulations, suggesting a maximum subhalo mass of $M_{\rm max} \lesssim 10^7 M_\odot$ within clusters. This limit is consistent with constraints derived from strong lensing observations of individual clusters and statistical studies of the galaxy cluster population.
