This study addresses the model reduction of a continuous-time stochastic process under noisy, partial observations. We introduce a straightforward procedure that adapts the discrete-time model reduction framework established by Lynch et al. (2019) and Ranganathan et al. (2021) for this specific context. The method involves two main steps: first, estimating the generator matrix of the high-dimensional discrete-time model using the Sum-of-Squares technique proposed by Li et al. (2021); second, applying the singular value decomposition method by Li et al. (2020) to reduce this estimated discrete-time model. We demonstrate that this reduction strategy is valid even when data is collected via a continuous-time partial observation process, and we illustrate its application using a hidden Markov model. Furthermore, we introduce a novel model selection criterion that integrates the BIC with the approximation error from singular value reduction, showing that this criterion can be applied to both discrete- and continuous-time settings. Finally, we validate the proposed methods through both synthetic and real-world applications. The results indicate that, although the discrete-time model is inherently misspecified due to the continuous-time data collection mechanism, the proposed reduction scheme successfully recovers the true underlying low-dimensional structure. Additionally, our numerical findings demonstrate that partial observations do not significantly hinder model reduction performance. Finally, we discuss the model selection outcomes relative to existing approaches in both continuous- and discrete-time contexts. The entire methodology is implemented in the R package `ctmrs`, which can be accessed at https://github.com/ctmrs/ctmrs. This package includes examples of both synthetic and real-world applications. This study introduces a real-time spatio-temporal event detection framework designed for social media streams, specifically targeting event mining in the tourism sector. The method relies on a two-stage local clustering procedure that first segments social media streams by geographic location and then assigns temporal tags using a sliding time window. A novel event detection technique is subsequently proposed, which integrates both local and temporal clusters while filtering out noisy clusters to isolate the most significant events. The Foursquare dataset was utilized to benchmark the proposed approach against two baseline methods. Furthermore, the efficacy of the system is demonstrated through the analysis of Twitter data collected from Venice, Italy. Results indicate that the proposed method outperforms the baseline approaches in terms of accuracy, computational efficiency, and event localization. Additionally, the method successfully identifies events occurring within a specific temporal tag using the defined time window, and the outcomes are presented in both textual and map-based formats. Finally, the approach is validated in a real-world scenario by analyzing Twitter data from Venice. In this scenario, a web application was developed to visualize events on a map, allowing users to browse and search for events within their desired locations. The results align with existing literature and successfully capture real-world events in Venice. To the best of our knowledge, no prior research has applied social media event mining to support tourism activities. Consequently, the proposed method is expected to assist tourists in discovering popular tourist spots and trending events before and during their visits. The source code is accessible at: https://github.com/abdullahaydin/twitter-event-mining. Keywords: Event Detection, Tourism, Social Media, Clustering, Real-time Event Mining.

This study establishes optimal regularity results for solutions to the elliptic equation div(A(x,Du)) = d\mu_1 + Mdu_2, where d\mu_1 and Mdu_2 are nonnegative distributional measures. Here, u belongs to W^{1,1}_{loc}, A is a Carath\'eodory function satisfying strict ellipticity and growth conditions up to a specific exponent \gamma, M is a nonnegative distribution, and du_2 denotes a signed Radon measure. The analysis covers two scenarios: an initial trace problem within a bounded domain \Omega \subset \mathbb{R}^n, where u vanishes on \partial \Omega, and a free boundary problem in \mathbb{R}^n. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the regularity of u is heavily influenced by the distributional structure of \mu_1, Mdu_2, the specific problem type, and the strict ellipticity condition on the matrix A. These findings generalize and extend numerous existing regularity theorems. Additionally, we provide counterexamples to illustrate the optimality of our conditions and the necessity of strict ellipticity. Finally, we explore applications of these results to regularity issues in free boundary problems. Notably, the conclusions of this paper are applicable to a broad spectrum of problems featuring degenerate or singular growth conditions. Many of these results represent novel contributions. Key concepts include: nonnegative distributional measures, degenerate elliptic equations, initial trace problems, and free boundary problems. High-performance permanent magnets are essential for numerous industrial applications, including electric motors and generators. Yttrium-cobalt-boron magnets possess the chemical formula $Y_xCo_yBo_z$ and are currently utilized in high-temperature environments. Although these materials are already established, their performance can be enhanced through an optimized composition. This study employs a multi-objective evolutionary algorithm to search for such an optimal composition. The method is grounded in the concept of the convex hull of a property space, which is discretized into a grid. The algorithm seeks a point within this grid that maximizes cobalt content while ensuring proximity to the convex hull. We applied this approach to identify high-cobalt compounds within the Y-Co-B system, yielding several promising candidates. Experimental studies on these proposed materials could lead to the development of high-performance magnets. The methodology is both general and versatile, capable of addressing diverse property optimization challenges. Furthermore, the algorithm is designed to be hardware-accelerated, such as on GPUs, to significantly enhance computational speed. A Python implementation of this algorithm is publicly accessible. The current version of the code is capable of optimizing Y-coordination number, total magnetic moment, and the ratio of magnetic to non-magnetic atoms. Future enhancements will incorporate additional objectives, including the Curie temperature, anisotropy, and mechanical properties. The implementation is available at https://github.com/alecstevens/NEO. Additional information can be found in our supplementary material. Our codebase will be expanded to enable the optimization of more objectives in future updates. Real-time bidding (RTB) has emerged as a dominant approach for programmatic display advertising, enabling advertisers to purchase impressions on a "pay-per-performance" basis. This study addresses the challenge of maximizing return on ad spend (ROAS) under budget constraints within the RTB environment. We introduce a new adaptive bidding framework that dynamically adjusts bids to adhere to budget limits while accounting for advertiser risk preferences. This solution comprises two core components: (1) a budget-aware bid allocation mechanism that sets target prices for each impression, and (2) a risk-aware risk adjustment factor (RAF) calculation method that determines the final bid based on the target price, advertiser risk attitude, and portfolio-level risk aversion. Extensive simulations using real-world data demonstrate that our proposed solution outperforms state-of-the-art methods. Furthermore, we provide theoretical proofs confirming the convergence of the algorithm and the optimality of the resulting solution. Empirical results from RTB simulations confirm that our approach significantly improves ROAS compared to existing alternatives. Additionally, we validate our theoretical findings through a large-scale simulation involving 100 advertisers, where our solution achieves a 10% increase in ROAS over current state-of-the-art methods. Finally, we collaborate with a leading display advertising technology provider to deploy this solution in live bidding systems, and we present empirical evidence from these real-world applications. The collaboration confirms that our solution effectively adapts to varying levels of risk aversion across different advertisers. Overall, this solution offers a flexible and effective solution for RTB budget management, making it a valuable tool for advertisers seeking to optimize their advertising investments. By adhering to budget constraints and incorporating risk preferences, our approach enables advertisers to make more informed bidding decisions, ultimately enhancing their advertising outcomes. This research contributes to the broader field of display advertising by advancing adaptive bidding techniques and promoting efficient resource allocation. Ultimately, our solution represents a significant step forward in optimizing advertising investments, ensuring that budgets are utilized effectively while considering risk considerations. By doing so, it helps advertisers achieve their performance goals and maximize the impact of their advertising efforts. Our results have potential applications in quantum error correction and the certification of quantum devices. The research specifically examines the secure bound analysis for the six-state protocol, evaluating its performance under both phase and Pauli depolarizing channels. Furthermore, the study highlights the security benefits of combining the six-state protocol with decoy states. The findings are supported by simulations that illustrate the key rate as a function of the seed's min-entropy. The methods presented in this paper are applicable to all quantum key distribution systems. Additionally, the work confirms that the intuitive argument regarding the secure bound analysis in privacy amplification, which relies on the conditional entropy theorem, does not hold in general. Finally, the paper proposes an alternative approach to address this issue and discusses its advantages and limitations. This study examines the sample distribution $D_n$ generated by a diffusion on the unit interval, governed by the forward Feller-KPZ equation with coalescing particles drawn from the neutral Chinese restaurant process. We analyze the expected value $E[D_n]$ and variance $\mathrm{Var}[D_n]$ for small and large $n$. Our findings demonstrate that while $E[D_n]$ converges exponentially to 1 as $n \to \infty$, $\mathrm{Var}[D_n]$ approaches 0 polynomially. These results are contrasted with those of the standard uniform sampling case. Additionally, we extend the analysis to the general Bessel process, which encompasses the radial Bessel and Feller processes, and compare these results with the standard uniform sampling scenario. Finally, we explore the connection between our findings and the Baik-Sinnet-Wang conjecture. A supplementary video illustrating the Bessel diffusion and the Chinese restaurant process is available at https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=4222222222. The design of this optimized delay relies on the observation that the delay typically employed in CPM systems is excessively long because the effective memory span is dictated by the duration of the longest significant channel impulse response. By leveraging this insight, we derive an optimized delay that is significantly shorter than the traditional approach. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this proposed delay achieves near-optimal detection performance while offering substantial complexity reductions. Numerical results confirm that, compared to conventional delay structures, the proposed approach yields significant complexity savings accompanied by a negligible degradation in bit error rate performance. Additionally, the extended delay metric can be computed offline, enabling its application to a wide variety of CPM signals. Finally, we illustrate that the proposed delay can also enhance the detection performance of delay-structured non-coherent differential detection. Consequently, this developed metric serves as a versatile tool for delay optimization across diverse CPM scenarios. We provide a theoretical analysis of our framework and validate it empirically across both grid worlds and continuous control tasks. The experimental results demonstrate that our approach achieves an order-of-magnitude reduction in human effort compared to state-of-the-art methods. Furthermore, our visual policy representation proves effective in capturing the intended behaviors specified by the human feedback. This study introduces a novel parameterization tailored for block maxima datasets, specifically designed for Bayesian inference within the extreme value framework. We model the block maxima using the generalized Pareto distribution with a known scale parameter. By reparameterizing the standard likelihood in terms of a threshold and an expected number of exceedances, we demonstrate that the resulting profile likelihood exhibits a simple interpretable form. This new parameterization is particularly effective for constructing highly efficient importance samplers. Furthermore, we extend this approach to a non-homogeneous Poisson process model of exceedances, which offers a more flexible fit for block maxima data. We develop conjugate priors and evaluate their performance through a case study involving a 100-year period of temperature records from the United Kingdom. Additionally, we address Bayesian model selection for selecting between parametric alternatives, employing both fractional Bayes factors and reversible jump Markov chain Monte Carlo methods for inference. Model selection criteria are also investigated, including versions of the Bayes factor, Deviance Information Criterion, and extended Bayes factor. Finally, we address the issue of label switching inherent in the Poisson process parameterization and its implications for Bayesian inference. Our Poisson process-based models are benchmarked against existing parametric approaches, demonstrating that the Poisson process models provide both efficient fits and accurate return level estimates. Furthermore, the Poisson process parameterization yields less noisy estimates for the threshold, thereby enhancing return level predictions. Finally, we show that fractional Bayes factors effectively distinguish between competing parametric models, while reversible jump Markov chain Monte Carlo successfully explores the label switching problem. We analyze first exit times within a regime where the observation window for detecting an exit event is small relative to the interval length, specifically considering $N$-dependent forces. Our findings indicate that when the interaction potential approximates a hard-core condition, entropic forces drive the particle toward the exit. Conversely, when the potential is attractive, the force pulls the particle away from the exit. We further demonstrate that at small lengths, first exit times follow a Poisson-like distribution. Additionally, we present results for various $N$ and $L$ values across different system sizes and interaction potentials. Finally, we derive exact analytical results for a free particle and establish the corresponding Poisson distribution for an interacting particle under a hard-core potential. Finally, we present approximate solutions for continuous models featuring soft interactions. Quantum mechanics is widely recognized as a distinctively new theory that fundamentally diverges from classical mechanics, primarily because of the wave-like characteristics of quantum states and the consequential inability to apply Bayes' rule in the same manner as in classical mechanics. This paper demonstrates that a novel formulation of quantum Bayes' rule can be derived, which is functionally equivalent to Bayes' rule when applied to the probability operators defining quantum states. Leveraging this formula, we illustrate that the consistency of measurement inferences in quantum mechanics aligns precisely with that of classical mechanics, provided one acknowledges that quantum states evolve via the von Neumann equation rather than the Schrödinger equation during measurements. Furthermore, the formula confirms that the collapse postulate in quantum mechanics is unnecessary for making measurement inferences. Consequently, this suggests that the measurement problem in quantum mechanics is not inherently problematic, as long as measurement inferences are understood as the consistency between the likelihood operator and the state operator. Finally, we contend that the primary obstacle in interpreting quantum mechanics lies in the lack of consensus regarding the definition of the operator representing a quantum state. To address this, we propose that the density operator should serve as the fundamental representation of a quantum state, as it can be defined without the ambiguity that plagues state vector representations. The density operator formulation successfully resolves the inconsistency problem inherent in combining the Copenhagen interpretation with the von Neumann measurement scheme. Additionally, we demonstrate that the density operator representation is compatible with both the decoherence program and the many-worlds interpretation, both of which are widely regarded as solutions to the measurement problem. Therefore, the density operator representation should be considered the standard framework for quantum mechanics. The paper concludes by outlining several applications of this representation. Notably, the density operator representation offers a solution to the measurement problem by clarifying the operational distinction between knowledge and reality. Specifically, the state operator represents reality, whereas the knowledge operator reflects the observer's knowledge of reality. This distinction is essential for formulating a version of the uncertainty principle that avoids the conflict between the uncertainty principle and the consistency of measurement inferences. The resulting knowledge-state interpretation of quantum mechanics offers a viable alternative to the state-vector representation, which has been the primary source of contention in the ongoing debate over the interpretation of quantum mechanics. The knowledge-state interpretation posits that the wave function represents an observer's knowledge of reality, whereas the state-vector interpretation asserts that the wave function represents reality itself. This study reports initial findings regarding finite volume corrections to the equation of state, trace anomaly, and speed of sound for two specific models: a free, massless scalar theory and quenched QCD utilizing periodic boundary conditions. Additionally, we provide preliminary results for quenched QCD under Dirichlet boundary conditions. Our analysis will focus on exploring the convergence characteristics of these equations of state as system volume increases, specifically examining the dependence on system shape and boundary conditions. These insights are crucial for understanding the thermodynamics of the Quark-Gluon Plasma generated in heavy-ion collisions, where the fireball volume remains small and boundary effects are significant. Furthermore, we outline potential extensions to QCD with dynamical fermions and investigate the feasibility of extracting the trace anomaly from QCD correlation functions on a lattice. This approach would utilize experimental data from high-energy heavy-ion collisions, where increasingly larger volumes are accessible as collision energies rise. Such an extension represents a necessary step toward fully developed lattice QCD applications within heavy-ion physics. Finally, I will present early results from these extended calculations. The early universe is primarily studied through its spectral imprints on intergalactic matter, such as the Lyman-$\alpha$ emission line from neutral hydrogen. Although these features are typically observed in the optical range via redshifts of $z \sim 2-3$, the corresponding rest-frame wavelengths lie in the Lyman ultraviolet. We propose a method to filter out Lyman ultraviolet photons from sky background light, allowing for the photometric detection of Lyman-$\alpha$ features in the rest frame. This approach involves building a Lyman ultraviolet filter and conducting sky background observations to characterize it. To achieve this, the filter must be constructed using materials that transmit Lyman ultraviolet light while effectively absorbing near-Lyman $\alpha$ and Lyman-$\beta$ lines. We have developed a filter prototype composed of a thin aluminum film and a thick magnesium fluoride film. This prototype demonstrated transmission rates of 99.9% at 1216 Å and 99.8% at 1026 Å. Furthermore, the filter's ultraviolet photon filtering performance was evaluated by observing the night sky spectrum. The results indicate that this Lyman ultraviolet filter is effective at removing Lyman ultraviolet photons from the sky background. Consequently, the combination of sky background observations and the use of Lyman ultraviolet filters can significantly improve the efficiency of detecting Lyman-$\alpha$ features in the Lyman limit region of the spectrum. This method is particularly valuable for studying intergalactic matter such as the neutral hydrogen fraction, Lyman-$\alpha$ forest, and deuterium abundance. Additionally, this approach is applicable to future space telescopes like the Chinese Space Station Telescope (SST) and the European Space Agency's (ESA) Ultraviolet Explorer (UVEX). These instruments are equipped with Lyman ultraviolet filters and will be capable of performing high-precision spectroscopy on intergalactic matter. Specifically, UVEX is expected to achieve a spectral resolution of $R \sim 10,000$ at 1216 Å, representing a 10-fold improvement over current capabilities. This enhanced resolution will enable the detection of intergalactic features that are currently unobservable. Ultimately, this will facilitate a deeper understanding of the evolution of the first galaxies and the formation of the first stars. Keywords: intergalactic medium; cosmology; early universe; Lyman-$\alpha$ emission line; ultraviolet filters; space telescopes.

This paper introduces a distributed algorithm designed to address two key challenges in networked linear dynamical systems exhibiting graph symmetry: distributed optimal control and distributed model reduction. These problems are addressed within a unified framework utilizing graph filters. The proposed distributed optimal control strategy achieves graph-symmetric matrices through the local integration of graph filters and star-symmetric functions. By exploiting the low-dimensional structure inherent in graph filters, graph-symmetric systems are simplified to a reduced dimension via the principal component corresponding to the smallest non-zero Laplacian eigenvalue. This model reduction approach relies exclusively on local computations, distributed graph filters, and distributed projections onto the principal subspace of the graph Laplacian. Numerical examples are provided to demonstrate the effectiveness of these methods. The study further extends to graph-asymmetric systems by incorporating local low-rank approximations, which rely on distributed singular vector computations. Finally, communication costs are analyzed, revealing that the distributed optimal control method incurs no additional cost over basic distributed coupling, while the model reduction approach requires only a single extra communication round per time step. These contributions significantly enhance scalability, efficiency, and privacy for distributed optimal control and model reduction in graph-symmetric systems. The communication efficiency of the proposed methods is also validated through applications to distributed Kalman filtering and distributed model predictive control. Simulation results indicate that the computational and communication overheads of the model reduction scheme scale linearly with the number of nodes, thereby improving scalability. The paper concludes by discussing potential extensions of these graph-filter-based distributed optimal control and model reduction techniques to graph-asymmetric systems. The core contributions of this work are: (i) a unified framework for solving distributed optimal control and model reduction problems using graph filters; (ii) a graph-filter-based distributed optimal control method utilizing star-symmetric functions, featuring the model reduction capability of graph filters; (iii) a model reduction technique based on local low-rank approximations derived from singular vector computations; and (iv) the extension of graph-filter-based distributed optimal control to graph-asymmetric systems. These contributions substantially improve scalability, efficiency, and privacy in distributed optimal control and model reduction for both symmetric and asymmetric networks. Image editing has become a ubiquitous skill, yet identifying specific edits or the individuals who performed them remains difficult. This is largely because modern digital cameras capture high-resolution images with sufficient detail to render every modification, including minor ones, detectable. In contrast, we propose that passive observation of active image creation offers a viable alternative for indexing edited content. We introduce the concept of active image indexing and demonstrate its utility through two key applications: detecting when an image has been altered and identifying the person responsible for that alteration. First, we develop an index based on image saliency maps to detect local edits. Second, we analyze pre- and post-edit differences using a graph-cut framework to estimate the underlying saliency map of the modification, leveraging this estimate alongside speaker characteristics to attribute the edit. Experimental results indicate that our indexing method outperforms state-of-the-art techniques for image editing attribution in a edit-vs-non-edit classification task and remains competitive in edit-vs-edit scenarios. Furthermore, our attribution technique surpasses existing methods for local image editing attribution and compares favorably against active image fingerprinting approaches. These findings highlight the potential of active image indexing for large-scale forensic analysis of user-generated content. This study explores a new approach to keyless authentication for independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) sources over additive white Gaussian noise (AWGN) channels. The proposed framework utilizes a deterministic, publicly accessible, error-resilient generator to produce a test sequence. Authentication is achieved by verifying if a target sequence falls within a predefined neighborhood of this test sequence. We determine the optimal neighborhood radius under a fixed false rejection rate to maximize acceptance probability for legitimate users. Furthermore, we connect this authentication framework to the statistical query model in database theory and offer a novel perspective on the well-known small subgraph testing problem. Finally, we assess the performance of our scheme using extensive simulations. Additionally, we link the statistical properties of Fourier coefficients for random phase sequences to the authentication results presented in this paper. Our findings indicate that the length of the test sequence required for a given error tolerance is significantly shorter than the sequence lengths typically required in existing literature for similar error rates. This study presents a flexible local projection method that extends Jordà's (2005) model to a non-parametric framework via Bayesian inference. The approach utilizes flexible splines to approximate the infinite series of coefficients for both dependent and independent variables. We introduce a penalty-based prior on the resulting coefficients to ensure convergence and induce sparsity, thereby capturing the empirical irrelevance of distant shocks. This prior effectively regularizes the estimation of both conditional means and variance-covariance matrices, thereby mitigating overfitting. Our empirical analysis investigates the "Great Moderation" shock responses of inflation and unemployment in the United States. The estimated impulse responses align with Jordà's (2005) findings while also revealing additional nuances. Furthermore, we introduce a new model comparison metric to facilitate the selection of the optimal specification when projecting infinite-dimensional functions. The results indicate that our proposed prior successfully identifies the empirical irrelevance of shocks beyond five periods, thereby enhancing model parsimony. Finally, we demonstrate that the uncertainty in these impulse responses is primarily driven by the irrelevance of remote shocks. Consequently, the primary challenge in estimating impulse responses via flexible local projections lies in balancing model complexity and the finite sample size. We conclude that the most effective strategy for inferring impulse responses in this framework is to select the specification that optimally balances these two factors. Our proposed scoring rule successfully accomplishes this optimization. Ultimately, the scoring rule proves to be a valuable tool for researchers aiming to improve the accuracy of impulse response estimates within the flexible local projection framework. Fine-Grained Named Entity Typing (FG-NET) involves classifying entity mentions into a vast array of types, often lacking clear semantic boundaries. To address this, existing research typically employs a hierarchical structure to organize these types, leveraging the inherent tree architecture of hyperbolic space to represent such hierarchies. This study proposes Fine-Grained Named Entity Tying through Refinement in Hyperbolic space (FGNET-RH), a method designed to capture both entity context and the hierarchical nature of the type system. The approach utilizes a hyperbolic neural network to learn embeddings for entities and their types, explicitly incorporating structural information from the type hierarchy. Furthermore, to manage the large number of types, we introduce a semi-supervised learning strategy that leverages type relationships to expand the training dataset. We validate our method using public datasets, and our results demonstrate that FGNET-RH outperforms existing state-of-the-art techniques. The source code is available at https://github.com/leeyang1991/FGNET-RH. Additionally, our implementation includes a pre-trained model that achieves state-of-the-art performance on the public FG-VOCaB dataset. The model is accessible here: https://huggingface.co/leeyang1991/fgnetrh. We hope this resource will be beneficial to the research community. In light of our findings, we recommend that future datasets adopt a hierarchical structure for entity types to better reflect their inherent relationships. We also intend to release a new dataset featuring a more granular type system in the near future. We welcome collaboration from researchers interested in advancing fine-grained named entity typing. Specifically, it is demonstrated that the second Hankel determinant for $\mathcal{U}$ is bounded by 1, whereas for the class of all univalent functions, the bound is 6. As the demand for cloud computing grows, so do the challenges associated with resource management. The primary objective in this domain is load balancing, which involves the efficient allocation of resources to meet user requests. This paper introduces Prepartition, a novel approach designed to distribute virtual machines (VMs) across a data center's compute nodes in a balanced manner. By utilizing a new data structure called the "Node Map," Prepartition enables rapid identification of nodes with sufficient resources. This mechanism allows for the efficient distribution of newly arriving VMs across all nodes and ensures that newly provisioned VMs remain in the same node throughout their execution. Furthermore, the approach incorporates a VM migration strategy to rebalance the system when nodes become unbalanced. Experimental results demonstrate that Prepartition outperforms other load balancing methods, achieving execution times that are 1.5 to 2 times faster. Additionally, the system maintains consistent memory and CPU usage across all nodes. Given its advantages, Prepartition is well-suited for cloud environments. Future research will explore extensions to the approach, such as implementing VM reservations based on specific VM types and nodes. To achieve this, a VM type map will be introduced to track node types and a node map will be established for each node to monitor resource availability. This will facilitate a VM type map to identify nodes with sufficient resources for new VMs. Furthermore, the current VM migration strategy will be replaced with a VM swap approach to enhance rebalancing efficiency. Finally, the Prepartition system will be integrated with the OpenStack cloud platform. To achieve this, the prepartition module will be embedded within the Nova controller, and the VM swap strategy will be implemented using the swapout and swapin features provided by Nova. These extensions are expected to result in improved execution times and memory usage. Additionally, the VM swap strategy will be evaluated against the live migration feature in OpenStack. Finally, the VM type map will be assessed against type-specific VM requirements, such as those for graphics-intensive applications. This will involve comparing the performance of specific VM types, including graphics cards, across different nodes. Finally, a VM affinity map will be introduced to track VM locations, enabling the system to balance VMs across all nodes. This will be tested to verify its effectiveness in achieving a balanced distribution. This paper introduces the Fixed Point Network, a new architecture designed to identify Nash equilibria in extensive-form games. We demonstrate that the behavior of a general multi-layer feedforward network can be linked to the Bayesian Nash equilibrium of a specific game, enabling the training of this model using only the concept of Bayesian incentives without relying on back-propagation. To enhance prediction accuracy, we also develop a novel, computationally efficient training algorithm. Our method is validated across several extensive-form games, and we show that it serves as a powerful tool for counterfactual reasoning, allowing for the effective detection of causal effects in real-world data. Furthermore, we apply the proposed model to the challenge of predicting criminal behavior. Our results indicate that the Fixed Point Network achieves performance comparable to state-of-the-art approaches while offering a substantial reduction in training time. Finally, we provide an open-source implementation of the model. Supplementary materials are available at https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/romanberezovskyi/extended-form-games-and-criminal-behavior-prediction. This paper presents an efficient method for monitoring linear-time invariant systems against stealthy attacks. We propose an online predictive monitoring approach that utilizes the future inputs and outputs of the controlled system to detect intrusions. The core concept involves comparing two distinct models of the system to identify attacks. Our focus is on scenarios where the system's input is an unknown, time-varying signal, which typically renders the control problem challenging due to an insufficient number of future measurements. To overcome this, we introduce a change of coordinates that transforms system measurements into both controllable and observable measurements. This technique is applicable to a broad range of systems, including those that are not both controllable and observable. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this method through numerical examples drawn from various engineering fields. Furthermore, we establish the method's efficiency by showing that the resulting optimization problem can be solved via a closed-form expression. Finally, we compare this approach with a recent method by Chen et al. (2020) to highlight its superior performance. The code required to replicate our findings is available at https://github.com/ahmedhassan123/EfficientPredictiveMonitoring. The method can be extended to systems with unknown constant disturbances. Our findings indicate that this approach is not only computationally efficient but also robust in detecting attacks even when disturbances are present. These results suggest that the method is highly general and can be adapted to various attack and disturbance scenarios. The extension to disturbed systems is detailed in our PhD thesis, available at https://github.com/ahmedhassan122/PhD_Thesis. Document summarization remains a difficult task, particularly for low-resource Indian languages characterized by their diversity and complexity. To address this, we introduce GAE-ISumm, an unsupervised model that leverages pre-trained multilingual models and adaptive graph-based scoring to generate summaries. GAE-ISumm demonstrates strong performance on the IndSummData dataset and establishes a new state-of-the-art within unsupervised document summarization. The concept of an S-ring of Krull type extends the theory of valuation rings of Krull type in commutative algebra. The developed theory finds applications in the study of covering groups and their factorizations. Furthermore, the new constraints on the masses and orbital separations of these companions are comparable to or tighter than those obtained from astrometric monitoring. The rapid expansion of the Internet of Things (IoT) has significantly increased security and privacy concerns within smart home environments. This paper introduces a low-cost SMART HOME MONITORING SYSTEM (SHMS) designed to enhance security and privacy for smart home users. To achieve this, the system employs private blockchain technology alongside a lightweight consensus mechanism known as Proof of Localization (PoLo). The primary objective of PoLo is to minimize the storage and computational burdens associated with blockchain operations in resource-constrained smart home devices. Our findings indicate that the proposed SHMS architecture is highly effective for smart home applications, offering superior efficiency in terms of storage and computational resources compared to other existing blockchain designs. Furthermore, the system demonstrates enhanced security and privacy, with the blockchain serving as an additional layer of protection. Finally, the system's scalability is demonstrated by its ability to add new devices without requiring modifications to existing network structures. This paper details the implementation of the PoLo consensus mechanism, the development of the SHMS prototype, and an evaluation of its performance regarding security, storage, and computational aspects. Additionally, the paper provides a comprehensive analysis of the system's advantages and limitations. The complete SHMS prototype code is available at: https://github.com/AbdulrahmanAlshammari/Smart-Home-Monitoring-System. This study introduces a deep learning-based quantization method for calculating likelihood values associated with Gray-coded modulations. The core concept involves training a neural network to approximate the original quantization function, enabling the network to output likelihood values for a given log-likelihood ratio vector. We also propose a neural network-assisted maximum a posteriori detector leveraging this quantization approach. By circumventing the expensive exponential operation required to convert probabilities into likelihoods via the Bayes rule, our method reduces the computational complexity of the detection process. Furthermore, we demonstrate that our design achieves near-optimal performance relative to existing state-of-the-art schemes. Although we focus on higher-order modulations in this paper, the proposed approach is also applicable to binary modulation. Our design is constructed using neural networks with ReLU activation functions, ensuring robustness and trainability. Extensive simulations confirm that our scheme delivers a significant computational complexity reduction while maintaining minimal loss in detection performance. Finally, we have designed our scheme for use with linear minimum mean square error equalization. The remainder of this paper is organized as follows: Section \ref{sec:system_model} outlines the system model, and Section \ref{sec:related_work} reviews related work. Section \ref{sec:proposed_scheme} details our proposed design, followed by numerical results in Section \ref{sec:results}. The paper concludes with Section \ref{sec:conclusion}. This study introduces novel parameterized algorithms for the classical problem of determining if an undirected graph admits an upward planar drawing within a specified partial order. The central challenge involves verifying whether there exists a partial order extending the given embedding such that the resulting directed graph is both planar and upward-oriented. The algorithm operates in $O(2^p \cdot p^2 \cdot n)$ time, where $n$ represents the number of vertices and $p$ denotes the count of fixed faces. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this upper bound is tight. We also present a parameterized algorithm with a running time of $O_p(n \log n)$ for the case where a single face is fixed. Additionally, we propose an $O_p(n)$ time algorithm for graphs where two faces are fixed, provided the embedding ensures that all vertices outside these two faces induce convex vertex chains. The proposed algorithms are practically efficient, as evidenced by experimental results. This work extends our PhD thesis, which can be accessed at https://www.tu-dortmund.de/fakultaet20/ulrichnagel/ulrich-nagel-phd.pdf. This study addresses the challenge of noise in crowdsourced datasets, which is common in both online and historical records. Traditional noise mitigation techniques often depend on prior knowledge about the noise distribution or assume that the majority of contributors are highly reliable, leading to the classification of noise as "one-hot" (i.e., treating noise as clear-cut errors). In contrast, this work proposes a novel ensemble modeling method that accommodates noisy crowdsourced data without requiring any prior assumptions regarding the noise. To achieve this, the study integrates "human softmax" probability distributions—distributions derived from human annotators—with various measures of uncertainty, such as entropy, to evaluate the overall uncertainty within the dataset. The effectiveness of this approach is demonstrated through two case studies: first, predicting the species of birds in historical wildlife illustrations, and second, estimating the reliability of online crowdsourced data for machine learning applications. The results indicate that ensemble modeling significantly outperforms other leading methods for noise management, including those relying on pre-existing knowledge of the noise distribution. Furthermore, this technique is easily extensible to other domains, such as estimating the species of plants from crowdsourced data or estimating the gender distributions of historical figures from online sources. Ultimately, the proposed method is expected to facilitate more accurate and robust machine learning applications in these fields. Finally, the code required to replicate our experiments is publicly accessible at: https://github.com/alextucker1992/Ensemble-Modeling-for-Noisy-Crowdsourced-Datasets. We demonstrate exponential decay in the Hölder norm for transfer operators acting on smooth observables within uniformly and nonuniformly expanding semiflows that exhibit exponential decay of correlations. These findings extend prior results, which were limited to semiflows. The method relies on a Rugh-type formulation of the Perron--Weiss formula, adapting techniques developed for expanding maps and diffeomorphisms to the context of semiflows. As an application, we establish exponential decay of correlations for smooth observables against the Riemann zeta function $\zeta(s)$ within the geodesic flow on the unit tangent bundle of the modular surface. This represents the first such result regarding L-functions. Furthermore, we prove the existence of a spectral gap for the transfer operator of the Riemann spectral flow on the unit disk of a weighted Sobolev space, a consequence of the main theorem. We also examine various applications of this approach, including the dynamics of the unit ball of a weighted Sobolev space and the decay of transfer operator norms on the space of continuous functions. Additionally, we analyze the transfer operator for the Riemann family of zeta functions, $\{ \zeta(s, t) \}_{t \in [0,1]}$, defined as $\zeta(s, t) = \sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{e^{2\pi i t n}}{n^s}$, on the space of continuous functions. We establish exponential decay in the $C^0$-norm and a spectral gap on the $C^k$-norm for $k \geq 1$. The dynamics of the transfer operator are investigated, revealing that the spectrum on the $C^k$-norm is not discrete for any $k \geq 1$. The family of transfer operators is quasi-compact, and we derive a lower bound for the essential spectral radius. The $L$-function associated with this family of zeta functions is $\pi \cot(\pi s)/2$. A strength-$t$ covering array, denoted $\textrm{CA}(N,M,t,q)$, is a specific arrangement within an orthogonal array where $N$ represents the number of rows, $M$ the number of columns, $t$ the strength, and $q$ the number of symbols. In 2018, Khuri and Liu demonstrated that all nonisotropic strength-$2$ covering arrays with $q=3$ possess a structural form characterized by an orthogonal array combined with extra column(s) containing repeated entries. This paper extends that finding to the small case where $q=4$. Additionally, we present a method for generating strength-$t$ covering arrays with $q=2$ using strength-(t+1) covering arrays with $q=4$, which can be viewed as pairing two such arrays with different symbol sets. This construction proves particularly effective for small-scale arrays. Leveraging these two structural results, we derive structural properties for covering arrays with strength $2$ and $4$ under these specific parameters. Furthermore, we characterize the structure of small strength-$2$ covering arrays with $q=4$ through examples and computational data, revealing additional properties. Finally, we provide characterization results for small size strength-$2$ covering arrays with $q=4$ by examining the structure of their subarrays. These findings on structure and characterization are expected to be valuable for improving covering array generators and for theoretical research, including the study of asymptotic properties. Our results also contribute to software testing methodologies, such as model-based testing, by offering insights into the properties of generated test cases. Additionally, we propose an alternative approach for generating random covering arrays. To support these contributions, we have created a Python library that implements the algorithms used in this work. The library is available at https://github.com/abertoni/smallCA4. It includes functions to generate covering arrays based on the methodologies described, as well as tools to verify user-generated arrays and assess their randomness. We demonstrate that for any local realistic bound on the success probability of a non-local game involving $N$ players, $D$-dimensional systems, and a purified input state with noise level $p$, calculating this bound is NP-hard when $D$ is NP-hard for pure states and the noise scales as $1/D^{O(\log D)}$ (which is $1/e$ for qubits). Conversely, we establish that if the noise scales as $1/D^2$, making it $1/4$ for qubits, the problem becomes solvable in polynomial time. This approach leverages the observation that the local realistic bound can be expressed as the optimal value of a semi-definite program, enabling the application of approximate semi-definite programming algorithms. Additionally, we prove that determining the local realistic bound for generic non-local games with $N$ players, $D$-dimensional systems, and noisy maximally entangled states is also NP-hard under the same dimensional and noise constraints. Our primary contribution lies in the second part of this work, where we exploit the structural properties of noisy maximally entangled states to bound the optimal value of the semi-definite program in polynomial time using a hierarchy of semidefinite programs. Consequently, the local realistic bound for these games can be computed within any desired precision $\epsilon$ using an algorithm that runs in polynomial time relative to $N$, $D$, and $1/\epsilon$. In the hierarchy, the rank corresponds to $O(1)$ for $\epsilon=1/D^2$, $O(\log D)$ for $\epsilon=1/e$, and $O(\log D)$ for $\epsilon=1/\text{poly}(D)$. Notably, this hierarchy does not converge to the exact value within polynomial time. This paper presents a preliminary and partial replication of a guided genetic algorithm designed for automated crash reproduction. For accessibility, we have included the Python source code used in our implementation alongside the resulting outputs. This study represents only the reproduction phase; optimization for novel bugs or diverse input generation is beyond the scope of this work. We believe that providing both the source code and results will facilitate future extensions and help identify potential limitations. Additionally, we welcome suggestions for improvements to the source code. Our analysis reveals that the algorithm is highly sensitive to the initial population, which was generated randomly. Consequently, we recommend that for automated bug reproduction, this random generation should be substituted with a more robust and informed strategy. We hope this report proves beneficial to the software testing community. In summary, we have successfully replicated only a segment of the original paper, and we apologize for any inconvenience or confusion this may cause. We are eager to assist the community in achieving a more complete reproduction of the work. Your guidance would be greatly appreciated. Thank you.

The existence of an intermediate square lattice phase within a vortex lattice has been theoretically predicted for high-$T_\textrm{c}$ cuprate superconductors. Photons are an ideal probe for nuclear collisions because of their neutral charge, which prevents electromagnetic interference, and their ability to escape collision zones without interaction. However, thermal photon production in heavy-ion collisions is low, making data analysis challenging. Additionally, existing models struggle to predict thermal photons across the full energy range. This study addresses these limitations by developing a robust analysis framework to extract thermal photons from experimental data. We employ a multi-stage photon generation model to simulate signals from different source regions. By comparing generated photons with experimental data, we determine the anisotropic flow coefficients $v_1$ and $v_2$ for thermal photons. Our results indicate that these coefficients vary with collision centrality and energy, showing a strong dependence on centrality but a weak dependence on energy. Furthermore, we find that thermal photon production in central Pb-Pb collisions at 2.76 and 5.02 TeV aligns with that of 200 GeV ppb collisions. Finally, we compare our findings with those of other collision systems. Since thermal photons are emitted by both quarks and gluons, their flow characteristics can reveal the momentum distribution between these two components in the quark-gluon plasma. This study examines magnetic ordering in three-dimensional systems featuring triangular and kagome lattices. Employing mean field and random field theories, we demonstrate that non-colinear magnetic orders, specifically 120-degree and pendulum phases, emerge in these geometries. For the kagome lattice, we analyze the evolution from paramagnetic to ferromagnetic and antiferromagnetic phases, as well as the formation of 120-degree and pendulum ordered states. Additionally, we investigate how temperature influences these various magnetic configurations. In the kagome case, we calculate the temperature-dependent free energy to identify the ground state. Finally, we discuss the potential to stabilize these distinct magnetic orders through exchange bias. Our findings may be applicable to a broad spectrum of other triangular and kagome lattice systems. Detecting treatment effects is a highly sensitive task, particularly when dealing with massive datasets containing numerous variables. While numerous methods have been developed to address the issue of false discoveries, most rely on treating variables as independent, often utilizing a Bonferroni correction. Although FDR-controlled procedures exist for handling dependent variables, they typically require strong parametric assumptions or prior knowledge of the dependence structure. This study introduces the TDEB method, which operates without requiring independence or pre-specified dependence structures. The technique employs a data-driven approach to learn the dependence pattern, enabling the use of a less conservative false discovery rate control compared to traditional corrections. We evaluated TDEB's performance using both simulated and real-world data, confirming that it maintains strong type-I error control while achieving higher statistical power than current alternatives. The fundamental concepts of cosmological inflation are examined. We derive the equations of motion governing the inflaton field, define the slow-roll parameters, and present the corresponding slow-roll approximation of these equations. Additionally, we outline how the slow-roll parameters determine both the evolution of the universe and the power spectrum of primordial perturbations. We derive an expression for the number of e-folds as a function of these slow-roll parameters and illustrate their application in the simplest inflationary model, where a single scalar field—known as the inflaton—drives the expansion of the universe. Finally, we provide our estimates for the numerical values of these parameters.

Keywords: Cosmological Inflation, Theory of the Early Universe, Scalar Field Theory, Perturbations of the Early Universe, Power Spectrum of the Early Universe, Reheating of the Early Universe.

Software query reformulation is a technique that automatically modifies or rephrases user inputs to address ambiguous or erroneous requests. This paper introduces QUICKAR, a novel approach that automatically generates query reformulations by leveraging crowdsourced software development history. QUICKAR employs a new scoring metric to assess the quality of these reformulations, with higher scores correlating with a greater likelihood of success in locating the intended concept. The method and evaluation dataset used to test QUICKAR are publicly accessible to facilitate future research. Our assessment utilizes an automatic classifier to predict whether a reformulation can successfully resolve a concept location query. The results, which utilize precision and F1 scores, indicate that QUICKAR effectively reformulates queries to aid in finding relevant concepts. The experimental outcomes demonstrate that the approach achieves an accuracy rate exceeding 80%. Additionally, we illustrate how QUICKAR enhances the usability of concept location tools through a case study. The code for QUICKAR is available at https://github.com/ahmedhassan/QUICKAR. Entrainment is a well-documented social-communicative mechanism where individuals subtly mimic specific utterance characteristics of their partners to foster rapport. This study introduces the inaugural application of neural networks to measure entrainment within conversational speech. We developed a deep neural network capable of predicting partner characteristics, such as fundamental frequency contours,Prosodic Units, and acoustic embeddings, from an opponent's output. We hypothesize that the divergence between these predicted and actual characteristics reflects the degree of entrainment. To validate this, we examined performance on established, labeled datasets and assessed prediction quality against known correlations between entrainment metrics and conversational outcomes. Furthermore, we demonstrate how this distance can be utilized to automatically detect entrainment in unseen data, a capability essential for analyzing continuous conversational datasets. Our findings indicate that the distance calculated on Deep Neural Network embeddings offers a robust measure of entrainment. Finally, we explore how this proposed distance advances current research into entrainment. (This work was supported by the National Science Foundation under Grant No. 1746097). **Keywords:** entrainment, neural networks, conversational speech, continuous monitoring, unsupervised metrics.

Domain adaptation is a widely adopted strategy for addressing distribution shifts across training, validation, and inference datasets. Recently, source-free domain adaptation (SFDA) has garnered significant attention due to its practical utility in scenarios where pre-trained models must operate without access to original training data. However, existing SFDA methods typically rely on storing intermediate models or hypotheses during adaptation, which imposes a high memory burden. To mitigate this memory bottleneck, we introduce a novel SFDA framework utilizing semi-supervised hypothesis transfer (HSHT). This approach leverages semi-supervised hypothesis transfer learning to eliminate the need for hypothesis storage, enabling resource-constrained devices to perform SFDA using only a single buffer buffer for intermediate representations. Additionally, we propose a hypothesis update mechanism that facilitates the refinement of hypotheses through lightweight gradient updates within the device. Experimental results demonstrate that our HSHT method outperforms state-of-the-art SFDA techniques across various datasets and tasks. Furthermore, we show that SFDA integrated with HSHT can be effectively deployed on edge devices, achieving superior performance in real-world applications. This study introduces a domain-informed neural network architecture tailored for particle interaction localization within astroparticle experiments, specifically for future direct detection of dark matter and neutronless fusion reactions. By leveraging the geometric symmetry of the detector volume, we demonstrate that a spherical neural network can achieve superior performance compared to a conventional feed-forward network. We evaluate both models using Monte Carlo simulations of particle interactions within the SuperNEMO and Super-Kamiokande detectors. Our results indicate that a feed-forward network with one hidden layer possessing spherical harmonics symmetry can determine the 3D position of super-KeV interaction vertices with approximately 1 cm precision. This approach offers a viable pathway for developing vertex reconstruction techniques in upcoming experiments, such as those searching for dark sector particles like dark photons and axion-like particles through nucleon coherent scattering. Furthermore, this domain-informed neural network serves as a proof-of-concept for extending domain knowledge from physics into machine learning architectures, a strategy that could enhance performance in astroparticle physics observables. Consequently, this may inform the design of future detectors and optimize the utilization of data from current experiments. Finally, our methodology is applicable to extracting localized vertices from general particle interaction data, including those from collider and beam experiments. Atmospheric retrievals for exoplanets and brown dwarfs necessitate precise and extensive cross-section data for molecules. This study introduces EXOPLINES, a database designed to support the retrieval of exoplanet atmospheres, featuring optimized line parameters and line-by-line cross-sections for the most prevalent molecules in these systems. Currently, EXOPLINES includes data for H2O, CO, CH4, and NH3, spanning temperature ranges of 30–1000 K, 30–1500 K, 50–2000 K, and 50–2000 K, respectively. These datasets are generated using the HITRAN2020 molecular line parameters. The study also addresses the impact of self-broadening coefficients on retrieval results, utilizing a self-consistent, line-by-line approach. The analysis indicates that H2O retrievals are significantly affected by the choice of self-broadening coefficient, whereas the effects on CH4 and NH3 are negligible. The paper includes a detailed description of the EXOPLINES database and its application. The datasets are accessible at https://github.com/astro-roma1/EXOPLINES. This work offers a foundational overview of grounding within Answer Set Programming (ASP) by extending well-founded semantics to include circular disjunctions and disjunctions with at least one default-free disjunct. We demonstrate that the entirety of the grounded ASP program adhering to these guidelines constitutes a necessary and sufficient explanation for every subset of the original program's atoms that cannot be determined true or false. Furthermore, we introduce a formal algorithm to implement this grounding process and provide a Satisfiability Modulo Theory (SMT) encoding for the computation of circular disjunction closure. Additionally, we present an algorithm for closure computation based on this encoding and empirically evaluate its performance using the ASP encoder ASPencore. Our empirical analysis, which compares our SMT encoding against existing ASP encodings of ASP ground, indicates that our SMT encoding achieves significantly better performance than the standard ASP encodings. Ultimately, we conclude that our approach provides a solid formal basis for understanding the core concepts of ASP ground, establishing a promising direction for future research. Specifically, this foundation enables the development of enhanced encodings for various ASP constructs and algorithms, leading to improved performance. We illustrate this potential by showing how our understanding can yield better encodings for transformations between different forms of ASP programs, thereby achieving superior performance outcomes. Finally, we demonstrate that incorporating this improved understanding of ASP ground into the open-source ASP compiler ASPencore results in notable performance gains. Specifically, integrating our SMT encoding of ASP ground into ASPencore produces a 2.5x performance improvement over the default ASP ground compiler and a 1.5x improvement compared to an ASPencore version with the SMT encoding disabled. These findings underscore the value of applying a rigorous formal understanding of ASP ground to the development of the ASPencore tool. In summary, this paper serves as a survey of recent research advancements in grounding, providing a formal understanding of the concept and exploring its application in enhancing the ASPencore tool. We believe that a formal understanding of ASP ground is essential for the continued advancement of the answer set programming field. Additionally, we present an SMT encoding for ASP ground closure computation, which can be utilized to develop formal verification tools for ASP ground computation. This approach holds the potential to facilitate formal proofs of correctness for ASP ground computation algorithms. Ultimately, this research contributes to the broader goal of advancing formal methods and tools within the answer set programming community. Specifically, our work supports the development of formal verification tools for ASP ground computation and provides a foundation for formal proofs regarding the correctness of ASP ground algorithms

This work establishes the change law for general quantum resources in quantum thermodynamics, quantum coherence, and qubit impurity. We demonstrate that for any quantum state, the variation of a resource's content during an operation equals the sum of that operation's Choi matrix's contribution to the resource and the state's divergence to it. These findings not only elucidate the change mechanisms of general quantum resources but also enable the derivation of conditions under which these resources remain monotonic. Specifically, we determine the monotonicity of quantum thermodynamic free energy, coherence measure, and impurity without relying on any assumptions. Furthermore, leveraging the change law, we derive expressions for quantum thermodynamic efficiency, coherence gain, and impurity increase during quantum processes. Finally, we construct quantum thermodynamic engines, heaters, and dephasing channels that defy the first law of thermodynamics, achieve non-monotonicity, or violate the second law. These results provide quantum thermodynamics with fundamental tools grounded in quantum information theory, thereby fostering its development. Additionally, the change law and monotonicity conditions derived here are applicable to the study of quantum coherence, discord, entanglement, and other resources. The full proof for the case of qubits is provided in the main text, while extensions to arbitrary quantum systems are detailed in the supplementary material. Our approach is based on the quantum relative entropy formulation of state content for general quantum resources, which is detailed in a companion paper. We anticipate that the resource content and monotonicity criteria established in this work and its companion paper will serve as essential tools for quantum thermodynamics and resource theory research. The concepts introduced here can be readily extended to the analysis of quantum resources in other physical theories. The change law and monotonicity conditions derived in this work are also relevant to investigating quantum coherence, discord, and entanglement. The full derivation of the change law for quantum thermodynamic free energy, coherence, and impurity for arbitrary quantum systems can be found in our companion paper. We believe the concept of resource content defined in this work and its companion paper will become a fundamental tool for quantum thermodynamics and resource theory research. The framework introduced in this work can also be easily generalized to the analysis of quantum resources in other physical theories. Furthermore, the change law for quantum thermodynamic free energy, coherence, and impurity for arbitrary quantum systems, derived in this work alongside its companion paper, is also relevant to the study of quantum coherence, discord, and entanglement. This study introduces a framework for measuring information based on its moments. The initial measure, termed information content, is derived from the first moment and exhibits characteristics akin to differential entropy for probability distributions. Furthermore, the positive and negative information content analogs correspond to the differential entropies of a distribution's convex and concave envelopes, respectively. By generalizing to infinite-dimensional moments, we develop an information variance measure that fulfills properties similar to those of Renyi entropy of order 2. Additionally, we demonstrate the optimality of Gaussian distributions regarding positive and negative information content and provide an intuitive probabilistic interpretation of the information content triangle. Finally, we establish an infinite system of inequalities for these measures and extend these inequalities to stochastic processes and random vectors. Our work offers an alternative method for information measures that complements existing approaches while retaining many of their properties. The proposed measures are calculable for specific classes of distributions and stochastic processes, including those with piecewise constant probability density functions. Various applications are illustrated, such as modeling the physical intensity of electromagnetic radiation, analyzing the reliability of complex systems, and generating random vectors with specified marginal distributions. These findings are supported by numerical simulations. This research was conducted as part of the author's thesis under the supervision of Dr. K. S. Namboodiri. This paper investigates inference regarding the parameters of a non-linear, non-stationary time series model characterized by heavy tails and high kurtosis. Specifically, I introduce a non-linear time varying parameter autoregression model featuring a time-varying leverage effect, VPAR($p$)-LE, which is estimated using a two-step procedure. The initial step employs an Expectation Maximization algorithm to determine the model's unknown features, while the second step calculates parameter estimates based on these inferred values. Additionally, a z-test is proposed to assess the significance of the estimated parameters. Simulation results indicate that the estimation procedure performs well, though the rejection rate of the significance test exceeds the nominal 5% level. This deviation is attributed to the fact that, despite being estimated as non-stationary, the finite sample data effectively behaves as a stationary process, causing the significance test to function similarly to one designed for stationary series. Finally, the VPAR$(p)$-LE model is applied to analyze the daily returns of the S&P500 and S&P500 Energy sectors, with a focus on comparing the two resulting models. The analysis confirms that the energy sector exhibits a more pronounced time-varying leverage effect, aligning with the intuition that riskier sectors experience more frequent crashes. Furthermore, the model demonstrates that time-varying parameters are most significantly reduced during the 2008 financial crisis, underscoring the necessity of employing time-varying parameter models during such periods. This finding is supported by the fact that the 2008 crisis represents the longest continuous period of negative returns observed in the dataset. Finally, it is concluded that the model performs adequately on this dataset, as evidenced by the fact that the estimated conditional kurtosis is consistently greater than three. However, it is noted that this model is not inherently superior to others; rather, it serves as a valuable tool for analyzing financial time series that display a time-varying leverage effect. We introduce a novel, explicit family of good quantum low-density parity-check codes equipped with linear-time decoders. These codes rely on a time-space lattice architecture, utilizing check and measurement matrices that are linear functions of the number of logical qubits, $n$. Within this framework, each bit in the matrices corresponds to a stabilizer, with row and column distances both exceeding $n^{0.5 - \delta}$ for some $\delta > 0$. Furthermore, the matrices possess a constant checkweight. Our findings thus establish the first explicit construction of a complete lattice of quantum LDPC codes that achieves constant rate and minimum relative distance. Additionally, the linear-time decoder guarantees that any error pattern with weight below the quantum distance can be identified and corrected with high probability. To substantiate these claims, we provide a rigorous analysis utilizing a quantum version of the X-Walk algorithm. This algorithm serves as the foundational step for developing a time-space lattice version of the minimum-weight decoder, which we demonstrate to be polynomial-time efficient. We then apply the quantum distance graph algorithm to this minimum-weight decoder, resulting in a complete decoder capable of correcting any error pattern with weight less than the quantum distance of the code. This approach achieves the optimal decoding trade-off between rate, distance, and decoding time, thereby fulfilling the objectives of the quantum HDPC code holy grail. This study investigates the bulk-boundary correspondence in the eigenstate problem of disordered higher-order topological insulators (HOTIs). The analysis begins with the clean limit, where the emergence of bulk-boundary correspondence is elucidated through the relationship between the bulk fractal dimension and the topological invariant. Subsequently, numerical simulations are employed to examine the correspondence in the disordered phase, revealing a shift from bulk fractal states to boundary or edge thermalization states. The simulation results confirm that the stability of these boundary and edge states against disorder is intrinsically linked to the bulk fractal dimension. Consequently, our findings offer valuable insights into the disordered limits of higher-order topological insulators. Furthermore, these conclusions are extended to higher-dimensional non-hermitian systems, including the skin effect and non-hermitian skin effect. Finally, the discussion is broadened to encompass general topological invariants characterized by multiple indices. To demonstrate this extension, we apply it to the rotated quantum spin Hall effect and higher-order non-hermitian skin effects, analyzing their respective bulk, boundary, and edge spectral properties. Ultimately, our results provide a theoretical foundation for understanding the spectral characteristics of disordered higher-order topological insulators. Additionally, the methodologies developed in this work can be utilized to investigate the spectral properties of other disordered topological systems. This contribution details recent findings on supersymmetry presented by the CMS experiment, specifically highlighting results from multilepton channels that offer robust discrimination against the Standard Model background. The presented searches target the production of charginos and neutralinos decaying into three jets and two leptons via supersymmetric partners. Additionally, we report a search within the three lepton channel for the associated production of charginos and neutralinos, also proceeding through supersymmetric intermediates. Furthermore, we examine a search for right-handed stops that decay into bottom quarks and bottom squarks, which subsequently decay into gluinos. Finally, we describe a search for neutral Higgs bosons that couple more strongly to down-type fermions, focusing on events featuring a bottom quark pair and a Higgs boson decaying into a W boson, muon, and neutrino. This search targets the $h_2$ state in two-Higgs doublet models and the $S$ and $A$ states in the MSSM, assuming down-type Yukawa couplings of $\mu_R = 2\cot\beta$, $\tan^2\beta$, and $\tan\beta$ relative to the Standard Model expectation. These analyses utilize approximately 20 fb$^{-1}$ of data collected at $\sqrt{s} = 13$ TeV. Collectively, these searches extend into unexplored regions of parameter space for various supersymmetric models. For further information, contact email: marcello.benetti@cern.ch. We introduce a new approach for rendering scenes captured via light field cameras, utilizing a multi-scale convolutional neural network that operates solely on pixel-wise data. This method eliminates the need for scene geometry or pixel relationships, thereby streamlining the acquisition and processing of pixel data. Our multi-scale framework yields superior results in both image and video synthesis, as well as in reconstructing the scene representation for novel views. Additionally, we incorporate a specialized loss function designed to enhance the training of dynamic scenes. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach achieves performance comparable to existing methods while requiring only 10 views instead of 15. We have made the code and pre-trained models publicly available. The results can be viewed here. Our code is available here.

This study presents speckle interferometric data for 100 stars, obtained using the high-speed imager HIIS on the SOAR telescope during the 2020 observing season. Although HIIS operations were frequently interrupted by a significant solar array fault, the instrument successfully executed speckle interferometry for 20 days across 11 sessions. The dataset includes 20 binary stars with measured separations and position angles, alongside 80 single stars where no HIIS companions were detected. For the 20 binary systems, we report precise astrometric measurements of companion positions and separations, with a median uncertainty of 0.007 arcsec. Additionally, we determined the speckle FWHM for the 80 non-binary stars, achieving a median value of 0.014 arcsec. These findings will be utilized to refine HIIS astrometric calibration for future ground-based direct imaging missions. The HIIS data for the 20 binary stars are accessible via the Extrasolar Planet and Stars Database (exoplanet.eu/survey/hiis/2020/binary/), while data for the 80 non-binary stars can be found at exoplanet.eu/survey/hiis/2020/nonbinary/. The HIIS binary stars are also listed in the Nasa Exoplanet Archive at exoplanetarchive.ipac.caltech.edu/hiis/2020/binary/. Furthermore, we have developed a Python package named HIISpy to facilitate the analysis of HIIS astrometry and speckle photometry, which is available at github.com/HiISpy/HiISpy. This package is particularly useful for analyzing HIIS data and planning observations for the upcoming HIIS campaign in 2022.
