We investigate celestial chiral algebras within celestial holography, with a specific focus on channel independence and the consequences of colour-kinematics duality. These concepts are naturally realized in the OPEs of holomorphic conformal primary fields in two-dimensional CFTs. We demonstrate that the full structure of the w algebra emerges from the conformal symmetry of two-dimensional CFTs, rather than being an independent celestial symmetry. Furthermore, the consistency of colour-kinematics duality in two-dimensional CFTs imposes a novel constraint on the central charge. We also examine the link between integrability and colour-kinematics duality in both gauge theories and gravity, deriving an exact relationship between soft theorems and conserved charges associated with large gauge transformations. Additionally, we establish the relationship between soft theorems and charges arising from null direction symmetries in the self-dual sector of (chiral) self-dual Yang-Mills theory. Finally, we prove the consistency of this relationship by explicitly constructing the corresponding symmetry charges in the w algebra. These findings suggest that the two-dimensional chiral algebra encodes essential information about self-dual field theories, including their soft theorems, symmetries, and null direction integrability. This insight may facilitate the construction of a two-dimensional chiral algebra for self-dual Yang-Mills theory, a task currently under investigation. Such an achievement would be highly significant for black hole physics, as it could provide a rigorous two-dimensional description of self-dual gravitational scattering amplitudes, thereby clarifying the nature of self-dual soft hair on black holes. In this context, the w algebra could serve as the appropriate chiral algebra for self-dual gravity. We propose that a self-dual sector of the celestial OPEs, featuring a colour-kinematics duality between the self-dual sector of Yang-Mills theory and self-dual gravity, would support this proposal. Solar eruptions frequently produce jets, and while their dynamics and origins are well-documented by the Solar and Heliospheric Observatory's (SOHO) LASCO coronagraph, the mechanisms driving the initial jet formation remain unclear. This study presents LOFAR observations of a radio source linked to a jet source within the low solar corona, offering the first detailed view of a jet-driven piston shock in the low corona. The source exhibits a morphology consistent with a piston shock, and its temporal profile aligns with the temporal-spatial evolution of the overdriven shock. We conclude that LOFAR is capable of detecting piston shocks in the low corona, thereby providing a tool to investigate the dynamics of jet-driven shocks and their role in coronal heating. Furthermore, these observations indicate that the onset of the piston shock is driven by the early phase of the jet. Although not directly observed, this early jet phase is likely magnetic in origin, suggesting that magnetic fields play a crucial role in the dynamics of the piston shock. Finally, the low-frequency emission is likely thermal in nature, suggesting that piston shocks can generate the low-frequency non-thermal emission previously observed. These findings are supported by a two-dimensional magnetohydrodynamic simulation. Our results suggest that similar low-frequency emissions from the low corona may be more common than previously thought, potentially explaining the missing low-frequency emission in the low corona. Additionally, this work demonstrates the value of multi-wavelength observations for studying the dynamics of solar eruptions. Future observations of similar events will be crucial for understanding the origins of jets and the processes driving them. This research introduces a new, efficient algorithm for simulating three-dimensional superfluid turbulence by solving functional stochastic differential equations (FSDEs) in a weakly turbulent regime. These equations govern random vortices that model the irrotational regions of a superfluid. The proposed method offers functional weak convergence, achieving a rate proportional to the square root of the time step, which matches the accuracy of standard simulation techniques in non-random contexts. Furthermore, the algorithm is applicable to arbitrary, potentially time-dependent, vortex configurations and geometric domains. We demonstrate its utility by presenting simulation results for fully developed three-dimensional superfluid turbulence, specifically simulating the decay of superfluid turbulence behind a decelerating blunt body, known as the wake of a bluff body. The results align with existing theoretical and experimental data regarding both the large-scale vortex structure and the three-dimensional drag coefficient. The software utilized is accessible at https://github.com/kenji-ichikawa/RandomVortex. This software is also featured in our companion paper, which details new numerical findings on the simulation of superfluid turbulence using random vortices. We introduce a deep learning approach designed to forecast the temporal evolution of high-dimensional datasets, such as time-lapse microscopy images or single-cell RNA sequencing results. This method leverages supervised learning to develop a neural network capable of anticipating future frames based on previous observations. By employing convolutional neural networks to extract features from sequence data and a recurrent network to model temporal dependencies, our architecture effectively handles short sequences and large dimensionality. To validate the model, we applied it to two datasets: time-lapse fluorescence microscopy images of developing zebrafish embryos and short 10x Genomics Chromium single-cell RNA sequencing data from human cells. The model successfully predicted image sequences with high accuracy and demonstrated the ability to learn and visualize cell cycle phases in zebrafish embryos. Furthermore, we trained the model on diverse datasets of developing embryos to create a classifier that can categorize new images into the correct developmental stage. These findings indicate that our approach holds significant promise for applications in developmental biology and immunology. Reinforcement learning focuses on agents interacting with environments to maximize cumulative rewards. However, because these environments are often partially observable, agents must manage both their belief states and actions. This work demonstrates that recurrent neural networks (RNNs) function effectively as belief representations within RLL by leveraging their inherent recurrent architecture to track beliefs over time. The study validates this hypothesis through experiments on a simple grid world and a complex, realistic scenario involving a self-driving car navigating a roundabout. Self-supervised training yielded promising results, notably in the self-driving car application. Consequently, this representation facilitates the transfer of self-driving skills to new roundabouts and supports model distillation for creating more efficient agents. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/alexschulz/Recurrent-belief-representation. Our findings indicate that RNNs can serve as a valuable tool for representing beliefs in partially observable settings. This result is significant for understanding how to design neural networks capable of learning from data and for developing efficient recurrent architectures. Furthermore, this outcome supports the broader hypothesis that recurrent architectures are essential for handling partial observability. Finally, this work offers a promising pathway for investigating how biological brains represent their belief states. The code can be found at https://github.com/alexschulz/Recurrent-belief-representation. This research was conducted as part of my Master's thesis at the University of Oxford. This paper addresses weakly-supervised action detection, which involves learning to identify action onset and offset from video through frame-level binary labels. While prior methods primarily focus on aggregating frame representations using pooling techniques to create vector or matrix summaries, we introduce a novel approach that aggregates spatial-temporal feature maps using a graph convolutional network. This technique highlights salient regions within the video while suppressing irrelevant details. Experimental results demonstrate that our method surpasses state-of-the-art models. The accompanying code will be released publicly. Furthermore, we have developed a new dataset, UCF-WACG, specifically for weakly-supervised action detection. This dataset features overlapping temporal annotations and frame-level labels, offering a more realistic and challenging evaluation than existing datasets. It includes ten human action classes, with temporal boundaries for actions derived from frame-level annotations across multiple samples. We anticipate this dataset will be valuable for research in action recognition, temporal action localization, and video retrieval. The dataset and evaluation tools will be made available to the research community. Additional details can be found at https://sites.google.com/view/ufm-ucsd-wsltl. This research examines diffusion processes halted or reflected at a domain boundary, where the generator consists of a second-order elliptic operator that may degenerate and a zero-order term that can be unbounded. The analysis addresses small perturbations of the stopped process and both the MST and T-martingale problems associated with perturbations of the full process. Furthermore, metastability findings are applied to analyze the homogenization of a class of randomly pertained stopped diffusion processes. Notably, the methodology does not require the original process to be conservative (i.e., the process is allowed to explode). The study encompasses several specific applications, including (absorbed) local time on a domain, (absorbed) Dirichlet and Neumann semigroups in a domain, and the first exit time from a domain. Additionally, the results remain valid when the domain is merely a closed set rather than an open one. Finally, the work addresses various aspects of the spectral theory for the considered operators. This framework is specifically applicable to analyzing the spectral theory of the Laplacian in a domain, the Neumann Laplacian on a manifold, and the Laplacian on a manifold. The analysis also covers the Laplacian on a manifold with conical singularities, the Laplacian on a manifold with singularities, and the Laplacian on a manifold featuring isolated conical singularities. Finally, the study addresses the spectral theory of the Laplacian on a manifold with finitely many points removed. This study investigates the properties of nuclear matter at zero temperature under strong magnetic fields using the lowest-order constraint variational (LOCV) method with the $AV_{18}$ nuclear potential. Our findings indicate that while the LOCV potential energy remains largely unaffected by the magnetic field, the symmetry energy shows clear sensitivity. Specifically, the symmetry energy decreases as the magnetic field strength increases, reaching approximately $20$ MeV at $B = 100$ fm$^{-2}$. These results suggest that the LOCV method is well-suited for analyzing nuclear matter properties within strong magnetic fields. Furthermore, the calculated LOCV potential energy aligns closely with relativistic LOCV (RLOCV) results, which employ the same potential but utilize the relativistic potential $AV_{18}^R$. This agreement confirms that the RLOCV method produces reliable outcomes for nuclear matter under such conditions. Additionally, the LOCV technique yields a magnetic moment roughly $10\%$ larger than that of RLOCV, a consequence of incorporating self-energies in the RLOCV framework. Finally, we observe that both LOCV and RLOCV methods produce similar spin polarization even at zero net density, a feature that matches the predictions of the mean-field (MF) approach. These consistent results across different theoretical methods provide strong support for the validity of the LOCV technique. Finally, the magnetic moment is found to be highly sensitive to the magnetic field, dropping to approximately $10\%$ of its zero-field value at $B = 100$ fm$^{-2}$. This significant reduction is attributed to the alignment of nucleon spins with the quantization axis defined by the magnetic field direction. Overall, the LOCV method proves to be a valuable tool for studying nuclear matter at zero temperature within strong magnetic fields. These conclusions are supported by comparisons to the MF and RLOCV approaches. This study addresses privacy and communication challenges within federated learning (FL) by introducing a novel framework called \emph{differential privacy recommendation for communication-efficient federated learning} (DP-REC). The primary goal of this work is to enhance privacy protection while minimizing communication overhead. To achieve this, we first leverage recommendation techniques to reduce the volume of data shared by the server, thereby improving the model's ability to learn from representative samples. Subsequently, we integrate a new communication-efficient FL algorithm with differential privacy mechanisms to further lower communication costs and strengthen privacy guarantees. We rigorously analyze the trade-off between utility and privacy under varying levels of differential privacy, establishing a specific bound on the number of learning rounds. Experimental results demonstrate that DP-REC outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods in terms of both privacy and communication efficiency. Additionally, we examine the impact of different FL strategies on the DP-REC framework, finding that it is particularly well-suited for heterogeneous data distributions. Overall, our findings indicate that DP-REC offers a promising solution for enhancing privacy and communication efficiency in FL systems. We conducted far-ultraviolet (FUV) observations of the Taurus-Perseus-Auriga complex using the Galaxy Evolution Explorer (GALEX) to study molecular clouds and their surrounding regions. These observations provide a novel, large-scale FUV view of the Taurus cloud, along with new data for the nearby L1551 and L1157 clouds, as well as the Perseus and Auriga clouds. FUV imaging of Taurus reveals a bright FUV emission region extending from the FUV-excessed IC 348 cluster to the FUV-bright IC 435 cluster, situated between the FUV-dark Taurus filaments. This emission likely originates from the surface of Taurus clouds, illuminated by massive stars in the nearby FUV-excessed IC 348 cluster. Additionally, we identified several FUV-bright emission regions around the edges of the L1551 and L1157 clouds, suggesting that the FUV radiation from the nearby NGC 1333 cluster is illuminating these areas. FUV imaging of Perseus shows bright emission regions around the NGC 1335 cluster and the FUV-excessed NGC 1333B2 cluster, indicating that these regions are also illuminated by massive stars in NGC 1335. FUV imaging of Auriga identifies two FUV-excessed clusters, IC 49 and IC 59, and several FUV-bright emission regions around the edges of the Auriga clouds, illuminated by the FUV radiation from the NGC 1960 cluster. These results suggest that the FUV radiation from the cores of the NGC 1333, IC 348, IC 49, and IC 59 clusters is primarily absorbed by the clouds surrounding them. Furthermore, we propose that the FUV emission regions observed around the edges of the Taurus, L1551, L1157, Perseus, and Auriga clouds may serve as indicators of the surface of the clouds. Finally, we speculate that the FUV emission regions around the edges of the Taurus, L1551, L1157, Perseus, and Auricha clouds may be the birthplaces of the Taurus, L1551, L1157, Perseus, and Auriga filaments, respectively. Tables are extensively utilized in scientific publications to organize data and summarize research outcomes. However, existing methods for retrieving tabular data from scientific articles often fall short, primarily because they neglect the unique characteristics of these documents. Specifically, the internal structure of a table and its content play crucial roles in determining the representation of table headers. This study investigates the application of graph neural networks (GNNs) to represent table headers. We first convert a table into a graph representation, where table cells function as nodes and adjacency relationships serve as edges. Subsequently, we employ a GNN to generate embeddings for the table's internal structure. Experimental results demonstrate that these GNN-derived embeddings outperform those from traditional embedding methods, such as word embeddings, in classifying header cells within scientific articles. Furthermore, we find that leveraging the structural information of headers significantly enhances performance in automatic table extraction for scientific papers. Our approach effectively handles edge cases, including rotated headers, tables lacking clear semantic boundaries, and those containing blank cells. Additionally, the proposed method is computationally efficient, requiring only a single forward pass during inference. We have made our code and pre-trained models accessible to facilitate future research. This work offers a novel perspective on representing tabular data, with potential applications extending beyond scientific articles to other domains. We introduce a cognitive hierarchy model tailored for multi-stage games of incomplete information, addressing the dynamics of belief formation and strategic reasoning throughout various stages and revealing equilibrium behavior. In this framework, players at different cognitive levels reason about their own and others' beliefs regarding both actions and types. Specifically, within this model, first-order players reason conditionally about their own private information, whereas second-order players form conditional expectations regarding their own types as well as those of others. Under a non-degeneracy condition, we demonstrate that in each stage, cognitive equilibrium amounts to a Bayesian Nash equilibrium, while the model predicts a unique path of behavior across multiple stages. We apply this model to repeated games, highlighting its ability to generate unique dynamics and equilibria even when participants exhibit significant uncertainty regarding one another. Notably, our findings indicate that cognitive hierarchy offers a superior explanation for experimental evidence suggesting that people do not fully reach Nash equilibrium predictions, even after an extended number of periods. Finally, we extend the model to multi-player settings, demonstrating its capacity to generate testable predictions that can be empirically validated. Specifically, we show that while first-order behavior is consistent with best response, second-order behavior exhibits the risk-averse traits of rational expectations. These results are supported by an experiment involving a repeated three-player game. Furthermore, we illustrate that the model can account for discrepancies between standard theoretical predictions and actual behavior in the market for used cars. Our analysis also suggests that cognitive hierarchy provides a compelling explanation for the persistence of the "lemons" market even after multiple transactions. We conclude by showing that the cognitive hierarchy model generates distinct, testable predictions that diverge from those of quantal response equilibrium and level-$k$ models. These predictions are confirmed by an experiment utilizing a generalized version of the three-player setting. We also present additional evidence from a real-world application, indicating that cognitive hierarchy offers a viable explanation for the behavior of used car markets. Finally, we demonstrate that the model can explain the failure of trade to occur in such markets. These contributions highlight the potential of the cognitive hierarchy model to provide a more accurate understanding of human behavior than existing alternatives. Our findings suggest that this approach can offer a better explanation for empirical observations, including the persistence of inefficiencies in repeated games and the dynamics of market transactions. In sum, the cognitive hierarchy model provides a more accurate description of human behavior than other existing models, such as level-$k$ and quantal response equilibrium. We also show that the cognitive hierarchy model can explain the failure of trade to occur in used car markets.

Accurate and timely population estimates are essential for formulating national policies. This study introduces a population estimation framework for Mozambique that integrates geospatial data with birth and death records. Specifically, we employ a Bayesian neural network to forecast annual population counts, utilizing satellite-derived nightlight intensity as a key feature. We assess the efficacy of this methodology by comparing estimated population figures against census data. Our findings indicate that, without adjustments, the estimates underestimate the total population by approximately 10% in 2010. Furthermore, we demonstrate that incorporating an age distribution model, which synthesizes population estimates with mortality rates derived from nightlight data, significantly enhances estimation accuracy. This improved approach reduces the underestimation of total population by roughly 5% in 2010. Additionally, we project the 2017 population for two provinces, providing the first-ever population estimates for these specific regions. The complete dataset and source code are accessible via a public repository. Ultimately, this methodology holds promise for generating accurate, sustainable population estimates in developing nations. By leveraging open-source datasets, the approach can achieve census-independent population estimation, thereby reducing reliance on costly national censuses. This work lays the foundation for developing sustainable, census-independent estimation systems in developing countries. Additionally, the public repository includes scripts for adjusting national estimates using provincial and district-level data. We believe this work will inspire further research into sustainable population estimation in developing nations. The source code is available at: https://github.com/abhishekkumar1992/PopEst. The underlying datasets can be found here: https://github.com/abhishekkumar1992/population-estimation-datasets. The adjustment code for provincial and district data using national estimates is located at: https://github.com/abhishekkumar1992/PopAdjust. Approximate membership query (AMQ) filters are widely used to efficiently test set element membership while tolerating a limited number of false positives. This paper introduces filters specifically designed to generate zero false positives for certain elements. We propose the zero-false-positive disjoint filter (ZFFD), which achieves a substantial reduction in storage space, utilizing 2.53 bits per element. Additionally, we present the ZFFD+ variant, which is optimized to minimize computation during insertion and testing, completing testing in just 1.01 CPU cycles per bit. Furthermore, we examine various methods for constructing these filters and demonstrate that their effectiveness varies depending on the specific application context. Our evaluations are based on three distinct datasets: a synthetic set, a set derived from a Wikipedia dump, and a set formed by concatenating passwords from the RockYou and Dropbox leaks. To facilitate broader research, we have made our dataset generation code and filters publicly available. This paper introduces a novel framework for the smooth particle hydrodynamics (SPH) method grounded in the multi-resolution property of multiwavelet basis functions. Within this approach, fluid and structural properties are represented and computed across varying levels of resolution. The method is validated through diverse fluid-structure interaction (FSI) scenarios, encompassing both single-phase and multi-phase regimes. To evaluate the multi-phase capabilities, the simulations incorporate a new equation of state (EOS) capable of handling large pressure variations, alongside a volume-of-fluid (VOF) technique for precise free surface tracking. In these scenarios, different resolution levels are assigned to the fluid and solid domains. Numerical results confirm the method's robustness and accuracy, demonstrating that lower levels of artificial viscosity can be utilized when resolving fluid-structure interfaces. Consequently, this capability significantly reduces numerical dissipation. Furthermore, the study confirms the method's stability and accuracy under such conditions. Finally, the proposed framework is shown to be effective in simulating complex FSI problems. Notably, the multi-phase FSI case involving a sphere falling into a water tank yields results that align well with experimental data. This agreement is achieved using a relatively small number of particles and without introducing numerical viscosity. These findings underscore the method's potential to substantially enhance the accuracy of FSI simulations. Finally, the paper concludes with a discussion on the broader applicability of this framework. Specifically, it suggests that the multi-resolution strategy can be leveraged to simulate complex flows and flows with high gradients by assigning different resolution levels to distinct regions of the fluid. Additionally, such distinct level assignments could facilitate the simulation of multi-phase flows. In both scenarios, the current multi-phase FSI problem serves as a proof of concept. This demonstrates that distinct resolution levels can be applied to different regions of the fluid without compromising accuracy or stability. This paves the way for future research into complex flow simulations and multi-phase flow modeling. In these future applications, multi-phase resolution will be utilized to achieve a more accurate representation of the flow field. Furthermore, this approach will enable the simulation of finer details in the flow field using a reduced number of particles. These advancements are expected to significantly improve the accuracy of the resulting solutions. To conclude, the proposed multi-resolution SPH framework offers a promising avenue for advancing the accuracy and efficiency of fluid and structure simulations. This is anticipated to have a significant impact on various engineering applications. Examples include, but are not limited to, aerospace engineering, hydrodynamics, and biomedical engineering. Machine learning is a computational method that enables devices to recognize patterns within vast amounts of data without relying on explicit programming. Although quantum computing has existed for several decades, the practical application of quantum algorithms for machine learning remains largely theoretical. This study presents a quantum algorithm designed for both unsupervised and supervised machine learning tasks, implemented on a superconducting quantum processor. The research demonstrates the implementation of these quantum machine learning algorithms alongside quantum circuit compilers and performance benchmarks using superconducting hardware. For the specific case of principal component analysis in unsupervised learning, the study reports the execution of an 11-qubit circuit taking approximately 100 microseconds. Furthermore, it highlights the successful execution of a 6-qubit circuit for the XOR problem in supervised learning, which took about 50 microseconds. These findings indicate that quantum machine learning can be effectively implemented on superconducting processors. The work includes a detailed analysis of errors within the superconducting quantum processor and provides insights into mitigating these errors through data post-processing techniques. Ultimately, the paper concludes that superconducting quantum processors are viable platforms for quantum machine learning, supported by the provided hardware analysis and error mitigation strategies. Additionally, the study explores potential extensions of these algorithms to larger qubit configurations and larger datasets. We introduce a technique for measuring the mass of the $W$ boson by analyzing lepton-pair events that occur in conjunction with a $b\bar{b}$ pair. This approach is highly sensitive to $b$-quark fragmentation, a factor that can be precisely calibrated using $b$-hadron spectroscopy data. By applying this method to the CMS and ATLAS datasets from the LHC, we achieve lepton-pair mass resolutions of 1.5 GeV and 1.2 GeV, respectively. These results surpass the 1.6 GeV precision of the direct $W$-boson mass measurements conducted by the D0 and CDF collaborations. Furthermore, we evaluate the systematic uncertainties associated with $b$-jet energy scale and calibration, as well as quark and gluon fragmentation, by incorporating $b$-jet data into our analysis. Our findings indicate that the uncertainty in $b$-jet energy calibration is negligible, while the uncertainty in parton fragmentation is comparable to the $W$-boson mass uncertainty itself. Consequently, the total uncertainty for the combined ATLAS and CMS datasets amounts to 1040 MeV, which is approximately 15% lower than the direct measurement uncertainties from D0 and CDF. This total uncertainty is dominated by the $W$-boson mass itself, rather than by $b$-jet energy scale or fragmentation considerations. Our results demonstrate that the $W$-boson mass can be determined with a precision of 1 GeV or better, provided that $b$-jet data from $b$-quark fragmentation sources are available for calibration. We anticipate that the LHC will soon provide sufficient $b$-jet data to enable a direct determination of the $W$-boson mass with a precision of 500 MeV. Additionally, we discuss the potential for improving this precision to 250 MeV by utilizing $b$-jet data from $b$-quark fragmentation sources that are currently unavailable, such as $Z\to b\bar{b}$ events. This highlights the critical importance of $b$-quark fragmentation data for $W$-boson mass measurements. Our findings are particularly relevant to the ongoing discussions regarding the $W$-boson mass anomalies reported by the CDF collaboration. Telepresence robots (TPRs) are widely used across various industries to facilitate remote communication and support human activities. As these systems have become more prevalent, ensuring a high-quality experience for remote users has grown increasingly critical. This study introduces a novel Quality of Experience (QoE) model designed to assess user satisfaction and the sense of presence during remote robot control. This model enables network operators to effectively manage network resources for TPRs, thereby enhancing the quality of experience for remote users. Mafia, also known as Werewolf, is a well-known party game that has become increasingly popular in online environments. This paper introduces a straightforward, unassisted mathematical model of the game, which is then applied to analyze game length and winner probabilities. Our findings indicate that a 3:3:12 ratio of Mafia, Villagers, and Police is optimal. Under these conditions, the Mafia's win rate reaches its peak at approximately 47%, winning an average of 2.1 games per 10, while Villagers win 52% of the time with an average of 2.2 games per 10. Additionally, the police win roughly 1% of the time, averaging 0.1 wins per 10 games. We conclude by discussing the influence of various game parameters on the Mafia faction's success rate.

**Keywords:** Mafia, Werewolf, mathematical model, probability, recurrence relations, game length, game theory, game analysis.

This study examines the simultaneous accretion of a gas accretion cavity within a giant planet mass range of 0.3 to 1.0 Jupiter masses. We simulate the simultaneous gas accretion process for two giant planets orbiting at 1.0 and 3.0 Jupiter masses within a protoplanetary disk, utilizing a fully coupled, multi-fluid, multi-dimensional disk model. Our findings indicate that the maximum mass a giant planet can reach is constrained by the strength of its gravitational perturbation on the disk. Specifically, the inner planet reaches a maximum mass of approximately 0.3 Jupiter masses, while the outer planet can grow to about 1.0 Jupiter masses. Furthermore, the gas accretion cavity created by the inner planet extends radially inward to the disk's inner edge, whereas the cavity formed by the outer planet is limited to a radial distance of roughly 10 astronomical units. We also observe that a significant gap is generated between the locations of the two gas accretion cavities. These results suggest that the gas disk migration model, which relies on gap opening, faces significant challenges in the simultaneous accretion scenario of a pair of giant planets. This study examines electron-phonon interactions within a macroscopic network of semiconducting armchair carbon nanotubes. By employing a two-terminal configuration on a highly ordered array of self-assembled nanotubes, we identify a distinct phonon signal characterized by a temperature-dependent peak in the current that aligns with the optical phonon energy gap. Furthermore, the detection of a current plateau at low electron energies serves as further confirmation of this phonon-driven mechanism. These findings constitute the first proof of phonon-assisted electronic current flow in a macroscopic CNT network, demonstrating that such systems can facilitate electron transport through the intertube phonon mode. The implications of these results are particularly significant for designing large-scale electronic devices that utilize optical phonons as an additional interaction pathway for electron interaction management. Additionally, the data offer a means to investigate the electronic properties of CNT films, including carrier density and mobility. The methodologies used in this research can be readily adapted for other materials possessing similar optical phonon characteristics. This study introduces a novel fuzzy k-means algorithm designed for high-dimensional data, incorporating variable feature weights. In many high-dimensional datasets, certain features are more critical than others for effective clustering; however, the standard fuzzy k-means method assigns equal weights to all features, often resulting in inaccurate clustering. Although quantum gravity is conjectured to forbid global symmetries, the absence of observed super-Higgs modes in gravitational wave data allows these symmetries to potentially survive within quantum gravity. We propose that measurements of cosmic birefringence can constrain which global symmetries remain unbroken. If an unbroken global symmetry exists, its associated super-Higgs mode would fail to propagate as a free field in a vacuum, thereby altering the polarization of distant radio waves. We establish an upper limit on the fine-structure constant based on recent cosmic birefringence observations and discuss the implications of this finding for quantum gravity. Furthermore, we note that future, more precise measurements of cosmic birefringence will significantly tighten these constraints. This approach offers a novel perspective on constraining quantum gravity models featuring nearly massless bosons, an area of broad interest. Additionally, our findings suggest that any proposed connection between global symmetries and dark sector physics must be carefully evaluated. Specifically, unbroken global symmetries would prevent the formation of stable, non-abelian dark solitons, thereby limiting the viability of certain dark sector models. We also address the issue of the shift anomaly, which generally obstructs the consistent quantization of theories based on unbroken global symmetries. Finally, we discuss the broader implications of our findings for quantum field theories with unbroken global symmetries and their relationship to quantum gravity. In conclusion, our results indicate that global symmetries cannot exist in quantum gravity. However, we emphasize that this conclusion relies on the accuracy of current cosmic birefringence measurements, and we look forward to future observations that will significantly refine these constraints. We report the discovery of five UV-bright stars within the globular cluster NGC 4147, identified through UVIT imaging. This study is the first of its kind to investigate UV luminosity in this specific cluster. Our analysis of the color-magnitude diagram indicates that these UV-bright stars are likely blue straggler stars (BSSs). We calculated the distance to UVIT 1FJ 0000.0+47.4 using the distance modulus ($\mu_0$) derived from the cluster's horizontal branch, yielding a value of $29.95 \pm 0.15$ mag. Additionally, the cluster's line-of-sight velocity was determined to be $-110.0 \pm 1.0$ km/s. We derived an age of $11.5 \pm 0.5$ Gyr and a metallicity of $-1.1 \pm 0.1$ dex for UVIT 1FJ 0000.0+47.4. Furthermore, the cluster's line-of-sight velocity dispersion was measured at $\sigma_{los} = 10.0 \pm 1.0$ km/s. Deep transfer learning represents a cornerstone of deep learning research and industrial applications. This study challenges two prevailing consensuses regarding transferability. First, it questions the widely accepted belief that the depth of neural networks determines transferability. By analyzing transfer learning across networks of varying architectures but similar depths, we found that transferability is primarily driven by the relationship between network depth and the specific downstream task, rather than depth alone. This insight led to the development of the Variable-length Multi-scale Multi-task Network (ViMS-MMTN), which utilizes lightweight sub-networks for pre-training to enhance efficiency. Second, we refute the common notion that model size and parameter count are primary determinants of transferability. Through a systematic examination of image classification transfer learning, we demonstrated that these factors are not the key drivers. This realization motivated the proposal of the Hierarchical Multi-scale Multi-task Network (HiMS-MMTN), which achieves high-accuracy transfer learning with minimal parameters by leveraging multi-scale features and multi-task learning strategies. Extensive experiments confirm the validity of our hypotheses, and the proposed methods have demonstrated superior performance on image classification and object detection tasks. Research on network information diffusion has traditionally concentrated on the structural properties of contact networks, such as degree distribution and assortativity. However, recent studies have demonstrated that dividing networks into communities based on modularity significantly improves the accuracy of predicting both the speed and extent of information spread. This study investigates how network modularity influences the speed of information diffusion during epidemic outbreaks. We show that a mid-level modularity of approximately 0.4 maximizes diffusion velocity, with this effect remaining consistent across various models, including the SIR, SIRV, and network epidemic models. Furthermore, we found that the average betweenness coefficient of outlets connecting different communities serves as an effective indicator of this modularity-induced effect. Finally, applying these findings to the 2019 novel coronavirus outbreak in China reveals that the country's provincial-level network exhibits moderate modularity, a characteristic that likely facilitated a rapid initial spread of the epidemic. These insights could inform future strategies for containing infectious diseases. Additionally, our comprehensive analysis of the relationship between network structure and diffusion speed may offer valuable guidance for designing efficient communication networks. This work extends the findings previously detailed in reference [1].

The widespread adoption of the Android operating system has heightened concerns regarding user privacy, as it hosts numerous applications and services. Consequently, researchers have investigated mobile malware to understand its mechanisms and the potential risks to users. While existing studies primarily focus on analyzing malicious applications, there is a notable gap in literature regarding Android malware that is hidden within the OS itself. To address this deficiency, this survey examines the architecture of the Android OS and its security mechanisms to explain how problem-space evasion attacks function within the environment. Finally, we outline possible future Android malware scenarios, providing a foundation for further research. Given that this work represents a shift from analyzing malicious apps to studying the Android OS from an attacker's perspective, we believe it will make a significant contribution to the field. Additionally, we believe this survey will be valuable to both mobile security researchers and practitioners. Building large-scale distributed systems is difficult due to the need to manage diverse components, such as databases, search engines, and machine learning models, which often have varying requirements for scaling, fault tolerance, and resource allocation. While distributed system administrators traditionally manage these parts individually, a trend is emerging to consolidate them within unified containers. Ozy is a general-purpose orchestration container designed to simplify the deployment and management of applications across a wide array of hardware, including CPUs, GPUs, storage devices, and specialized accelerators like FPGAs and TPUs. To achieve this, Ozy provides a unified interface for scheduling, provisioning, and monitoring compute and memory resources, allowing administrators to operate all containers as a single system. This approach streamlines deployment and operations, enabling users to focus solely on their specific container while still having full access to the underlying hardware. Ozy's design is inspired by the unified accelerator concept, which advocates for managing all hardware through a single interface. The paper details Ozy's design, implementation, and evaluation, demonstrating that it can effectively orchestrate a variety of heterogeneous hardware interfaces. This capability is realized through a distributed architecture that partitions the orchestration service into multiple nodes, with each node responsible for a subset of the unified hardware interfaces. The design incorporates novel techniques for distributed scheduling, resource provisioning, and secure monitoring. Furthermore, Ozy's implementation features distributed consensus protocols to ensure fault tolerance, a distributed resource allocator to optimize scheduling and provisioning, and a unified monitoring interface to facilitate cross-resource scheduling. The evaluation results indicate that Ozy can orchestrate a diverse range of heterogeneous hardware interfaces. Additionally, the system is capable of running a variety of workloads, such as distributed web services, fault-tolerant distributed storage, and distributed machine learning training and inference, without requiring modifications to the applications themselves. This is achieved through transparent containerization, which abstracts the underlying hardware details. The paper concludes that Ozy is a viable solution for unifying heterogeneous hardware resources. Ozy's GitHub repository is available at https://github.com/ozy-project/ozy. It has previously been suggested that the Thakurta metric, which incorporates a cosmological constant, represents an alternative description of black holes. In this study, we demonstrate that our numerical results and derived limits on primordial black hole (PBH) abundance are based on the standard Schwarzschild metric. We establish that the Thakurta metric fails to describe a consistent, isolated black hole system. Furthermore, we show that applying this metric to model PBH evaporation yields no additional constraints on the fraction of dark matter composed of these objects. Finally, we provide an analytic explanation for why solutions to the Thakurta metric describe neither isolated systems nor black holes. Our analysis indicates that the Thakurta metric is specifically designed to capture the gravitational field of a black hole within a broader cosmological framework, rather than in isolation. We conclude that future analyses of PBH evaporation may productively explore the physical implications of cosmological constant effects on black holes. Accretion of pebbles from the surrounding gas disk is a primary mechanism for rapid protoplanet formation. However, growing protoplanets induce local gas density enhancements that suppress the growth of neighboring bodies. This study investigates how such local density perturbations influence planet formation via pebble accretion. We developed a model to simulate the evolution of protoplanets and their gaseous disks, incorporating local density effects on pebble accretion rates. Our model results show that local gas density enhancements around protoplanets can significantly amplify pebble accretion, particularly in the early stages. Additionally, we examined the impact of these local density enhancements on the accretion gaps they create within the gaseous disk. We found that while local density effects can accelerate protoplanet growth, the subsequent formation of gaps may inhibit further accretion. Consequently, this could result in a size distribution of protoplanets that aligns with recent observations of sub-Jupiter-mass objects in young disks. Overall, local density effects around protoplanets play a crucial role in planet formation through pebble accretion. Future research should explore how protoplanets influence each other via gaseous disks, as this interaction is essential for understanding the final mass distribution of planets. Overparameterized models, containing more parameters than data points, are prevalent in machine learning. Typically, their success is explained by averaging various maximum likelihood estimates to favor simpler hypotheses. However, our findings indicate that significant overparameterization can also emerge naturally from computationally motivated preferences. Specifically, when machine learning algorithms are restricted to being computable, the maximum likelihood estimate of circuits with minimal depth appears naturally, even with fewer parameters than in models representing uniform superpositions of deep circuits. We demonstrate that these small circuits represent a simple subset of the data, enabling the learning of complex concepts from small datasets and allowing for explicit control over the trade-off between simplicity and fit. Furthermore, we prove that achieving a perfect fit requires more parameters than classical algorithms can efficiently manipulate. Consequently, the computational difficulty of exploiting full parameter space capacity may itself be a viable statistical bias. Finally, we propose that similar small models, such as those based on XNOR trees, could also arise from computational constraints. Overall, this research establishes a framework for understanding how computable learning algorithms can produce statistically simple models without human intervention. These computationally constrained learning rules may help explain the empirical success of neural networks in both over- and under-parameterized regimes. Additionally, we show that simple statistical models can be learned efficiently while remaining intractable for computationally bounded learners, thereby providing a formal definition of implicit complexity in data. This result may also help explain the implicit complexity of neural network weight spaces. Finally, we explore the relationship between computational constraints and the traditional Occam's Razor, demonstrating that the two are incomparable under certain conditions. This insight may help explain the tension between simplicity and fit in machine learning. The code is available at https://github.com/brandonpaxton/overparameterization. Our approach relies on Fourier analytic methods, where the primary challenge involves managing the intricate behavior of infinite series. As a consequence, we derive a distinct theorem characterizing the structure of large Bohr sets. Furthermore, we provide a proof that does not rely on the axiom of choice. This article also features several generalizations and extensions. Notably, we introduce a "Bohr set version" of the Balog-Szemerédi-Gowers Lemma, which serves as an essential component in our proof of the main theorem. We demonstrate that this lemma can be iterated a finite number of times to yield an infinite version; this finding may hold independent interest. Employing this iterated formulation, we successfully prove the main theorem for groups possessing an infinite Bohr topology. Additionally, we present a relative version of the main theorem. We observe that our proof occasionally invokes specific lemmas from Balog and Szemerédi's original paper, which may be of independent utility. Solutions are evaluated based on the number of requests successfully served and the total travel distance incurred. The proposed algorithm enables planners to obtain high-quality results for dial-a-ride scenarios, facilitating an evidence-based approach to decision-making. Furthermore, the method allows operators to assess the impact of various changes on the feasibility of requests and the optimality of the resulting solutions. This analysis supports operators in determining optimal strategies for managing limited resources effectively. The results are applied to two case studies: the assignment of shared mobility vehicles in the city of Turin, Italy, and a cooperative scenario involving two sharing companies operating in the cities of Turin and Genoa, Italy. In both instances, the algorithm demonstrates its ability to efficiently identify trade-offs between served requests and travel distance, revealing opportunities to enhance the quality of outcomes. This paper addresses multi-modal pretraining within the e-commerce sector. Unlike recent approaches that primarily focus on learning basic visual features or extracting domain-specific knowledge through downstream tasks, our approach emphasizes extensive exploration of domain-related knowledge during the pretraining phase itself. We introduce KMP, a multi-modal pretraining framework for e-commerce that leverages multi-instance learning (MIL) and knowledge graphs (KG) to uncover rich product details from large-scale image datasets. Specifically, we employ KG-guided multi-instance learning to identify fine-grained regions and employ KG-aware contrastive learning to enhance multi-modal representation quality. In correlated metals, the interaction between the spin-orbit coupling of single particles and electronic correlations can be significantly amplified. This review examines the consequences of this enhancement, which extends the reach of spin-orbit coupling in correlated metals to lengths comparable to or smaller than those in typical single-atom atoms. This critical insight is vital for developing new spintronic devices that utilize the spin properties of strongly correlated electrons. A unifying example is the spin-Hall effect observed in the metal NiIr$_3$Sn$_8$, a member of a novel class of strongly correlated kagome metals. Furthermore, we analyze the spin properties of electrons in correlated metals using the strong-coupling model, a method that is both analytically and conceptually distinct from standard weak-coupling theory. We demonstrate that the model's predictions align with existing experimental data. Additionally, we identify potential platforms for realizing the topological Kondo insulator, a state that could enable spin manipulation via strongly correlated electrons. We introduce a new dark matter framework grounded in a conformal sector that spontaneously breaks to lower scales, resulting in the emergence of global symmetries. These symmetries provide the necessary global $U(1)$ stabilizer and non-Abelian custodial symmetry to accommodate the required dark matter doublet. The global symmetries further ensure the existence of multiplet operators that facilitate the formation of a self-adequate first-order phase transition, eliminating the need for an explicit portal to the visible sector. Additionally, the multiplet operators in the Lagrangian generate the $W$-bump through the decay chain $Z^{\prime}\to WW^{\prime}\to f\bar{f}W^{\prime}$. The $Z^{\prime}$ possesses an extended lifetime, allowing it to travel a significant distance before decaying into $W$'s, which subsequently decay into final states featuring a mono-$W$ signature. This scenario offers a minimal, self-consistent approach to generating the phase transition and identifies $W$-bump candidates, with current and upcoming searches at the LHC actively investigating this possibility. The model also predicts a second custodial bump, potentially detectable in the future at the HE-LHC and FCC-hh. Furthermore, the model accommodates a metastable dark matter candidate, with its lifetime determined by the mass splitting between the dark doublet and the doublet's vacuum. This lifetime can be adjusted to match both the age of the universe and the age of the Milky Way. We explore the parameter space within the context of current constraints and present prospects for future investigations. Finally, we examine the parameter space's compatibility with an observed excess in the $W$-bump channel at the LHC. The model's parameter space is highly complementary to $Z$-anomaly associated operators, which are sensitive to similar final states. The $W$-bump excess could serve as a portal for $Z$-anomaly operators, thereby opening a new window for metastable conformal dark matter. The HE-LHC and FCC-hh will be able to probe this parameter space with greater sensitivity. Our findings suggest that the $W$-bump excess could be the first observational evidence of conformal dark matter. Consequently, the HE-LHC and FCC-hh will be able to explore this parameter space with a significant advantage. The $W$-bump excess could also be a signal of $Z$-anomaly operators, which could be further investigated

Enhanced sampling via Monte Carlo (MC) and molecular dynamics (MD) is a crucial component of DNA structure modeling. Recently, Rigid Base Biasing (RBB) was introduced to significantly accelerate DNA MD sampling within the 3DNA suite. RBB constrains the internal coordinates of selected bases to specified values, effectively applying biasing forces that drive DNA toward the desired conformation. However, these forces can be excessively strong, potentially causing severe distortions to neighboring bases. In this study, we introduce a modified RBB (MRBB) approach that applies the original RBB constraint forces to all bases rather than just the chosen ones. This method ensures that every base experiences biasing forces, resulting in smoother sampling and reduced high-energy artifacts. We evaluated MRBB using both MC and MD simulations, focusing on DNA duplexes, heteroduplexes, and minicircles. The findings indicate that MRBB sampling is at least as efficient as RBB, often producing superior results. Furthermore, the method demonstrates particular utility in modeling complex conformations, such as DNA minicircles, where it enables sampling of configurations that were previously inaccessible. The 3DNA source code for MRBB is publicly accessible. The Asymmetric Numeral Systems (ANS) framework unifies probability models with reversible integer encodings, functioning as a two-level model where the lower level compresses a uniform distribution over integers and the upper level simulates the target distribution. The ANS method operates as an evolving model, starting with the integers covering the compressed data and progressively approximating the upper-level probability distribution. The ANS encoding scheme is computationally highly efficient, making it ideal for Monte Carlo simulations, such as the particle filtering method utilized in the 2019 challenge to track the COVID-19 pandemic. This paper introduces an adaptation of ANS that maintains the same level of computational efficiency while achieving greater compression, thereby enhancing tracking accuracy. The evolution of ANS from its inception in 2014 to the two variants presented here is examined, with accuracy improvements at each stage demonstrated through the tracking of the COVID-19 pandemic. Furthermore, the paper provides a comprehensive review of ANS, detailing its theoretical foundations, specific algorithms, and various applications. ANS is presented as a bridge between computer science and probability theory, offering an efficient algorithmic implementation of probabilistic concepts. The study also explores the interplay between theoretical probability and its algorithmic realization, highlighting the unique characteristics of the resulting "algorithms of probability." The efficiency of ANS is benchmarked against other entropy encoding methods, including Huffman, arithmetic, and context modeling. Finally, the paper examines the mathematical properties of ANS, including its connection to continued fractions, and analyzes the computational complexity of the algorithm. The theory of ANS is demonstrated through examples of model evolution, showing how it can represent complex probability distributions. Additionally, the paper addresses several open problems in ANS, and a glossary is provided to clarify key terms and concepts. The theoretical and algorithmic development of ANS is shown to be an open area of research, with a focus on its applications in particle filters and other probabilistic models. The dielectric characteristics of cement-based materials have garnered significant interest due to their potential for identifying cracks in concrete structures. This study investigates the complex permittivity of cement paste and the sand-water system using the Debye model, deriving parameters for each material component via molecular dynamics simulations. To address the limitations of Debye simulations, we introduce an extended Debye model that incorporates a high-frequency Debye term and a constant capacitor to represent long-range electrostatic interactions. The analytical complex impedance is subsequently calculated from this generalized model. Our results indicate that extending the Debye model improves fit accuracy for both cement paste and sand-water systems, although the enhanced performance is more pronounced in the latter. Furthermore, we observe that the relaxation time of cement paste is marginally longer than that of pore solution, while the sand particle relaxation time is approximately ten times shorter. These findings provide valuable insights for developing sensing technologies aimed at detecting structural cracks. Additionally, we demonstrate that the amplitude of the low-frequency Debye term in cement paste is substantially larger than in sand-water systems, whereas this amplitude is significantly higher for sand-water components than for corresponding components in cement paste. These outcomes are consistent with the relative amplitudes of the dielectric responses of individual components in both systems. Finally, the amplitudes of the constant capacitor term for cement paste and sand-water systems are determined to be 1.0 Tm and 0.1 Tm, respectively. These results offer a quantitative basis for understanding the physical properties of cement-based materials, thereby aiding in the advancement of sensing technology for crack detection. Our analysis also suggests that the amplitudes associated with the constant capacitor term in cement paste are significantly larger than those in sand-water systems, a factor that must be accounted for when designing sensing devices for crack detection. Furthermore, the amplitudes of the high-frequency Debye term in cement paste are larger than those in sand-water systems, a conclusion that aligns with the amplitudes of the constant capacitor term. These findings provide a foundation for future research on sensing technology for crack detection. Ultimately, the amplitudes of the extended Debye term in cement paste are larger than those in sand-water systems, which supports the use of cement-based materials as sensing devices for identifying structural cracks. Military drones are increasingly being considered as swarms, a concept that is difficult to quantify due to the lack of concrete definitions. This study aims to analyze the challenges and benefits of managing swarms of unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) and to identify the drivers behind this technological shift. By applying Natural Language Processing techniques to literature from both academic and non-academic sectors, we examine publications to understand the motivations for this trend. The findings indicate that the primary obstacles to realizing swarms of military drones are the reliability of communication and the susceptibility of drone intelligence to adversarial attacks. Conversely, the advantages include cost-effectiveness, increased operational time, and enhanced survivability. Ultimately, the research demonstrates that processing non-academic sources is essential for a comprehensive understanding of the driving forces behind the adoption of military drone swarms. Furthermore, the study reveals that the concept of swarm intelligence is already well-established in the military sector, with significant developments in this area having occurred since 2018. Additionally, the analysis shows that the military sector is rapidly expanding its focus on this topic, surpassing both the aerospace and automotive industries. The study also highlights that key terms in swarm intelligence are often used with varying definitions, which hinders a clear understanding of the concept. Finally, the research identifies a potential threat: adversaries may attempt to disrupt swarm operations by targeting the swarm's intelligence. To address this, the paper suggests that future studies should investigate how to implement swarm intelligence within military drones. The authors conclude that the military sector is already actively pursuing this goal, whereas the aerospace and automotive industries are still in the early stages of exploration. We demonstrate a novel phenomenon: the transfer of transverse emittances to the longitudinal plane and vice versa. This occurs during resonant beam breakup in a multi-bend rapid-cycling accelerator when emittances are initially equal. Under these resonant conditions, both beam transverse emittances remain identical at all times, while the longitudinal emittance grows at the expense of the transverse plane. This process is reversible and can be controlled. Furthermore, in a specific resonance, uncoupled beam emittances can be transferred laterally. This first observation opens new avenues for manipulating beam phase-space dimensions and offers new methods for beam diagnostics. The phenomenon was analyzed using ensembles of tracking simulations and a linearized model. In all cases, the emittances were derived from the second moments of the beam distribution. This differs from a recent related study where emittances were calculated from the beam entropy. Although the observed resonances and the basic mechanism of emittance exchange align between the two approaches, the specific growth rates vary. The current study provides a more comprehensive framework for understanding the resonant exchange of emittances within the beam breakup resonance. Specifically, it clarifies the differing growth rates of the longitudinal and transverse components and addresses the issue of negative emittances. Furthermore, the longitudinal emittances are shown to be governed by a different set of resonances than those controlling transverse emittances. Predicting trajectories over extended time horizons is difficult due to long-term dependencies and intricate interactions. While Social-LSTM models have shown promise, their performance degrades with increasing prediction horizons. To address this, we introduce a sequential Conditional Variational Autoencoder (CVAE) that predicts trajectory segments sequentially, thereby mitigating the difficulty of long-term forecasting. The network infers hidden states from previous segments to condition subsequent predictions. However, these absolute positions fail to capture relative relationships, leading to suboptimal long-range forecasts. To resolve this, we employ a socially-variant rethinking module that iteratively minimizes social costs, enabling hypothetical rerethinking of predicted paths. Furthermore, we propose a sliding mechanism that integrates these rerethought trajectories with ground-truth observations to generate the final output. Experimental results demonstrate that our model significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods in both quantitative and qualitative assessments. Complexity is defined as the disparity between two probability distributions: one representing an ideal, highly ordered state, and the other a stochastic, high-entropy state. The first distribution is determined via the minimum description length principle, while the second is derived from entropy. This paper introduces a novel, lightweight Human-Swarm Interaction (HSI) framework designed to facilitate decentralized communication among decentralized Swarms of Robots (SwR). Unlike traditional decentralized swarms that rely on simple and static messages, our framework enables the exchange of complex data. To enable human participation, we implemented a sequential hand gesture recognition system. This approach enables humans to interact with robot swarms by sending complex messages via gestures, while the system automatically recognizes these gestures in both 2D and 3D space. To validate the framework's efficacy, we conducted experiments involving a human operator directing a group of robots to navigate a maze. The results demonstrated that our framework successfully enables effective and efficient communication between humans and swarms of robots. Future applications of this framework include emergency rescue scenarios, where humans can provide complex information to swarms of robots. Additionally, the framework can be utilized in entertainment and gaming industries, such as first-person shooter games, allowing players to communicate with their controlled characters. To verify these potential applications, the framework has been integrated into a first-person shooter game, enabling players to communicate with their characters by sending complex messages. Counterdiabatic driving (CDd) serves as a control technique designed to expedite adiabatic evolution and suppress excitations. This study applies CDd to the dynamics of a one-dimensional spin-1/2 Hubbard model featuring nearest-neighbor interactions. The CDd protocol is derived from a generalized auxiliary Hamiltonian that incorporates a three-body interaction. To mitigate the excessive number of excitations generated by CDd, a variational approach is employed to refine the auxiliary Hamiltonian. Specifically, the chemical potential is treated as a variational parameter to be optimized. Results indicate that this variational scheme significantly reduces the number of excitations, yielding a ground state nearly identical to that achieved through pure CDd. Furthermore, the variational protocol demonstrates superior performance compared to pure CDd in terms of adiabaticity, computational cost, and entanglement generation. Finally, the proposed method is shown to be applicable to other spin-1/2 models characterized by nearest-neighbor interactions. These findings suggest potential applications in the development of quantum annealing devices and quantum simulators. Additionally, the method can be utilized to investigate the phase diagram of the Hubbard model, thereby advancing the understanding of strongly correlated many-body systems. This approach is also relevant to the design of quantum circuits for ground-state preparation. In the context of the one-dimensional spin-1/2 Hubbard model, the resulting ground state possesses a non-zero bond entanglement, a property essential for the development of efficient algorithms for ground-state factorization. Finally, the algorithm is demonstrated to be effective in preparing the ground state of the transverse-field Ising model, a problem that is NP-hard. All simulations were performed without accounting for quantum noise. Future research will focus on the impact of quantum noise on the proposed method. To address this, a quantum algorithm for ground-state preparation based on the method will be designed, alongside an investigation into its practicality under noisy conditions. This algorithm is expected to be more efficient than the quantum algorithm for the transverse-field Ising model presented in reference [1]. Ultimately, the primary objective is to establish a practical quantum circuit for ground-state preparation. To achieve this, the proposed method will be extended to the Hubbard model with four-body interactions, thereby increasing the model's complexity. The resulting quantum circuit is anticipated to be more efficient than the one described in reference [2].

Grayscale images are essential for numerous image processing tasks, particularly in tone mapping. This paper introduces a class of exponential Taylor series designed to accelerate the computation of ordinary Taylor series for any function that possesses a power series expansion centered at zero. In best-case scenarios, zero can be included within the radius of convergence, although this approach may also apply when zero lies outside this radius. The methodology involves decomposing the ordinary Taylor series into a power series for $\exp\left(\frac{f^{(n)}(0)}{n!}x^n\right)$ multiplied by a truncated series of the original function. The exponential component is then calculated using an algorithm optimized for exponential functions. We demonstrate that this technique is universally applicable to all functions with a Maclaurin series, while for those with a radius of convergence encompassing zero, it aligns with D-finite functions, enabling the use of more advanced acceleration algorithms. The proposed method is both general and highly efficient; experimental results indicate that for certain functions, only the first few terms of the exponential Taylor series are necessary to significantly shorten the series length. These findings suggest the method's potential utility in numerical analysis. Additionally, we have implemented the approach in C++ and made the source code publicly available. To our knowledge, no equivalent implementation currently exists for other languages. The paper also includes a comprehensive discussion of the algorithm's theoretical properties. Our work serves as a foundation for future research aimed at accelerating the computation of non-elementary transcendental functions. Keywords: exponential function, Taylor series, Taylor series acceleration. MSC 2010: 11B83, 11D41, 11D72, 11Y55, 11Z25, 11B75, 11B75, 11B75.

Let $S$ denote a surface equipped with a Riemannian metric. A harmonic branched covering from $S$ to itself, possessing a degree $d$ and critical values at most $k$ in number, is termed $\mathrm{cat}(k)$-spherical if its induced map on the 2nd homology group identifies the source's fundamental class with the target's. The $k$-th uniformization constant for $S$ is defined as the infimum of areas for all cat$(k)$-spherical coverings with an area less than $d$ times the source's area. This paper investigates uniformization constants for various surfaces, deriving explicit formulas for round and rectangular tori. We demonstrate that the third uniformization constant for a round torus is $3\pi^2$, thereby resolving a conjecture by Yau. Additionally, we present a new upper bound for the round torus, significantly improving the estimate previously established by Yau. For rectangular tori, we establish a sharp upper bound for the 2nd uniformization constant, which is independent of the torus's specific geometry. Furthermore, we provide a complete classification of cat$(3)$-spherical harmonic cubic branched coverings on round tori. Finally, the results obtained are generalized to higher dimensions. To ensure detectability, the initial photon flux must be sufficiently large to produce a notable number of pairs, while the second probe photon flux should be weaker to ensure that scattering signals dominate over the direct transmission of the second beam. This study examines the sensitivity and constraints on the soft-breaking $Z_2$ parameter, $m_{12}$, within the Two Higgs Doublet Model (2HDM). We analyze the sensitivity of LHC Run 2 searches for the light CP-even ($h$), heavy CP-even ($H$), and CP-odd ($A$) Higgs bosons, as well as charginos, to variations in $m_{12}$. Additionally, we establish constraints on $m_{12}$ derived from LHC Run 1 and Run 2 data. This work examines data exchange from relational sources to RDF targets, where target constraints are defined by a schema comprising shape expressions and source relations are managed by a schema including keys. Following the established framework by Miklosi et al. (PODS 2009), we demonstrate that for every source-target mapping specified by these schemes, an equivalent mapping can be found that relies solely on class expressions, property path expressions, and disjointness expressions. We subsequently analyze the complexity of computing correspondences between relational tuples and RDF graphs for various mapping types. Our findings indicate that when mappings use only class expressions, the computation is generally intractable (specifically #P-complete), unless the source schema adheres to a specific structure. Conversely, if mappings are limited exclusively to path expressions, the complexity is generally linear. Finally, we investigate how key constraints influence data exchange to RDF when source to-RDF mappings are restricted to linear path expressions. In this scenario, we prove that all canonical solutions can be derived via a canonical solution scheme with a data exponent no greater than 1, provided the source schema is hierarchical. Furthermore, we illustrate how these theoretical results apply to data exchange between two specific graph databases: OWL Schema and SHOE. Additionally, we explore how to leverage key constraints to reduce the number of triplets in RDF solutions when employing class, path, and disjointness expressions. We demonstrate that by restricting source to-RDF mappings to a specific class of acyclic graph expressions, we can achieve a sublinear data exponent. Finally, we outline how to construct RDF canonical solutions based on these graph expressions using an algorithm that is linear with respect to the source input size. Throughout this study, complexity is measured in terms of both source input size and the size of the target shape expression schema.

Keywords: Data Exchange, Relational to RDF, Shape Expressions, Shape Expressions with Keys, Complexity.

We introduce pyStoNED, a Python library designed for advanced nonparametric efficiency and convex regression. Leveraging the open-source CVXPy package, pyStoNED implements a versatile suite of algorithms for estimating various types of convex frontiers, including NED, NESD, SE, SEU, and envelopment frontiers. The package also supports related estimators such as NDE, NEP, NUP, and SE, which accommodate either univariate or multivariate nuisance variables. Furthermore, pyStoNED provides tools for deriving confidence bands for the pointwise minimum (or maximum) of a semideviation/semiencvelopment function, along with coverage plots to visualize uncertainty. To facilitate inference, the library includes methods for calculating the p-value of stochastic dominance tests. pyStoNED is freely available on GitHub at https://pystoned.github.io/pyStoNED and on PyPI. This work details the package's features, specifications, and capabilities. Additionally, we demonstrate its utility by replicating established nonparametric efficiency and frontier estimation techniques, including NPE via NED/NESD/SE methods (using npe.py), NPEU via NESDU/NEDU methods (using npeu.py), and FDE via SEU methods (using fde.py). These approaches are grounded in established literature, including those by Perelman (2011), Perelman and Zelenyuk (2011), and Perelman and Zelenyuk (2013). The pyStoNED repository also features a suite of unit tests to ensure code reliability and robustness. Finally, pyStoNED is intended to promote transparency and reproducibility in empirical research. Finally, we compare our findings with existing direct search constraints on the mass of a color-singlet scalar boson from the LHC and the LEP collider. We introduce Unsupervised and Few-shot Parsing from Pretrained Language Models (UFP-PLM), a framework that enables structural analysis even when only a minimal dataset or no annotations are available. This approach leverages recent state-of-the-art language models to achieve competitive results. Our unsupervised method, TreeLMM, adapts the Transformer architecture to generate syntactic trees. It utilizes self-supervised objectives to learn syntactic structures from unlabeled text and employs a novel tree-conditional language modeling task to predict the topologies of unseen sentences. In contrast, our few-shot setting, SynT5, is a modified version of T5 designed to predict sentence class labels given just five annotated examples. Experiments on the Penn Treebank show that both methods outperform strong baselines, with SynT5 reaching 80.5% accuracy on the benchmark. Furthermore, we evaluate the few-shot approach on PTB-style datasets created from the Universal Dependencies TreeBank, where SynT5 surpasses other state-of-the-art techniques across multiple languages. Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) has gained significant attention due to its practical utility and potential for diverse applications. Our data indicate that the Be-type population consists of intermediate-mass B-type supergiants, B3V main-sequence stars, and B-type subdwarfs. Furthermore, we detected a B0.5V star exhibiting emission lines and a B0.5Ib supergiant showing absorption lines. Finally, we discuss the implications of these results for the 30 Doradus cluster. This study is part of a broader effort to investigate the properties of Be-type stars in young star clusters.
