Aspect-based sentiment analysis focuses on determining the sentiment polarity of specific aspects within product reviews. However, identifying the relevant aspects and their corresponding sentiments remains a significant challenge in current research. Although recent approaches have leveraged aspect embeddings to mitigate this issue, they predominantly depend on the availability of external aspect labels. To address the scarcity of such labels, we introduce a pre-training strategy that generates supervised aspect embeddings by first isolating potentially relevant aspects and subsequently modeling the relationships between them and the review context. This pre-trained model is then applied to the final sentiment analysis task. Our method achieves state-of-the-art performance on the SemEval 2014 benchmark for aspect-based sentiment analysis. Mediation analysis serves as a vital tool for elucidating the pathways through which an exposure influences an outcome, yet standard methods often fail to account for sampling strategies like case-control designs. This study introduces a flexible mediation framework that accommodates both full and partial case-control sampling. Within this design, we examine an identification region for the interaction parameter between a binary exposure and a binary mediator on a general outcome, specifically under an additive logistic model. We demonstrate that the conditional mean of the mediator on the exposure remains unidentified in case-control settings; consequently, we propose a reweighting strategy to rectify this. Furthermore, we develop an estimation procedure for the exposure-mediator-interaction parameter and its confidence interval. Through simulation studies, we evaluate the performance of this approach regarding coverage probability and bias. Additionally, we apply the proposed method to data from the Women's Health Initiative to explore the pathway from obesity to postmenopausal breast cancer risk via estrogen levels. In this context, we illustrate how the method can be adapted to handle scenarios where the mediator is measured with error. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/SebastianKlein1990/MediationDesign. The statistical package `MediationDesign` is available on CRAN. Furthermore, we have created a user-friendly web application, `MediationCalculator`, accessible at https://mediationcalculator.app. This calculator enables users to visualize the identification region for the exposure-mediator-interaction parameter and obtain point estimates for this region under various sampling designs. Users can also view the coverage probability of the 95% confidence interval and the bias associated with standard mediation methods. A detailed tutorial is available at https://mediationcalculator.app/tutorial. The underlying code for the application can be found at https://github.com/SebastianKlein1990/MediationCalculator. This study examines a secure, multi-user radio over Gaussian channel where an RIS-assisted base station (BS) transmits to multiple users and multiple eavesdroppers. Accounting for hardware imperfections at the BS and reflecting element errors on the RIS, the goal is to maximize the sum secure rates of all users by jointly optimizing the BS's transmit vector and the RIS's reflection vector. This optimization is subject to the RIS's power budget and the requirement that reflection elements be semi-unitary matrices. Since the channel is open, hardware impairments at the BS can introduce significant errors into channel state information (CSI), complicating estimation. To address this, an analytical derivation of the upper bound for the total estimation error is provided, and the problem is reformulated into two subproblems. A hybrid algorithm combining the interior point method and the block coordinate descent method is proposed to solve these subproblems. Furthermore, a suboptimal algorithm utilizing a two-stage least squares approach is developed to reduce computational complexity. Numerical results demonstrate that the proposed algorithms outperform existing schemes in terms of performance. Additionally, it is observed that secure communication benefits from the presence of hardware impairments, as they introduce errors into the users' CSI that eavesdroppers do not possess. Finally, the study analyzes the asymptotic behavior of the proposed algorithms. In summary, this work offers a theoretical and practical framework for designing secure RIS-assisted radio over Gaussian channels despite hardware impairments. The proposed algorithms are computationally efficient and achieve near-optimal performance, making them suitable for real-world deployment. This research paves the way for developing secure RIS-assisted wireless systems in practical environments where hardware impairments are inevitable. We introduce Executive Function (EF), a contrastive value policy designed to re-sample and re-label an agent's perceptions through hindsight summarization. This approach enables the agent to learn from simulated or cached world states, facilitating unsupervised skill discovery, curriculum generation, and reinforcement learning from demonstration. Unlike traditional methods that rely on the temporal difference (TD) error for policy updates, EF contrasts a perception against the hindsight summaries of its successor perceptions to derive an EF value signal. Consequently, this value function approximates the count of reachable hindsight goals from a given state, guiding the agent to resume from the current perception along a path toward a reachable skill. Empirical results demonstrate that EF successfully uncovers multiple skills during unsupervised exploration, optimally designs a curriculum from a fixed set of perceptions, and learns from a few-shot demonstrations with superior sample efficiency. Furthermore, when integrated with Deep Deterministic Policy Gradient (DDPG), EF achieves performance comparable to TD-learning baselines using up to 10 times fewer samples. We anticipate that EF will serve as a versatile, perception-level module, seamlessly integrating with various existing algorithms to facilitate skill discovery, curriculum design, and demonstration learning. Our code, pre-trained models, and experiments are publicly available at https://github.com/ChenYi2020/Executive-Function. Finally, we hope that EF will inspire further research into the perception-level design of intelligent agents.

Assuming Rabi coupling remains constant, the findings indicate that, under typical conditions, the Rabi coupling mechanism effectively transmits the centrifugal term to negative parity scissors modes, resulting in their moments of inertia being approximately twice as large as those of corresponding positive parity states. Furthermore, the study demonstrates that the Rabi coupling between negative and positive parity scissors modes can be derived from the properties of these modes at zero excitation energy. Additionally, it is shown that the wave function overlap parameter can be accurately estimated using the normalized frequency separation between negative and positive parity scissors modes, provided the Rabi coupling is sufficiently weak. Finally, the model is applied to analyze experimental data for negative parity scissors modes in two isotopes of gadolinium. The results confirm that negative parity scissors modes in these isotopes exhibit significantly larger moments of inertia compared to their positive parity counterparts, a feature that the generalized Two-Rotors Model successfully explains. Inspired by finite volume schemes, we introduce a neural network approach grounded in cell averages. This method leverages conservation laws to construct the neural network framework, ensuring exact conservation within the discrete solution. Furthermore, the use of finite volume-based cell averages guarantees a numerical solution with a total variation bounded by that of the initial data. Consequently, this property prevents data oscillation, even when dealing with discontinuous or rough initial conditions. We rigorously prove that the proposed neural network method achieves first-order accuracy, provided the underlying finite volume scheme maintains first-order accuracy. Additionally, we demonstrate that if the finite volume scheme attains $k$-th order accuracy, the corresponding neural network method can reach $(k-1)$-th order accuracy. To validate these theoretical findings, we apply the proposed method to various finite volume schemes across several one-dimensional and two-dimensional test cases, including the Burgers equation, wave equation, heat equation, and the shallow water equations. The results confirm that the proposed method yields conservative solutions with no spurious oscillations. These outcomes underscore the method's potential utility for solving both hyperbolic and parabolic partial differential equations. Furthermore, numerical experiments reveal that the neural network-based algorithm converges rapidly, requiring fewer iterations compared to standard gradient descent optimization. The Unruh effect, which posits that uniform acceleration induces entanglement between future and past light cones, is notoriously difficult to observe due to the need to manipulate massive numbers of particles. This study demonstrates that the associated Berry phase can instead be detected through experiments involving ultracold atoms within engineered electromagnetic fields. These fields are constructed using a superposition of two specific components: one representing future and past light cones, and the other exhibiting rotational symmetry. The proposed scheme builds upon the method introduced by J. Zhang et al. (Phys. Rev. Lett. 123, 260403, 2019), utilizing atoms confined in a 1D optical lattice and subjected to a time-dependent geometric gauge field. The study analyzes the influence of various noise sources on the Berry phase and the corresponding entanglement entropy, accounting for both white and colored noise. Furthermore, the analysis addresses the impact of numerical errors inherent in the discrete approximation of the continuum acceleration field. Finally, the research evaluates the feasibility of the proposed scheme by leveraging existing experimental capabilities. The findings indicate that the scheme is viable, with the maximum deviation in the detected Berry phase remaining below 10%. Consequently, this work establishes a foundation for further investigations into the Unruh effect, the black hole information paradox, and related quantum phenomena. Additionally, the proposed approach may be applicable to other accelerating systems, such as those found in black holes and during cosmological expansion. Consequently, this work paves the way for additional research into various Unruh-like effects. Specifically, the scheme can be adapted to detect different forms of timelike entanglement, including those arising from the Unruh effect, Hawking radiation, and cosmological expansion. Such detections would enable a comprehensive understanding of these phenomena and their unification within quantum field theory in curved spacetime. In this context, it is essential to investigate how noise affects the detected Berry phase and entanglement entropy, as well as to explore the relationship between these quantities. This understanding is crucial for developing more efficient protocols to detect unifying characteristics of black holes and their information paradox. Ultimately, the proposed scheme may facilitate the development of more practical tools for detecting unifying features of black holes and their information paradox. This could lead to the discovery of new phenomena and deepen our understanding of gravity. Furthermore, the scheme may contribute to the unification of quantum mechanics and general relativity, thereby advancing our understanding of the fundamental nature of spacetime. Finally, the proposed approach may have applications beyond fundamental physics

Event extraction remains a difficult task, primarily because of the "open schema" challenge, where events can appear in an unlimited variety of types and instances. Furthermore, researchers have largely concentrated on extracting events from English, leaving other languages severely underexplored. This study introduces a novel method for identifying event arguments in other languages by first detecting the event type, followed by event argument extraction. We developed a new dataset for Chinese and Japanese, featuring 1,000 sentences drawn from Baidu and Nihon Keizai Shimbun, covering 25 distinct event types. To our knowledge, this is the inaugural public dataset dedicated to multilingual event extraction. We evaluated our model on both datasets, demonstrating that it significantly surpasses a baseline approach. Our code is accessible at: https://github.com/DeepSparsha/MEE. We invite researchers in natural language processing to participate in event extraction competitions on our newly launched platform: http://www.multilingualeventextraction.org. We anticipate that this method and dataset will facilitate multilingual analysis in various domains, including business, law, and journalism. We hope this work encourages greater interest in the field of event extraction. Finally, we look forward to advancing the frontiers of multilingual analysis through event extraction. This paper examines the universal characteristic forms of universally defined vector bundles on classifying spaces for formal groups over commutative rings. We establish positivity properties for these forms and derive generalizations of push-forward formulas originally proposed by Mumford. Leveraging these universal findings, we demonstrate several prominent conjectured positivity properties regarding characteristic forms of symmetric and quasi-symmetric classes, as well as their double negatives. Additionally, we verify a conjecture by Baker and Brown concerning the weak index conjecture for very ample line bundles on projective spaces. Finally, we outline several extensions of our methodology. This work serves as a foundational step toward a comprehensive push-forward theory within chromatic homotopy theory. Specifically, our universal results align with the push-forward theory anticipated by various researchers in this field. Furthermore, our universal double-negative push-forward aligns with a conjecture by Baker and Baker regarding universal characteristic classes for formal group laws, thereby substantiating their conjecture. This provides one of the most substantial independent validations to date for their universally defined very ample line bundles on projective spaces. Our universal push-forward also connects to a conjecture by Baker and Baker concerning universal characteristic forms for symmetric classes, offering strong evidence in support of that conjecture. Additionally, our universal quasi-symmetric push-forward appears to address a question posed by Baker and Lazarevic. Finally, our universal quasi-symmetric findings appear to confirm a conjecture by Baker and Baker regarding the weak index conjecture for very ample line bundles on projective spaces, extending their previous results within the ample cone. We conclude by presenting several extensions of our approach and verifying their consistency with various conjectures within the realm of chromatic homotopy theory. Our universal results thus offer valuable insights and direction for future research in this area. To facilitate this, we have structured the paper to be largely independent of the references it supports, thereby enhancing its accessibility and utility as a starting point for further inquiry. We anticipate that this work will serve as a valuable foundation for universal and chromatic homotopy topological research. The interaction between the accretion flow and the wind from the companion star in binary systems like Cyg X-1 remains a poorly understood area of X-ray astronomy. This study utilizes XMM-Newton data from Cyg X-1 in its hard state to examine how the companion star's wind influences the spectral and timing characteristics of the X-ray emission. We developed a new phenomenological model that incorporates the stellar wind's effects on both the continuum and line profiles within XIS spectra. Applying this model to the dataset reveals that the wind significantly impacts the observed spectral-timing properties, specifically the soft X-ray continuum, Fe K$\alpha$ emission, and the lag between soft and hard X-rays. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the companion star's wind can account for the observed increase in the soft-to-hard X-ray flux ratio and the associated changes in timing behavior as the accretion flow transitions from a wind-dominated to a non-wind-dominated regime. Consequently, our findings suggest that the stellar wind plays a crucial role in determining the spectral and timing properties of the hard state in Cyg X-1. These results also provide a framework for studying the impact of winds in other black hole binaries. Finally, we propose that future observations of Cyg X-1 during the non-wind and wind-dominated phases will offer valuable insights into the effects of the companion star's wind on its spectral and timing properties. This will ultimately aid in understanding the dynamics of the accretion flow and the wind from the companion star. This understanding is essential for predicting the behavior of future black hole and neutron star systems. This paper is part of a series of studies investigating the effects of the companion star's wind on the spectral and timing properties of Cyg X-1. This compromise stems from the necessity of creating a shared intermediate layer to fuse signals from both grammatical and lexical sources. We introduce an alternative approach that enables separate but interactive parsing of syntax and semantics, thereby accommodating both homogeneous and heterogeneous data. Specifically, we permit syntax and semantics to influence one another through a unified Poisson factor model. Empirical results demonstrate that our method achieves superior accuracy in joint syntactic and semantic parsing, attaining state-of-the-art F-scores on two independent benchmarks: the Universal Dependencies treebank and the ConceptNet 17 knowledge graph. Furthermore, our framework is compatible with a broad spectrum of alpha-dependent probabilistic factor models. By allowing syntax and semantics to interact conditionally within the same graph structure, this approach enhances interpretability and facilitates downstream conditional generation tasks. We also provide an open-implementation of the interactive joint parser. To our knowledge, this work represents the initial application of factor models to joint syntactic and semantic parsing. Additionally, it marks the first instance of utilizing interactive graph-based alpha-optimization for this purpose, as well as the first use of the Poisson factor model to jointly parse syntax and conditionally generate knowledge graphs. Finally, we present an extensive analysis of syntax-semantics interactions across various alphabets, factor models, and data configurations. The neutrino-dominated accretion flow (NDAF) is a magnetized neutrino-cooled disk surrounding the remnant black hole formed after a core-collapse supernova. This flow is a potential source for post-merger outflows, such as those in core-collapse supernovae and binary neutron star mergers. Outflows from NDAFs are driven by neutrino heating, magnetic reconnection, and general relativistic magnetohydrodynamic (GRMHD) jets. Outflows with low mass loss rates are expected to be adiabatic, whereas those with high mass loss rates are likely to be radiative. We utilized the GRMHD code \texttt{HARMRAD} to simulate post-merger outflows from magnetized NDAFs. Our results indicate that adiabatic outflows have lower mass loss rates than radiative ones. Furthermore, adiabatic outflows exhibit lower heating rates from neutrino heating and magnetic reconnection, resulting in lower energy fluxes. However, the Lorentz factor of adiabatic outflows is higher than that of radiative outflows. These findings suggest that the early-time, high-speed outflows observed in binary neutron star mergers may be adiabatic. Additionally, the radiative outflows predicted by our simulations may correspond to the high-energy X-ray flares seen in some core-collapse supernovae. Our results also imply that the high-energy X-ray flares in binary neutron star mergers may originate from the post-merger phase rather than the merger itself. We utilize the Hyper Suprime-Cam Subaru Strategic Program (HSC-SSP) to analyze the morphology of massive early-type galaxies (ETGs; $M_{Ks} < -24.5$ mag) across redshifts $0.01 \leq z \leq 0.7$. By employing HSC-SSP imaging alongside Hubble Space Telescope data, we identify tidal features linked to HSC-SSP galaxies and quantify their flux fractions. Our findings indicate that the flux fraction of these features declines as HSC-SSP galaxy luminosity increases, though this trend is not statistically significant. We observe a strong correlation between the flux fraction and the morphological classification of ETGs, where more irregular galaxies exhibit higher flux fractions. Furthermore, galaxies displaying prominent features are predominantly irregular. We also detect a significant relationship between the flux fraction and the specific star formation rate (sSFR) of ETGs, with more irregular galaxies showing larger flux fractions. Finally, we estimate the merger rates of massive ETGs by combining morphological and flux fraction data with Hubble-based dynamical models. These models suggest that irregular galaxies possess higher merger rates than regular ones, a result supported by our flux fraction and sSFR measurements. This evidence implies that irregular galaxies are the primary progenitors of current merging ETGs. Our results align with the hypothesis that irregular galaxies represent the end product of recent mergers, while regular galaxies may result from mergers occurring several Gyr ago. This study revises the previous paper, where we introduced a new gravitational theory. In that work, we derived the field equation from the modified principle of least action, incorporating a novel term with opposite sign and different sign dependence compared to the standard Poisson equation. This new term generates repulsive gravitational forces along the z-axis within the x-z plane of a coordinate system aligned with outflow symmetry axes. The magnitude of this effect scales with the square of the axis' linear mass density. In this current paper, we apply the derived field equation to model bipolar outflows, assuming them to be thin bipolar shells with azimuthal symmetry. This approach yields a new analytical solution to the field equation that aligns with observations. Furthermore, this gravitational law creates a stable region along the z-axis where the attractive and repulsive forces reach equilibrium. We demonstrate that the axis of the bipolar outflow aligns with the z-axis by showing that the velocity component parallel to it is negligible. Additionally, we prove that the attractive and repulsive gravitational forces are balanced at the center of the outflow along the z-axis, consistent with the observed symmetry of these structures. Finally, we provide evidence that bipolar outflows function as bipolar nozzles, exhibiting a convergent-divergent shape along the z-axis. We show that the shape of these nozzles is determined by the geometry of the flow surface, which is derived from the azimuthal symmetry of the bipolar outflow. This shape aligns with the observed bipolar nozzles in bipolar outflows. We also demonstrate that the nozzle shape is governed by the attractive and repulsive gravitational forces, alongside the pressure of the outflow material. Furthermore, we show that the nozzle shape can be modeled using a simplified version of the Bernoulli equation, which incorporates the attractive and repulsive gravitational forces. Finally, we illustrate that the velocity of the outflow increases as it moves away from the center, aligning with the observed acceleration in these outflows. Overall, the results indicate that these gravitational effects are essential for the formation of bipolar outflows. Additionally, we show that these novel gravitational effects can be derived from the modified principle of least action, which differs from the standard Poisson equation. This demonstrates that the proposed gravitational theory represents a new framework. We conclude that this theory offers a new perspective on gravitational theory. This study examines the optical emission from ten well-localized fast radio bursts (FRBs) that occurred between 2007 and 2021, utilizing new and archival data from the Canada-France-Hawaii Telescope (CFHT) and Las Campanas Observatory (LCO). The analysis reveals no significant radio-optical correlation in any well-localized FRB, with upper limits on radio-optical flux density ratios generally falling between $10^{-3}$ and $10^{-5}$. Furthermore, we establish upper limits on the optical luminosity of FRBs, ranging from $10^{29}$ to $10^{31}$ erg s$^{-1}$, which are approximately 100 times lower than the most stringent constraints previously reported. Additionally, we conducted a simultaneous and delayed photometric search for emission from the repeating FRB 20201124A using the CFHT and LCO. The simultaneous photometric search yielded no detection of optical emission from FRB 20201124A, with upper limits on its optical flux density varying from $10^{-9}$ to $10^{-7}$ erg s cm$^{-2}$. Finally, we analyzed the optical light curves of FRB 180916.J0307+62 and FRB 20201124A, finding no evidence of delayed optical emission. These results suggest that the emission mechanisms responsible for FRBs are not accompanied by copious optical radiation, whether simultaneously or with a short delay. The absence of delayed optical emission is particularly significant for constraining the contribution of magnetars to the FRB population. We conclude by discussing the implications of our findings for FRB emission models. Our results suggest that the magnetospheres of magnetars are unlikely to be the primary sites of FRB emission, as they would be expected to produce observable optical emission. Instead, the emission may arise from other sites, such as the inner light cylinder or the current sheet surrounding the neutron star. Our findings also constrain models in which the FRB population is dominated by young neutron stars, as these objects are expected to be optically bright. Overall, our results support the hypothesis that the FRB population is dominated by young neutron stars. High-power lasers are currently central to numerous scientific and industrial fields, including spectroscopy, photochemistry, laser surgery, and defense. Typically, these systems are expensive and complex, often involving multiple interdependent components. Consequently, the design and optimization of laser systems present significant challenges. This paper introduces a reverse-engineering framework utilizing a novel multi-objective optimization algorithm based on the Cuckoo Search method, which mimics the cuckoo bird's unique breeding habits. We apply this framework to optimize three laser systems: (i) a laser surgical system, (ii) a laser ranging system, and (iii) a laser ranging system derived from open-source code. The results demonstrate that our framework can effectively reverse-engineer laser system parameters from available data and optimize them using established algorithms. Furthermore, the framework is highly adaptable to other high-power laser systems, such as those employed in LIDAR applications. This flexibility stems from the framework's reliance on abstracted laser model parameters rather than system-specific details. Ultimately, we show that this framework can facilitate the design and optimization of high-power laser systems for various scientific and industrial purposes. The framework is now publicly available on GitHub. This work was conducted as part of the 2020 Summer Undergraduate Research Fellowship (SURF) at the University of Rochester. Although language models excel at processing visual data, their vision capabilities remain modular and isolated from their textual processing modules. This paper explores decoding-time visual control during pre-trained language model generation, introducing flexible mechanisms to adjust model outputs based on visual input. Specifically, we examine internal model features to manage how visual information influences text generation. We demonstrate that internal visual controls can be extracted and reused across different tasks and datasets. Furthermore, we present VL-Aware Selective Repeat (VL-SR), a proposed framework designed to enhance text generation quality and visual accuracy by leveraging internal model visual controls. Our research advances the decoding-time visual control of pre-trained language models and demonstrates that simple, efficient, and interpretable methods can significantly improve visual performance. We hope these findings encourage further investigation into the internal capabilities of vision-language models. Reproducible code and experimental results are available at: https://github.com/brandon-wu/INTERNAL-VCAP.

Our key contributions are as follows:
*   We demonstrate that internal model visual controls can effectively enhance performance on vision-language detection and captioning tasks.
*   We propose a straightforward yet effective method for achieving VL-SR, which enhances both text generation quality and visual accuracy.
*   We introduce VL-Interference, a new metric to assess the extent of internal visual controls within pre-trained vision-language models.
*   We present VL-Activation, a novel dataset for evaluating the internal visual controls of pre-trained vision-language models.
*   VL-SR enhances performance on Image Captioning datasets MS-COCO, Flickr30k, and MSCOCO-Val by 1.5%, 1.0%, and 1.1%, respectively.
*   VL-SR improves accuracy on the VL-Interference dataset across four datasets: Object Detection (ImageNet), Semantic Segmentation (ADE20K), Semantic Parsing (Visual Genome), and Visual Question Answering (VQA 2.0). We introduce Delegated RingCT, a novel ring signature and ring proof-of-knowledge framework designed to enhance the RingCT protocol for blockchain applications. This approach reduces both the size and count of group elements needed to validate memberhood in unknown rings, thereby accelerating ring verification. Additionally, we develop a corresponding ring signature scheme that maintains security as a proof-of-knowledge, enabling signature delegation and homomorphic operations while ensuring strong anonymity resistant to computation-limited adversaries. Experimental results demonstrate that our proposed ring signature scheme outperforms existing solutions by an order of magnitude. Furthermore, our theoretical analysis establishes that the lattice-based ring signature scheme relies on the security of the underlying signature scheme, with only minor modifications needed to extend this proof to other proof-of-knowledge properties, thereby ring-proving delegation and homomorphic capabilities against computational constraints. Finally, we implement a ringCT protocol using our proposed scheme on a blockchain, evaluating its performance and showing significant improvements over the current RingCT implementation. The code is publicly accessible on GitHub. Additionally, we detail how Delegated RingCT can be seamlessly integrated with MIMC to create a ringCT protocol with cryptographic agility. This integration allows for the easy substitution of cryptographic primitives, facilitating the migration to post-quantum ringCT or the adoption of alternative solutions to mitigate specific vulnerabilities. We also outline the necessary modifications to address the problem of pre-generated rings. Overall, Delegated RingCT offers a versatile solution for blockchain applications, providing flexibility in the choice of ring signature schemes. Future work will focus on addressing various open problems, such as enhancing transparency, minimizing trust assumptions, and strengthening security against malicious users. Specifically, we aim to strengthen the security proof by considering malicious actors who deviate from the protocol, such as block pruners who attempt to reconstruct secret keys by retaining all blocks from the chain. Additionally, we plan to improve the zero-knowledge proof component by utilizing Groth16 instead of SACSNIZK to achieve better verification times and more compact proof sizes. Finally, we intend to explore the application of zero-knowledge ringCT to solve the issue of pre-generated rings.
Keywords: RingCT, RingCT++, Ring signature, Ring proof-of-knowledge, Delegated ring signature, Cryptographic agility.

The paper presents a new method for determining beam emittance, specifically tune scans. It addresses a longstanding debate regarding the optimal scan strategy by suggesting a novel approach: the luminosity scan. This technique is applicable to any detector, though it is particularly advantageous for pixel detectors. The study includes a detailed explanation of the procedure and an illustrative example utilizing ATLAS's inner detector data. Additionally, numerical simulations were conducted to validate the proposed methods and to assess their performance under realistic conditions. The research concludes that luminosity scans offer superior results compared to emittance measurements at both low and high statistics, as well as when accounting for realistic beam dynamics. Furthermore, it is demonstrated that specific emittance measurements can be derived from luminosity scans without loss of information, provided that certain assumptions are met. Finally, a detailed discussion explores the implications of these assumptions. Overall, this work establishes a foundation for the development of advanced beam diagnostic techniques. The presented methods are broadly applicable to all colliding machine experiments. Furthermore, the authors propose that future studies should investigate the use of track density distributions from fine-grained pixel detectors to conduct luminosity scans, thereby enabling precise tracking of beam evolution along the collision season. This would facilitate fine-tuning for maximum luminosity and post-collision monitoring of performance degradation due to beam dynamics. Such an approach would enhance the efficiency of existing beam diagnostics. The paper ends by discussing potential challenges and outlining future research directions. Driven by the growing demand for interpretable, data-driven models in life sciences, this work leverages the inherent interpretability of linear regression to establish a new framework for sharing regression coefficients among collaborators. By formulating this as a multi-objective optimization problem, the study demonstrates how to balance the trade-off between the global data fit and the significance of individual coefficients. Furthermore, it outlines strategies for optimizing these coefficient values to serve either a local collaborator or to enhance the overall model quality driven by multiple contributors. Applications within a distributed setting are explored through a case study involving a distributed data association problem in wireless sensor networks. The results indicate that, under conditions of significant data heterogeneity, the proposed method can substantially improve the global objective function. Additionally, the authors observe that the final local objective function value for any collaborator is guaranteed to be at least as good as the value obtained by that collaborator independently. Finally, the study examines the relationship between the significance of individual coefficients and the local significance of the global objective function. Supported by these properties, the significance test for local optimality can be efficiently resolved as a linear program, thereby eliminating the need to solve additional non-convex problems for each collaborator. The paper concludes by demonstrating the efficient resolution of the local significance test using a wireless network case study. To our knowledge, this marks the first application of coefficient sharing in a distributed context. Overall, the proposed approach facilitates the solution of distributed regression problems without requiring the exchange of raw data, thus preserving data privacy. Furthermore, the framework is highly flexible, allowing for the consideration of various types of significance for both individual coefficients and local collaborators. Finally, the paper concludes by discussing the potential for extending this work to other regression methods, such as Lasso and Gaussian processes. Keywords: distributed data association, data sharing, interpretability, significance test, cooperative modeling, graph signal processing, graph neural networks.

This paper introduces AskewSGD, a novel algorithm designed to train deep neural networks using quantized weights. By employing a non-standard probability distribution for weight initialization, the method effectively mitigates quantization-induced skewness, thereby maintaining the independence of convolutional feature maps. This characteristic facilitates the application of the powerful cross-channel orthogonality constraint during optimization. Furthermore, the algorithm incorporates a new technique for handling the anisotropy of stochastic gradient descent by utilizing an interval constraint to enforce an unbiased gradient update. Numerical experiments confirm that AskewSGD enhances both the accuracy and stability of quantized neural networks during both training and inference. Additionally, results on various benchmarks demonstrate that quantized networks trained with AskewSGD can achieve performance comparable to that of their full-precision counterparts. Soft robots are gaining significant attention due to their ability to interact smoothly with complex environments, adapt to deformable objects, and operate effectively under high static loads. Driven by the need for high performance, model-based control strategies offer a promising solution for achieving precise manipulation and dexterous handling. This strategy utilizes the inherent dynamics of the robot to design controllers that enhance performance. While model-based control has been extensively researched in rigid robotics, it remains an underexplored area for soft robots, where model development and advanced control techniques present unique challenges. This survey examines state-of-the-art model-based control methods for soft robots and identifies key challenges and future research directions. Specifically, we analyze various approaches for robot modeling, including continuum, finite element, and discrete methods. We then present an overview of model-based control strategies, highlighting techniques such as inverse kinematics, inverse dynamics, optimal control, and machine learning. Furthermore, we address critical issues related to sensing, actuation, and materials. Finally, we explore promising applications in soft robotics and highlight potential future advancements in model-based control. We conclude that model-based control will play an increasingly vital role in achieving the high performance required by many soft robot applications. The comprehensive literature list provided covers over 100 papers, offering valuable insights and a strong foundation for future research. Additionally, we have made our compiled data available to facilitate further exploration in the field. (Data access: https://github.com/ashishkumar1997/MBC-Soft-Robots). Our survey can be accessed at https://arxiv.org/abs/2201.06001. Given the rapid evolution of the field, we anticipate that many exciting new developments will emerge in the near future. We hope this survey serves as a valuable resource for advancing model-based control in soft robotics. This article is part of the T-RO Special Section on Soft Robotics. The real Jacobi group extends the affine line by incorporating a positive definite symmetric $2\times 2$ matrix. This paper examines the geometry of the real Jacobi quotient space, exploring various characteristics through the lens of functions defined on the line that rely on the matrix variable. We demonstrate the application of these functions in resolving boundary value problems associated with the wave equation. Furthermore, we establish an extension of Gindikin-Karpelevich formula and provide the boundary value formula for the Klein fourfold Green function. Finally, we derive an extension of the Schrödinger operator and examine the boundary conditions of the Klein-Fourier transform. Ultimately, we formulate and address a specific boundary value problem for the Klein-Fourier transform within the context of the real Jacobi quotient space. This formulation relies on a specific boundary value problem involving the Schrödinger operator, which we term the "real Jacobi problem." We anticipate that the methods and findings presented here will find applications in both physics and the solution of boundary value problems within the Schrödinger-Klein-Gordon framework. Additionally, we illustrate an application of real Jacobi quotients to a variational problem concerning functionals dependent on the Hessian matrix of their arguments. In this scenario, we derive an extension of the Euler-Lagrange equation and identify boundary conditions for the corresponding functional. We anticipate that this work will contribute to mathematical physics, mathematical economics, and various other fields. The paper is structured into five sections: the first three address fundamental properties of the real Jacobi quotient space, while the fourth section focuses on mathematical physics, and the fifth applies these concepts to a mathematical economics problem. This structure ensures that the results can be utilized in diverse applications. We acknowledge that this work serves as a foundation for further research in mathematical physics and economics. Consequently, we have intentionally omitted detailed proofs of certain claims, instead providing comprehensive references for readers interested in those specific aspects. We believe this approach is appropriate, as it aligns with the standard practice of citing foundational research in the relevant fields. We are confident that readers will appreciate this decision. We conclude by expressing our gratitude to all researchers in these diverse disciplines for their invaluable contributions. We trust that this work will inspire future applications of mathematical physics and economic theory. We look forward to your valuable feedback. Verifying facts using structured data is crucial for ensuring the credibility of information disseminated on social media. However, many statements are not directly tabular and require a translation step to identify the relevant source table. Furthermore, determining the specific tuple within that table necessary for verification remains an unmet challenge. To address these issues, we introduce a method for decomposing fact verification into subtasks: first, jointly predicting the appropriate table and a verifiable query, and second, confirming whether the statement is true based on the database information from the first step. Our subtask model demonstrates superior performance in both table selection and statement extraction compared to current baselines. Additionally, we show that combining our model with existing verification techniques yields significant improvements in verification accuracy. A complete implementation of our framework will be released on GitHub. The associated dataset, TabFact, can be accessed at https://cihangizt.github.io/tabfact/. This work appears in the Proceedings of the 58th Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics. This is the final version. Bayesian nested sampling is designed to simultaneously determine parameter estimates and assess their evidence. It achieves this by combining a prior sampler with a negative log-posterior function, utilizing nested sampling to explore the resulting nested posterior. The core mechanism involves iteratively drawing samples from a nested prior, progressively eliminating the lowest-energy samples, and calculating the evidence. However, the nested posterior often features complex geometry, making it difficult to sample from efficiently. To address this, various importance samplers have been introduced to sample from distributions approximating the nested posterior. This study evaluates several proposed methods, including the nested nested sampler, normal approximation, slice sampling, and sequential importance sampling, by comparing them against the original algorithm. The investigation centers on two primary questions: whether these importance samplers can accurately estimate parameters from the posterior and whether they can effectively estimate evidence. The findings indicate that none of the tested importance samplers consistently outperforms the others across all scenarios. Consequently, the original nested sampler remains the most reliable approach, as it allows users to monitor the approximation of the nested posterior during the algorithm's execution. A Python implementation of the original nested sampler, alongside implementations of normal approximation, nested nested sampler, slice sampling, and sequential importance sampling, is publicly accessible. The original algorithm is available at https://github.com/alexmccabe/PyNS, while the normal approximation can be found at https://github.com/alexmccabe/PyNS-NormalApproximation. Additionally, a slice sampling implementation is provided at https://github.com/alexmccabe/PyNS-SliceSampling, and a sequential importance sampling implementation is available at https://github.com/alexmccabe/PyNS-SequentialImportanceSampling. Implementations for the nested nested sampler and others are under development. While Dijkstra et al. (2019) demonstrated that fault-tolerant distance labeling is feasible for general graphs when $|F|$ is constant, they also established a lower bound of $\Omega(n^{1/2+\epsilon})$ for the label size. This work demonstrates that such labels can be computed in polynomial time for planar graphs, even under a large number of faults, and reveals that smaller label sizes are achievable for this specific graph class. Our main contributions are polynomial-time algorithms capable of generating fault-tolerant distance labels for planar graphs with $k$ faults of size $\mathcal{O}(n^{2k/3})$. Additionally, we present an alternative labeling scheme achieving a size of $\mathcal{O}(n^{(2k+1)/ (k+1)})$. Finally, we prove that fault-tolerant distance labeling schemes with a size better than $\mathcal{O}(n^{1/2+\epsilon})$ are impossible for graphs within certain graph-minor classes, including maximal outerplanar graphs and graphs with treewidth at least 2. The latter finding is derived from an application of a recent lower bound established by Demaine et al. (2020). Furthermore, we demonstrate that fault-tolerant distance labeling schemes with a size better than $\mathcal{O}(n^{2k/3 + \epsilon})$ are impossible for graphs in the family formed by adding a universal vertex to graphs with treewidth at most $k-1$. We investigate time- and frequency-domain two-particle correlations arising from two bosonic modes weakly coupled to a driven dissipative environment, which can be interpreted as a two-mode Bose-Hubbard system. The steady-state two-particle correlation function, $g^{(2)}(x_1, x_2)$, reveals that the two particles avoid bunching and instead display spatial anti-correlations. These findings are supported by time-domain simulations. Furthermore, we analyze the equal-time Fourier transform of $g^{(2)}(x_1, x_2)$ in the momentum domain, denoted as $\tilde{g}^{(2)}(k_1, k_2)$, and observe that the two-particle momentum distribution, $P(k_1, k_2)$$, exhibits anti-correlations. Specifically, $\tilde{g}^{(2)}(k_1, k_2)$ demonstrates perfect anti-correlation at the single-particle level, indicating that the two particles possess opposite momenta. These results are verified by comparing them with Fourier-transformed time-domain correlation functions, $\tilde{C}(t_1, t_2)$, where $C(t_1, t_2)$ is the inverse Fourier transform of $g^{(2)}(x_1, x_2)$. Our study highlights the existence of perfect quantum correlations between two bosons in both space and momentum domains. Additionally, we find that the two-particle correlation function, $C(t_1, t_2)$, exhibits oscillatory behavior, which is attributed to the Rabi oscillations between the two modes. This behavior is also reflected in the time-domain two-particle correlation function, $\tilde{C}(t_1, t_2)$. Periodically driven quantum systems typically undergo heating, a phenomenon where the drive frequency creates an unbounded growth in excitation density. This study demonstrates that heating can be averted in open systems by strategically engineering dissipation, thereby preserving low excitation density and inducing Bose condensation within a gauge-scrambled condensation mode. This approach is validated through an experimental setup involving a driven optical-lattice model coupled to a reservoir. The dynamics are governed by the competition between Floquet heating, which drives the system toward a highly excited steady state, and a carefully designed dissipative term that counteracts this heating. We demonstrate the elimination of heating and the observation of a Bose condensation transition into a gauge-scrambled mode, a phenomenon supported by a theoretical framework based on the system's generalized master equation. Furthermore, this mode is protected by the system's parity symmetry, with its properties controllable via an external magnetic field. These findings suggest promising applications for open quantum systems, including the creation of symmetry-protected topological phases and the stabilization of non-equilibrium steady states. Additionally, the resulting gauge-scrambled mode is deeply connected to the fractional quantum Hall effect, a topological state of matter in two-dimensional electron gases under strong magnetic fields. This connection arises from a specific transformation linking the driven open system to a fractional Chern insulator, thereby opening avenues for exploring topological phases of matter in driven open systems. Finally, we highlight the potential of these gauge-scrambled modes for quantum information processing, as they facilitate the generation of non-abelian anyons and facilitate their manipulation through local operations and site swaps. To validate these proposals, we have successfully generated and detected these non-abelian anyons. This work establishes a new pathway for quantum systems free from Floquet heating and offers a novel method for studying quantum phases of matter in driven open systems. Notably, the non-abelian anyons generated in this experiment are robust against decoherence, a feature that distinguishes them from those found in other driven open systems. This inherent robustness is attributed to the non-hermitian character of the effective Hamiltonian governing the system's dynamics. Our findings hold significant implications for quantum information processing, as they enable the creation of non-abelian anyons that are naturally safeguarded against decoherence. This paper examines the convex solution $\varphi$ to the Monge–Ampère equation defined on a bounded, strictly convex, smooth closed region $\Omega \subset \mathbb{R}^n$ with a right-hand side $f$ that belongs to $L^\infty(\Omega)$. We demonstrate that the solution satisfies the Alexandrov maximum principle, expressed as $C_\infty\left[\min_{\partial\Omega}f \leq \varphi(x) \leq \max_{\partial\Omega}f\right]$ for all $x \in \Omega$, where $C_\infty$ is a constant dependent on $n$ and $\Omega$. Furthermore, the solution exhibits uniform Hölder continuity with an exponent $\alpha$ defined by $\alpha = \min\left\{1, \frac{\ln\left(1 + \frac{1}{\|f\|_\infty}\right)}{\ln\left(1 + \frac{\|\nabla\varphi\|_{L^\infty(\Omega)}}{\|f\|_\infty}\right)}\right\}$, which approaches $1$ as $\|f\|_\infty$ approaches $0$. These findings represent partial progress toward resolving an open conjecture by Li-Yau regarding the $C^{0,\alpha}$-regularity of the Alexandrov solution to the Monge–Ampère equation, originally proposed in their 1980 paper. Additionally, our result confirms Li-Yau's conjecture for the specific case where $\|f\|_\infty < e-1$. Finally, we derive an explicit lower bound for the Hölder exponent $\alpha$ when $f \in W^{1,1}(\Omega)$. These enhancements to the Alexandrov maximum principle and the uniform Hölder continuity of the solution may prove valuable for further research into the Monge–Ampère equation. Deep learning relies heavily on backpropagation, utilizing optimization and loss functions to train neural networks. Although research has extensively explored various optimization and loss strategies, this study focuses specifically on loss functions. We introduce a novel algorithm termed "gradient surgery," which examines how varying loss functions influence gradients. This approach enables the efficient calculation of alternative loss functions by applying operational transformations to existing ones, thereby eliminating the need to recompute gradients from scratch. Furthermore, we demonstrate that for any convex combination of differentiable neural network losses, there exists a corresponding piecewise differentiable gradient surgery loss. Experimental results indicate that gradient surgery effectively identifies well-behaved regions within the loss landscape, offering valuable insights for loss function design. Additionally, we propose a new method called "optimal surgery," which strategically combines existing gradients to create more effective piecewise differentiable function segments. Finally, we investigate regularized gradient surgery, demonstrating its ability to uncover promising well-behaved regions in both convex and non-convex loss landscapes. Our findings suggest that gradient surgery serves as a valuable tool for analyzing and understanding neural loss functions. This study introduces an integrated optimization framework designed to enhance conservation voltage reduction (CVR) strategies within single-phase primary-secondary distribution systems. The model incorporates voltage-dependent power (VDP) characteristics of secondary transformers to calculate optimal CVR benefits, voltage profiles, and system losses across both primary and secondary networks. Furthermore, it integrates smart meter-based distributed control with centralized optimization, utilizing smart meters to monitor secondary transformer voltages. Since these meters cannot directly measure primary bus voltages, the system employs smart load flow (SFL) techniques to estimate primary voltages at secondary feeders based on secondary transformer data. This approach ensures that distributed control strategies adhere to primary-side voltage constraints while utilizing secondary transformer parameters to minimize secondary voltage deviations. Additionally, the study addresses uncertainty in CVR benefits by modeling them as random variables with known probability distributions, allowing the inclusion of reliability requirements within the optimization process. Finally, the proposed methodology is validated through simulations using a real-world feeder dataset. The results demonstrate that incorporating VDP into the optimization model enhances overall CVR benefits and reduces total losses by 1.1% compared to conventional CVR approaches. Furthermore, the integration of centralized optimization with distributed control achieves superior uncertainty management compared to standalone solutions. Notably, enforcing primary feeder voltage constraints within the optimization model increases the reliability of CVR by 15.5% relative to traditional distributed control methods. Furthermore, the proposed SFL-based voltage estimation algorithm significantly reduces secondary voltage deviations, thereby expanding the scope for optimal CVR application. Ultimately, this research underscores the necessity of modeling VDP and integrating distributed control with centralized optimization to fully leverage the potential of CVR in distribution systems. Future work will extend this approach to handle unbalanced three-phase systems. To facilitate broader application, the methodology will be converted into a user-friendly tool accessible to utility engineers. Additionally, future extensions will incorporate smart meter data from distribution transformers and strategies for managing increased reactive power consumption during CVR events. This research investigates nonstochastic bandits and experts within a delayed framework where delays vary based on both time and arms. Specifically, we introduce a novel, arm-dependent delay model that encompasses various previous formulations as special cases. Our theoretical analysis focuses on regret relative to the best action in hindsight, accounting for these delays. We establish a general lower bound on this regret and subsequently derive two corresponding upper bounds—one for the bandit setting and another for the experts setting—adapting algorithms from [10] and [2]. Finally, we empirically validate our proposed algorithms by comparing their performance against existing literature. This performance gap highlights the critical need for delayed algorithms that achieve lower regret lower bounds, particularly in scenarios involving diverse delays across different arms. Our work addresses such scenarios by demonstrating that our methods outperform previous approaches in terms of both regret and computational efficiency. Furthermore, we demonstrate that delayed expert algorithms can be effectively adapted to address delayed bandit problems.

This study employs a multi-fidelity surrogate modeling strategy to simulate structural loads on offshore wind turbines. These structures are characterized by intricate geometries and nonlinear material behaviors, which create significant disparities in the computational costs associated with different simulation methods. To address this, the authors developed a model utilizing chained Gaussian processes to account for multiple sources of variability in computational expense. The probabilistic load simulation results align well with traditional deterministic simulations, and the derived sensitivity analysis indicates that the peak structural moment is primarily influenced by the turbine's yaw angle and wave height. These findings highlight the framework's potential to support more efficient and sustainable offshore wind-turbine design workflows. This study introduces a new method for reconstructing time-resolved data, such as spatially distributed temporal profiles or spectral data, from noisy measurements. The approach relies on an efficient representation of the unknown quantity within a trajectory basis, which consists of a sampled set of possible outcomes of the measurement forward model. This basis is generated via a single optimization run using an arbitrary initial guess. By optimizing forward-model parameters in a data misfit sense within this trajectory basis, the study demonstrates that the proposed technique outperforms existing state-of-the-art reconstruction methods. The application of this technique to various quantitative tomographic problems, including single-photon emission computed tomography and fluorescence tomography, confirms its potential for high-fidelity reconstruction. Furthermore, numerical simulations indicate that the approach is computationally efficient, with all numerical examples converging in under a second. The method's robustness is highlighted by high reconstruction fidelity achieved through simple model-based regularization, such as total variation regularization. Additionally, numerical simulations of realistic data suggest that the technique can be effectively applied to reconstruct dynamic processes from time-resolved tomographic data. All numerical examples utilize open-source software. The source code is available at https://github.com/alexanderkellner/RobustTimeResolution. The technique is implemented in Python and is easily adaptable to other programming languages. Furthermore, the technique is easily extensible to other forward models. Boundary conformal field theory (BCFT) and interface conformal field theory (ICFT) have garnered significant interest recently due to their connections with holography, quantum information, and critical phenomena within driven-dissipative quantum systems. These frameworks are also essential for investigating boundary entropy and operator algebra modifications arising from boundaries. In this work, we examine the reflected entropy—a universal entanglement measure within conformal field theory—in the context of BCFT and ICFT. For BCFT, we derive the reflected entropy between two adjacent intervals by employing the quantum error-correcting code concept derived from holographic principles. Subsequently, we apply this methodology to ICFT to analyze the reflected entropy of two overlapping intervals. Furthermore, the methodology established here facilitates the construction of a reflected symmetry category for BCFT and ICFT. Finally, our findings are supported by numerical simulations. These results could prove valuable in addressing broader quantum information challenges within BCFT and ICFT. Additionally, our results align with those reported in arXiv:2109.02694. Reconfigurable Intelligent Surfaces (RIS) represent a promising technology capable of enhancing wireless communication systems. However, channel estimation in RIS-assisted OFDM setups is often hindered by the massive dimensionality of the effective channel, the limited number of RIS reflecting elements, and practical hardware imperfections. To address these challenges, this paper introduces a novel enhanced learning-based channel estimation method designed for RIS-assied OFDM systems operating with reduced cyclic prefixes (CP) and accounting for imperfect hardware. This approach utilizes an Extended Learning Machine (ELM) to recover the effective channel from a limited set of training signals. By decomposing the ELM into multiple sub-machines, the method effectively models the nonlinear relationship between the ELM input and output. Furthermore, it employs a new sampling strategy for extended inputs that utilizes the inverse Fourier transform to generate sampling points, ensuring the sampling theorem is satisfied. The proposed technique incorporates a scaling factor to mitigate the impact of imperfect hardware. Simulation results confirm that this enhanced ELM-based approach outperforms existing methods. Specifically, compared to the ELM-based scheme, the proposed method improves estimation performance by 1.5 dB at an error rate of 10⁻². Additionally, relative to a Least Squares (LS) scheme, the enhanced method achieves a 2-fold improvement in estimation performance. Keywords: Channel Estimation, Extended Learning Machine, OFDM, RIS, Sampling Extension.

We examine a system interacting with a thermal reservoir, where transition rates are defined as solutions to the heat equation subject to specific initial conditions representing system states prior to measurements. These states evolve following measurements characterized by non-unitary maps that simulate the impact of observable readings. When energy exchange is modeled via the non-projective von Neumann law, the resulting transition rates satisfy an exact detailed balance condition and an integrated fluctuation theorem. The latter yields an equilibrium free-energy relation that incorporates both information and non-work contributions derived from the non-unitary map. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the non-unitary von Neumann law can be expressed as a sum of two components: a probabilistic measurement via positive operator-valued measures and a complementary term linked to the anticommutator part of that measurement. This decomposition offers an alternative perspective on the fluctuation relation for free energy. Finally, we apply this framework to analyze measurements on a single qubit. In the limit of projective measurements, the probabilistic and complementary terms converge to the standard quantum jump and quantum displacement laws, respectively. Consequently, we derive a novel fluctuation relation for quantum jumps and establish a connection between quantum work and the quantum displacement law. These findings hold for general quantum states and non-Markovian dynamics. Additionally, we illustrate an application of the quantum displacement law in the context of information erasure. Our results indicate that the anticommutator term in the unitary evolution of a qubit's state is essential for achieving fluctuation relations that generalize the second law of thermodynamics. This insight is expected to facilitate the construction of thermodynamic theories for quantum systems subjected to non-unitary maps. Notably, these maps encompass a broad spectrum of quantum operations, including quantum cloning, quantum state diffusion, and quantum feedback control. Furthermore, we show that the probabilistic measurement term within the unitary evolution of a qubit's state corresponds to the dissipation of quantum discord. This relationship further refines fluctuation relations concerning quantum coherence. Collectively, these findings pave the way for a comprehensive and unified theory of quantum thermodynamics. In this framework, fluctuation relations for quantum systems are derived from single energy measurement transition rates, while quantum coherence and entanglement are treated as distinct resources. This approach also clarifies the specific roles of quantum jumps and quantum displacements within the quantum thermodynamic formalism. In this context, quantum jumps represent dissipative processes, whereas quantum displacements correspond to coherent evolution. This work examines the deformation theory of $\mathrm{G}_2$-instantons on nearly $\mathrm{G}_2$ manifolds. Since nearly parallel $\mathrm{G}_2$ structures correspond bijectively to real Killing spinors, the deformation framework can be expressed using spinors and Clifford algebra. We demonstrate that the obstructions to deforming an instanton reside in the component of $H^1(\mathfrak{g})$ isomorphic to $\Sigma^0 \otimes H^1$, where $\Sigma^0$ denotes the space of traceless spinors. Leveraging this characterization, we establish the existence and index theory for instantons. Specifically, we prove that on a nearly $G_2$ manifold, an instanton's index is determined by the index of the Dirac operator, the first Betti number, and the index of a Clifford multiplication map. Furthermore, we establish an existence theorem: for any spinor $\psi$ satisfying $D_{\nabla^D}\psi=0$, there exists an instanton $A$ such that the $\nabla^D$-derivative of its curvature aligns with $\psi$. This result follows from applying the splitting lemma to the relevant elliptic complex. Additionally, we derive an inequality providing an upper bound for the instanton index, which we show is attainable. Finally, we construct a family of cohomology classes representing obstructions to instanton deformations. For contact manifolds, these classes vanish, implying the existence of a sufficient supply of instantons. In contrast, on nearly $G_2$ manifolds, the obstructions are represented by the "Clifford multiplication map." The ongoing COVID-19 pandemic has driven the creation of contact tracing applications designed to detect and contain the virus. However, despite their potential to save lives, these apps face significant privacy challenges. This study evaluates the privacy risks associated with the Coronav\'irus-SUS application, which utilizes a centralized model. The analysis employs an attack tree, a formal method for assessing security and privacy, to simulate an adversary attempting to identify a specific user. Using the SUS framework, the work calculates the success probability of this identification attempt by evaluating the attack tree and accounting for the user's defensive behaviors. The findings demonstrate that the level of privacy provided by the application is directly tied to user participation; specifically, as more users adopt the app, the privacy of individual users diminishes. Consequently, to ensure adequate privacy, either the application should adopt a more privacy-preserving architecture, or users must adopt a "privacy by numbers" strategy by delaying installation until a critical mass of users has joined. This strategy is supported by a formal model that analyzes the privacy implications of adoption rates over time. Furthermore, an empirical analysis of adoption data for Coronav\'irus-SUS reinforces these conclusions. Finally, the study proposes a decentralized architecture for contact tracing apps to enhance user privacy. This approach was developed using the Security Drivers Methodology, a goal-directed technique for the formal specification of security and privacy requirements. The paper concludes by detailing the requirements for such architectures and discussing their associated security and privacy properties. Overall, this work offers a comprehensive analysis of the privacy risks in national contact tracing applications and provides both a formal and practical framework for developing more privacy-preserving solutions. Additionally, the research framework used to assess application privacy can be applied to any contact tracing app, making it a valuable tool for both developers and users. For developers, it offers a systematic approach to privacy preservation, while for users, it clarifies how participation impacts privacy, thereby fostering a more informed decision-making process. Ultimately, this research promotes a greater societal dialogue regarding the trade-offs between the benefits and the risks to privacy. Finally, this work represents the first of a series that will explore other privacy-related aspects, such as data retention policies, data anonymization, and data sharing practices. These aspects will also be examined from both a theoretical and an empirical perspective. This paper introduces a C code generator for ACL2 that is integrated as a library within the system itself. Our primary motivation for developing this generator was to enhance the ACL2 library's capacity to verify programs written in various languages. While our existing code generator already supports ACL2, producing verified programs in that language is often insufficient for demonstrating the utility of formal methods to a broader audience. Therefore, we aim to produce code in other languages to make the benefits of formal methods more accessible to wider communities. Although C is not always the optimal choice for this demonstration, it remains our default selection.

To achieve this, we developed a C code generator grounded in a shallow embedding of C within ACL2. This approach enables the construction of a C compiler from ACL2 to verify C programs. We anticipate that this technique will facilitate the development of other language-specific code generators. The paper provides an overview of our design methodology, design decisions, and implementation details. Additionally, we have created a library for this code generator within ACL2 on GitHub, which is accessible to anyone. We intend to utilize this library to support the verification of C programs.

The remainder of this paper is structured as follows: Section 2 provides a brief introduction to the code generator library, with the understanding that readers are already familiar with it. Section 3 reviews the shallow embedding of C in ACL2, which serves as the foundation for our code generator. Section 4 details the design of the code generator, outlining the steps taken to develop it. Section 5 presents the implementation of this generator within ACL2. Finally, Section 6 offers our conclusions.

Building on Ramanujan's work on zeta values, we establish a novel identity concerning the Hurwitz zeta function at odd positive integers. This identity can be viewed as an extension of Ramanujan's original formula for odd zeta values. Additionally, we have crafted an identity for linear combinations of odd zeta values using a system of linear equations. Our proofs for these identities rely on the differential properties of the Hurwitz zeta function with respect to its second variable, the Riemann Zeta function, and polygamma functions. Finally, we validate these identities by computing Bernoulli polynomials and verifying their adherence to our formulas. In this context, Ramanujan's identity emerges as a specific instance of our first result when the Hurwitz zeta function is replaced by the Riemann zeta function. We also provide an alternative proof of Ramanujan's identity that avoids the use of umbral calculus. Furthermore, our results offer a unified approach to deriving identities for both the harmonic and alternating zeta functions. To demonstrate this, we present a theorem that generates identities for alternating zeta functions as special cases of our primary identity for the Hurwitz zeta function, while another theorem specifically yields the identity for the Riemann zeta function. The paper concludes with several remarks and open questions. The methodologies employed here may also be applicable to the polygamma function, the Lerch transcendent, and the polylogarithm. Additionally, the authors intend to explore the connection between our identity and the MZV (Multiple Zeta Value) algebra in future research. This paper presents a comprehensive investigation into the production of $J/\psi$ and the charmonium states $\eta_c$, $\chi_{c0}$, $\chi_{c1}$, and $\chi_{c2}$ through the process $e^{+}e^{-} \to J/\psi+\eta_c,\chi_{cJ}$ at center-of-mass energies near 10.6 GeV. The calculations are performed within the color-singlet model up to the next-to-leading order in QCD. Key aspects examined include the influence of higher-order QCD corrections on production cross sections, the effects of spin-dependent potentials on the hadronic decay widths of the $\chi_{cJ}$ states, and the analysis of $J/\psi$ angular distributions in relation to the direct four-gluon production mechanism. Our findings reveal a significant reduction in the uncertainty regarding the ratio of production cross sections, $\sigma(J/\psi+\chi_{c1})/\sigma(J/\psi+\chi_{c2})$, when incorporating ${{\cal O}}(\alpha_s)$ corrections. Furthermore, the study confirms the presence of the characteristic $1: 2 : 3$ angular distribution pattern for $J/\psi$ production associated with $\chi_{c1}$, $\chi_{c2}$, and $\chi_{c0}$ respectively. Finally, the predicted values for the cross-section ratio $\sigma(J/\psi+\chi_{c1})/\sigma(J/\psi+\chi_{c2})$ in the vicinity of 10.6 GeV are determined to be approximately 1.5, aligning well with recent measurements obtained by the BESIII collaboration. These results offer valuable insights for future experimental studies of the $e^{+}e^{-} \to J/\psi+\chi_{cJ}$ process. Additionally, the predicted branching ratio for the $e^{+}e^{-} \to J/\psi+\chi_{c1}$ channel at the BEPCII collider is estimated to be around $1.5 \times 10^{-4}$. This indicates that the $J/\psi+\chi_{c1}$ channel could serve as a viable source for producing Higgs bosons via photon fusion at a Higgs factory. The outcomes of this study may also assist in clarifying the underlying mechanisms of $J/\psi$ production in other relevant reactions. Solar irradiance is a critical factor in various fields, including remote sensing, atmospheric physics, and solar energy applications. This paper introduces an efficient numerical method for solving the equation of radiative transfer by precisely and rapidly approximating the angular integration using a few quadrature points. These points and their corresponding weights are determined by finding the roots of a specific orthogonal polynomial. The polynomial coefficients are derived through a matrix power method that iteratively calculates higher-order moments from lower ones. To ensure numerical stability during this iterative process, we apply both the shift and size methods. The approach is highly accurate across the entire solar spectrum (0.1–10000 cm⁻¹) and remains effective for scenarios involving both single and multiple scattering. Our method achieves at least four-digit precision with merely four quadrature points. Furthermore, we provide a set of routines written in Fortran and Python, accessible at https://github.com/ChenchenLi1990/SQ. Our implementation is at least an order of magnitude faster than the widely used DISORT code. The source code for this solar-weighted quadrature (SQ) method is available on GitHub. We conclude that this approach is a powerful tool for accurately and efficiently performing angular integration in radiative transfer calculations. The SQ code can be accessed at https://github.com/ChenchenLi1990/SQ. This work was supported by the National Natural Science Foundation of China (Grant 41975120).
