The curvature information provided by the Hessian or its generalized Gauss-Newton (GGN) approximation is essential for numerous machine learning (ML) tasks, including model-based optimization, uncertainty quantification, and robustness analysis. However, the substantial size and sparsity of these matrices make them impractical for storage, rendering traditional methods reliant on iterative matrix-vector products. While recent approaches have attempted to address this by exploiting low-rank properties, they often suffer from prohibitive communication costs during matrix-vector products or produce highly inaccurate approximations. This paper introduces ViViT, a novel matrix-based estimator that combines low-rank compression with the enhanced variance-based variance inflation (eVIV) technique. ViViT is designed to approximate any low-rank Hessian by leveraging the low-rank structure inherent in the product of two GGN factors. By utilizing the Gram matrix of these factors, ViViT can compute a compressed Hessian with significantly reduced communication overhead, thereby enabling efficient and scalable algorithms. We demonstrate the effectiveness of ViViT across a wide range of tasks, including deep residual networks, variational inference, and generative adversarial networks. Furthermore, we provide a comprehensive theoretical analysis of its statistical properties. Our extensive experiments confirm that ViViT achieves state-of-the-art performance in various applications, offering both superior accuracy and substantial computational gains. The implementation is available at https://github.com/DeepMind/vivit. Theoretical proofs can be found in our arXiv submission: https://arxiv.org/abs/2102.01087. Additional code and proofs are located at https://github.com/DeepMind/vivit/tree/main/vivit_theory. Our code repository also includes examples for model-based optimization and uncertainty quantification. For instance, when compared to eVIV, ViViT reduces training time by 2.5x while maintaining equivalent test accuracy. In contrast to the previous Hessian sketch method, ViViT improves test accuracy by 3.5% while achieving a 3x speedup. Finally, regarding uncertainty quantification in MNIST training, ViViT lowers the KL divergence by 20% compared to Hessian sketch, while delivering a 2x speedup. Finally, regarding GAN training, ViViT achieves a 2x speedup over Hessian sketch while maintaining identical test accuracy. This research investigates how grammatical gender influences word representations in neural language models within languages featuring gender agreement. By utilizing morphologically rich mark-up in morphologically tagged tokenized (MMT) corpora, the study demonstrates that gender features can be automatically derived from these resources. The analysis reveals that n-gram models trained on gender-annotated MMT resources successfully capture gender distinctions within gender-relevant contexts, specifically targeting morphemes. Furthermore, the study examines how gender-sensitive training data impacts the quality of vector space representations for natural language inference tasks. Although the datasets employed are relatively small, the findings are considered robust due to the inherent difficulty of the tasks involved. The research concludes by discussing potential applications of these insights for natural language processing and linguistic theory. Finally, the authors outline directions for future work, including the automatic annotation of gender features and the development of larger gender-sensitive datasets. This article is anticipated to stimulate further inquiry into the effects of gender on lexical and syntactic representation. We examine charmeneability within arithmetic groups, deriving several key results, beginning with a substantial theorem on stiffness. Specifically, if $\Gamma$ denotes an irreducible lattice in a semisimple Lie group $G$ that does not possess real rank one, and $H$ is a semisimple Lie group containing an irreducible lattice $\Lambda$, then any continuous charmeneability action of $\Gamma$ on $\Lambda$ is necessarily trivial. This finding offers a partial resolution to a inquiry posed by D. Osin. Furthermore, we demonstrate that every charmeneability action of $\Gamma$ on any locally compact second countable group $K$ with a compact center is virtually nilpotent. These findings extend various established results concerning amenability and minimality within the framework of dynamics. Additionally, we establish that every such action on a compact space is minimal and uniquely ergodic. Finally, we illustrate that, in contrast to amenability, charmeneability does not imply minimality. Our methodology involves constructing specific actions on various spaces and analyzing their dynamics through the examination of stabilizers of points within the Poisson boundary. This work extends several instances of prior research on amenability and minimality in dynamics. To facilitate this, we also present an alternative proof of a theorem by G. Gongora and J. Packer regarding the nonexistence of minimal dynamical systems arising from amenability actions of irreducible lattices in semisimple Lie groups of real rank at least two. Furthermore, we provide a characterization of the dynamics on transitive spaces under such actions. To achieve these results, we develop techniques involving lattices within algebraic groups, drawing upon methods from algebraic and Lie theory. We also characterize dynamics on minimal spaces arising from these actions. To support this, we characterize dynamics on transitive spaces, thereby extending various examples from the amenability literature. Object pose estimation is a critical element within 3D vision systems, which are increasingly deployed in autonomous driving and robotics. However, current state-of-the-art methods are typically restricted to specific categories and require extensive training on pose data for each individual class. This limitation significantly hinders their practical utility in real-world scenarios. To address this, we introduce ZOPED, a zero-shot framework designed for category-level pose estimation. Our approach leverages a pre-trained large-scale simulator to generate diverse pose samples for target categories, leveraging the fact that these samples often differ only slightly. Consequently, our method can train a pose estimator using just a single 3D bounding box, avoiding the need for multiple views or 3D object models. Furthermore, we propose a novel pose prediction technique that utilizes both 2D bounding boxes and keypoint annotations to enhance performance. Extensive experiments on the AI4Bench platform demonstrate that ZOPED achieves an 18% increase in pose estimation accuracy compared to the baseline, establishing it as the new state-of-the-art in category-level pose estimation under zero-shot conditions. This paper introduces a framework for identifying key road segments and traffic patterns from extensive, high-resolution traffic forecasting datasets. We demonstrate that this identification process is vital for forecasting, showing that it significantly enhances the accuracy of large-scale sparse traffic prediction tasks. Our approach relies on the similarity between road segments, which is derived from the similarity of their historical traffic patterns. We evaluate the efficacy of our framework using a traffic forecasting dataset from New York City. The experimental results confirm that the proposed method outperforms state-of-the-art techniques. Furthermore, we reveal that the similarity-based feature extraction technique is inherently scalable to massive datasets. We anticipate that the proposed solution will be valuable for big data applications in the transportation sector. The source code can be accessed at: https://github.com/ahmedhassan1234/SS-FE. The dataset used is available at: https://drive.google.

This paper introduces VACA, a new class of variational graph autoencoders designed for causal inference when only an observed causal graph and data are available. VACA learns an approximate causal model via graph regularization within the variational framework, enabling the computation of interventional and counterfactual estimates. Our empirical results demonstrate that VACA outperforms state-of-the-art approximate causal models in classification tasks involving interventions and counterfactuals. Furthermore, we establish a connection between VACA and recent Bayesian causal models, offering guidance for the development of future approximate causal models. This work serves as an initial step toward making causal inference more accessible. The code is accessible at https://github.com/alexschwaab/VACA. In this study, we present VACA, which constructs approximate causal models using graph regularization within a variational framework, thereby enabling causal learning from observational data under observation independence faithfulness assumptions. VACA facilitates causal reasoning by allowing the estimation of causal effects for interventions and counterfactuals. Empirically, VACA surpasses state-of-the-art approximate causal models on synthetic datasets and achieves comparable performance to CausalVAE on the MNIST dataset. For the synthetic datasets, we have established connections between VACA and Bayesian causal models. For the MNIST dataset, our results indicate that VACA is competitive with Bayesian causal models. Given these empirical findings, we propose that graph regularization is a viable approach for learning causal models, and we suggest that future research should explore the application of graph regularization to other learning scenarios. We introduce the REAL-time Transient Acquisition backend (REALTA), a new module developed for the Irish LOFAR station. This system is designed to identify and record transients in real time, enabling immediate analysis and follow-up. LOFAR data captured by REALTA can be rapidly re-acquired and reprioritized for interferometric analysis. The system's processing pipeline achieves a time resolution of 10 milliseconds and a frequency resolution of 200 kHz. Additionally, we demonstrate a successful detection of the fast radio burst FRB 20190520A. This paper details the REALTA architecture and its performance, while also outlining future enhancements and potential applications. The REALTA system is now fully operational. Over recent years, the convergence of machine learning and metaphotonics has driven significant advancements in both artificial intelligence and photonics. This integrated discipline offers a novel pathway to create intelligent metaphotonics, enabling the design of superior optical devices and systems alongside the development of superior machine learning algorithms. This book chapter explores recent progress, potential, and future prospects within the realm of intelligent metaphotonics. Specifically, it examines how machine learning is transforming metaphotonics, detailing the foundational principles, methodologies, and practical applications. Furthermore, the text addresses recent breakthroughs in the intersection of these two fields, highlighting emerging opportunities for the development of smart metaphotonics. Finally, it outlines key challenges and proposes future directions for this rapidly evolving domain. The content is structured into seven sections: an introduction to the convergence of machine learning and metaphotonics; an overview of supervised learning methods for optical device design; an analysis of unsupervised learning, generative adversarial networks, and reinforcement learning in metaphotonics; a survey of recent applications of intelligent metaphotonics; an introduction to neural architecture search; a discussion of open challenges; and a concluding summary. Section 2 provides an overview of supervised learning, covering backpropagation, the Levenberg-Marquardt algorithm, and their application to optical device design. Section 3 introduces unsupervised learning, generative adversarial networks, and reinforcement learning within the context of metaphotonics. Section 4 presents recent applications of intelligent metaphotonics. Section 5 introduces neural architecture search. Finally, Section 6 addresses open challenges, and the Conclusion offers a summary of the field. The authors aim to inspire further research into intelligent metaphotonics, potentially leading to superior solutions in this area. This paper introduces a comprehensive, current dataset containing over 150,010 movies, which has been made publicly available. Built upon attributes from IMDb, we have further incorporated release date information and gross revenue figures. The inclusion of revenue data is particularly significant, as this metric is a primary motivator for both audiences and film distributors. Additionally, we conduct a topological analysis of the movie-actor graph derived from the dataset and examine how various movie characteristics influence revenue performance. Our findings indicate that growth potential is a critical factor in determining a film's success. We also demonstrate that including genre information enhances predictive accuracy, whereas relying solely on release type yields the least effective predictions. Ultimately, this research aims to assist industry professionals in making more informed decisions regarding movie production. The dataset can be accessed at https://github.com/abdullahkaya1994/IMDb-Data.

This study examines secondary frequency control (SFC) within interconnected microgrids (IGs) characterized by frequency-dependent damping, low inertia, and significant voltage dynamics. Initially, a stabilizing controller is designed to ensure stable voltage behavior, followed by an analysis of the system's small-signal dynamics. To accomplish this, we derive an equivalent model utilizing a reduced system of nonlinear differential equations, which is proven to possess asymptotically stable equilibrium points under specific damping conditions. Furthermore, the equilibrium trajectories of the original nonlinear system are shown to converge asymptotically to those of the equivalent model. Additionally, local asymptotic stability is demonstrated through a Lyapunov function, revealing a linear relationship between frequency and voltage deviations at the primary controlled bus. Finally, the paper presents insights into the linearized system's dynamics, including its eigenvalue configuration and modal participation factors (MPFs). The proposed stabilization method is validated through simulations on a 10-bus test system. Results indicate that the modal spectrum of the linearized system comprises low-damped modes, yet all modes exhibit sufficient damping margins to prevent instability. Consequently, SFC-based stabilization successfully ensures stable voltage dynamics in power networks where voltage dynamics are non-negligible. This methodology is particularly advantageous for modern power grids featuring high penetration of power electronics-based distributed energy resources (DERs), which are typically equipped with fast secondary frequency control. A key benefit is that voltage dynamics can be stabilized without necessitating additional phase-shifting transformers. Furthermore, the approach is inherently scalable, as it relies on local measurements at the controlled bus. Finally, the technique is applicable to both AC and DC power networks. To facilitate this, we introduce a novel test system for analytical and numerical investigations, which is made available to the research community. The associated MATLAB code is also provided to support reproducibility. This work extends the findings of [1].

Cyberphysical systems (CPS) are anticipated to become increasingly ubiquitous, though the specific contexts in which they will operate remain unclear. Currently, the prevailing approach to designing large-scale CPS is a centralized one, where an external entity manages the interactions among numerous CPS. This paper introduces the emerging concept of Cyberphysical Systems of Systems (CPSoS), which posits that a higher-level supervisory entity will shift from being an external manager to an intrinsic integral component of the system itself. This trend is driven by the growing capability of artificial intelligence (AI) to enable learning and reasoning within the systems, facilitating knowledge transfer and the intelligent coordination of complex CPS interactions. This work explores the foundational challenges of designing CPSoS, emphasizing the critical role of intelligence in achieving this objective. Furthermore, it examines the foundational issues surrounding the integration of artificial intelligence into cyberphysical systems. We examine the analytic continuation of multivariate functions using complex landscape analysis. Introducing a concept of dimensionality based on Lipschitz constants, we establish an upper bound for the required sample size and demonstrate that the bound scales quadratically with this quantity for multi-modal functions. Furthermore, we present an algorithm for analytic continuation in $\mathbb{R}^d$ built upon multivariate Lagrange interpolation, showing that the computational cost grows no faster than that of the sample size squared. These results apply specifically to functions representable as finite sums of known functions. Our techniques are utilized in multidimensional signal processing to interpolate signals from a minimal set of samples. Additionally, we illustrate the relevance of complex landscape analysis in this context by examining the Zeta function and signal recovery challenges. Our findings are supported by numerical examples. This work was partially funded by the Ministry of Science and Higher Education of the Russian Federation (Grant No. 0728-2020-0021). We present a quantum algorithm that employs on-demand adaptive measurements to identify any $N$-qubit symmetric pure state, requiring a complexity of $O(\log^k(N))$. This approach achieves an optimal complexity of $O(\log(N))$ when adapted to use entangled measurements. Our general identification algorithm is extended into a quantum search algorithm capable of locating a target symmetric pure state within a symmetric superposition, utilizing on-demand adaptive measurements to reduce the linearly encoded target search amplitude to zero through a minimal number of measurements. With potential for further optimization, this proposed algorithm represents a significant advancement in many-body quantum information processing. Additionally, we outline the necessary hardware requirements for experimental implementation. **Context:** The Sun's rotation rate varies with latitude, a phenomenon known as the differential rotation (DR). The solar equator rotates faster than the poles, a pattern that has persisted for over a century.

**Aims:** This study investigates whether the observed DR is truly intrinsic to the Sun or if it is influenced by large-scale flows, particularly those surrounding active regions (SARs).

**Methods:** We analyzed the primary dataset used to detect DR, utilizing the helioseismic inverse method **GREGOR** (Global Reconstructions of the Earth's Gravity Oscillations). We identified SARs within the input data by applying a standard method involving the removal of data from regions with significant active regions.

**Results:** The analysis reveals that flows around SARs can account for up to 50% of the differential rotation. Specifically, when SARs are present, the difference between poleward and equatorward travel times is reduced by 50%. This effect is primarily driven by SARs in the northern hemisphere, where flow patterns are generally poleward, and in the southern hemisphere, where patterns are generally equatorward.

**Conclusions:** The observed differential rotation is not purely intrinsic to the Sun; it is significantly modulated by flows around active regions. Consequently, the true DR is likely smaller than previously measured. This finding has significant implications for solar dynamo models, as the rotation rate is a critical parameter. Furthermore, this result may impact the interpretation of potential differences in rotation rates between the Sun and other stars. Future research should aim to quantify the contribution of SARs to the DR in the solar interior. Additionally, the current analysis was limited to the solar surface; therefore, we propose that the next target for SAR removal is the **GREGOR** 3D velocity field. This would allow for the investigation of how SARs influence the observed DR at the base of the convection zone, a key factor in solar dynamo models. Ultimately, this approach may help explain the "tilt" observed in the solar cycle. By eliminating SAR-related effects, the resulting 3D velocity field could reveal a more accurate, intrinsic DR pattern. This could help explain the **Spörer's Law**, which states that active regions in the northern hemisphere are typically closer to the equator than those in the south at the same latitude. Pulsar Timing Array (PTA) observations in the nanohertz frequency range have recently yielded significant results, including the detection of a common red noise signal across multiple pulsars and the establishment of the lower bound of the square amplitude of the common signal, which has yet to be explained. We propose that primordial magnetic fields (PMF) generated during the early universe could account for this enigmatic signal. Our analysis indicates that a root mean square (rms) magnetic field strength of approximately $10^{-10}$ G within a characteristic scale of $10^{-1}$ pc is sufficient to produce the observed common red noise. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the PTA lower bound for the square amplitude of the common signal can be utilized to constrain the magnitude of PMFs in the early universe. Specifically, for a correlation length of $10^{-1}$ pc, the PMF rms amplitude is bounded from below by roughly $10^{-11}$ G at the 95% confidence level. Additionally, PMFs may generate stochastic gravitational waves (GWs) that could potentially be detected by future PTA experiments. We show that a GW strain amplitude of approximately $10^{-17}$ in the nanohertz range is feasible, contingent upon specific conditions of the PMF. Consequently, PTA data can impose constraints on both the amplitude and spatial scale of PMFs, offering a valuable tool for investigating cosmological magnetogenesis. Moreover, PTA observations have the potential to uncover a stochastic GW background originating from PMFs. If such a signal is detected, it would provide a means to constrain the amplitude and correlation length of PMFs, thereby elucidating the mechanisms responsible for their generation. Finally, we examine the viability of this proposal and explore the implications of the PTA common red signal in relation to PMFs. If the common red signal is indeed attributed to PMFs, it implies that the rms amplitude is at least $10^{-10}$ G and the correlation length does not exceed $10^{1}$ pc. Conversely, if the common signal arises from unmodeled gravitational waves, the corresponding GW strain amplitude must be greater than $10^{-17}$ in the nanohertz range. Additionally, if the PTA common signal is not caused by PMFs, the rms amplitude of the PMF is constrained to be below $10^{-10}$ G at the 95% confidence level. Light field technology has garnered significant interest due to its capacity to capture extra spatial and temporal data through the sampling of ray-directional information. However, the high resolution of light field data renders it unsuitable for storage or transmission. To address this, the paper introduces a learning-based approach utilizing deep neural networks for the compression of light field or light field-derived images. The disparity-aware compression model (DACM) is developed to simultaneously optimize structural similarity (SSIM) and rate-distortion (RD) performance. To enhance the model's ability to represent depth, the disparity map is incorporated into the loss function, which minimizes the difference between the actual and predicted disparity maps. Furthermore, the system is evaluated using synthetic light field images generated from standard still images through ray-slicing and defocusing. Experimental results indicate that the proposed model achieves superior SSIM and RD performance compared to state-of-the-art methods. Additionally, the framework is extended to handle real light field images by employing free-form deformation-based transformation matrices derived from the disparity map to map pixel positions from the input to the output. The model's efficacy is further validated using raw data from digital light field (DLF) cameras. Interactive and non-interactive frameworks represent the two prevailing paradigms in vector-based cross-lingual information retrieval (V-CLIR). While recent studies show non-interactivity offers greater scalability and efficiency, particularly for large query sets, we demonstrate that interactive models achieve superior performance. To combine the benefits of both approaches, we introduce a lightweight method that leverages precomputed noninteractive embeddings to enhance interactive models. This method requires minimal fine-tuning resources and computational overhead. Evaluation on six parallel corpora indicates substantial improvements, with an average MRR@10 gain of 11.5% over strong baselines. Furthermore, our model outperforms the EFIRv2+interactive+Rerank framework by 12.3% in MRR@10 while being 1,100 times faster and requiring 1,000 times less training data. Finally, we assess robustness across diverse contexts, including multilingual query generalization, domain adaptation, and low-resource languages. Although current models show limited robustness in these areas, our approach yields significant gains, with up to a 2.5-fold improvement in performance. This study presents design- and model-based estimators for small-area direct and indirect surveys, with a specific focus on low- and middle-income countries (LMICs). We utilize public health data from the 2017 Demographic and Health Survey conducted in Malawi to evaluate these methods. Our primary objective is to assess the relative performance of these estimators on outcomes where data is sparse. We examine three metrics: the prevalence of HIV in women of reproductive age, maternal mortality ratios, and child stunting rates. To achieve this, we analyze three design-based estimators—domain jackknife, domain generalized domain, and domain domain empirical Bayes—alongside two model-based estimators: Bayesian generalized linear mixed models (GZMM) and Bayesian small-area estimation models (BSAE). Data were preprocessed using two techniques: weighting adjustments via post-stratification and model-based estimation. The results indicate that while all methods performed adequately for survey data, the domain generalized domain estimator yielded the lowest bias. Furthermore, model-based approaches proved particularly beneficial when sample sizes were limited. Finally, we conclude with recommendations for future small-area estimation techniques. We investigate a quantum version of the betting framework introduced in [Ker18], specifically within the context of quantum optical communication channels. In this model, a gambler possesses an initial capital and may allocate a portion of it across various betting options offered by the world. The return on these bets is determined by the light received from a quantum channel, which the world selects according to a strategic policy. The gambler's objective is to determine an optimal betting strategy that maximizes the asymptotic growth rate of capital. In the quantum formulation, both the available betting options and the outcomes are represented by continuous-variable quantum states (coherent states). This specific setup was previously analyzed in [FMSV17] under the name "universal portfolio," and we examine its relationship with that study. By applying the quantum i.i.d. assumption, we derive an exact formula for the gambler's optimal growth rate. Furthermore, in the low-loss limit, we demonstrate an analogue of the horse betting result from [Ker18]: the optimal growth rate corresponds to the quantum relative entropy between the world's strategy and the uniform strategy. Finally, we analyze a scenario where the world's strategy consists of i.i.d. sampling from a fixed law, showing that the optimal growth rate equals the channel's capacity. This finding offers a new interpretation of quantum capacity and suggests a method for estimating it. Additionally, we explore an entanglement-assisted extension of the model. To support these findings, we provide a Python library implementing the model for the coherency set, alongside a program that numerically validates our theoretical results. This library is available on our repository.

Keywords: Quantum betting, optical communication, quantum relative entropy, universal portfolio, quantum capacity, quantum entropy.

The quasiparticle band alignments and optical properties of monolayer MA$_2$Z$_4$ (where M = Mo, W, Ti; A = Si, Ge; Z = N, P, As) were investigated using density functional theory combined with the GW approximation and Bethe-Salpeter equation. Results indicate that these materials possess direct band gaps and exhibit a stacking-independent excitonic peak, with the band alignment varying based on the specific element. Notably, the conduction band minimum (CBM) is located at the $\Gamma$ point for MA$_2$N$_4$ compounds, whereas it resides at the Q point for MA$_2$Ge$_4$ and MA$_2$As$_4$. Furthermore, the calculated optical absorption spectra for these materials show strong resemblance to those of monolayer MoS$_2$. These findings offer a comprehensive understanding of the electronic and optical characteristics of the entire MA$_2$Z$_4$ family, thereby facilitating the targeted design of novel two-dimensional materials. Additionally, the study provides a systematic analysis of the accuracy levels associated with various common approximations. Finally, the methodology established in this work is applicable to investigating the electronic and optical properties of other two-dimensional materials. Our analysis of the resulting protostellar system reveals a mass distribution of $M_{\rm disk} = 0.001M_{\rm star} = 0.001M_{\rm tot}$, a temperature of $T_{\rm disk} = 1000$ K, and a characteristic radius of $r_{\rm disk} = 100$ AU. These outcomes are consistent with previous numerical simulations and observational data. Furthermore, the simulated disk exhibits a size of $r_{\rm disk} = 100$ AU and a temperature of $T_{\rm disk} = 1000$ K that align with the conditions of the Taurus L1151 protostellar disk, as reported by Meeus et al. (2013). Additionally, the spectral energy distribution (SED) of our simulated system matches the SED of L1151, which was derived by Meeus et al. (2015). This agreement supports the conclusion that the internal disk structure of L1151 can be explained by the collapse of a prestellar core. Consequently, the SED serves as a critical tool for understanding the formation of disk structures around young stellar objects. Ultimately, we find that the prestellar core collapse model effectively accounts for the disk properties of young stellar objects. This suggests that the prestellar core collapse model is a viable explanation for disk formation around these objects. Atmospheric dispersion correctors (ADCs) are extensively utilized in ground-based telescopes to mitigate atmospheric dispersion introduced by the line-of-sight. This study focuses on atmospheric dispersion measurements (ADMs) conducted at the Very Large Telescope (VLT) using the FORS2 instrument, which is equipped with an integrated ADM. By analyzing 1,000 observations from the ESO Strategic Programme "The First 100 Billion Years," we developed a model for atmospheric parameters, including temperature, pressure, water vapor, and zenith angle. Our results indicate that the combined model accurately reflects atmospheric conditions, with a standard deviation of 0.5 K for temperature, 0.001 bar for pressure, 0.15 mas for water vapor, and 0.05 degrees for zenith angle. Additionally, we examined the impact of these parameters on ADM performance and provided recommendations for future enhancements to the ADM. These findings are particularly relevant for the upcoming ELT/METIS instrument, which will rely on an ADC operating at 1.0 microns, necessitating precise ADM functionality. This study addresses multi-period time series modeling within the deep learning framework. The objective is to forecast multiple future time series by decomposing predicted outputs into linear combinations of a limited number of latent basis time series. The proposed Bayesian Sparsity Regularization for Time Series Modeling (BS-Sparsity) utilizes sparse regularization to achieve this. We introduce an efficient variational inference algorithm grounded in the generalized mean field method, which approximates the Bayesian solution. We demonstrate our approach's effectiveness in short-term wind speed forecasting using the Wind-Pred dataset, showing superior performance compared to several leading deep learning methods. Additionally, application examples involving the GEOTRACE dataset are provided to further validate the method's capabilities. We introduce a supersymmetric extension of the minimal $U(1)_X$ model, incorporating right-handed neutrinos, at the TeV scale. Within this framework, both dark matter and electric charge can originate from the $U(1)_R$ symmetry associated with right-handed fields. By analyzing experimental constraints and incorporating a relic dark matter density consistent with observations, we investigate the resulting parameter space. Our analysis identifies viable scenarios where the dark matter candidate is the lightest neutral right-handed neutrino. Furthermore, we demonstrate that these scenarios naturally account for the neutrino oscillation data through the mechanism of seesaw neutrino mass generation. Finally, we discuss the potential detectability of these scenarios at future neutrinoless double beta decay experiments and at the LHC. A comprehensive parameter space map will be provided in an accompanying publication. Additionally, we examine a specific point in this space that predicts a neutrinoless double beta decay half-life within the current sensitivity range of experiments such as KamLAND-Zen and CUORE. Finally, we outline the signatures of this model at the HL-LHC and its potential distinguishability from the supersymmetric minimal $U(1)_L$ model. The detailed analysis of the parameter space, along with discussions on neutrinoless double beta decay and LHC signatures, is reserved for a forthcoming series of papers. We introduce a new machine learning-driven control algorithm designed for robotic manipulation and locomotion, specifically to enhance sample efficiency. Our method utilizes cost functions that integrate both task-level and state-level cost components. In task-level costs, the controller learns the policy mapping from states to actions. Conversely, costs at the state-level provide additional information regarding the reachability of specific future states, a piece of information that bypasses the need for the controller to explicitly understand the system's dynamics. We propose Cost-Guided Policy Optimization (CGPO), a novel control algorithm capable of utilizing these combined cost functions. We demonstrate the potential of using state-level costs to achieve precise, direct control of both linear and angular motion. Our approach relies on a new gradient estimator that utilizes first-order approximations of the costs. We validate our method by showing it can learn to navigate, walk, swim, and fly using a single motion data set. Furthermore, we demonstrate its effectiveness on a new robotic manipulation task: precisely cutting a piece of paper with a robotic knife. In both applications, our method achieves its objectives within a single trial, exhibiting a significant reduction in the number of required trials. Finally, we provide theoretical insights into the relationship between our approach and established policy gradient methods. These results collectively indicate the promise of combining task-level and state-level cost functions to achieve precise, controllable, and direct movement and manipulation in one trial. Toda conformal field theories represent natural extensions of Liouville conformal field theory and are expected to possess rich conformal symmetries. This work examines $\mathfrak{sl}_3$ Toda conformal field theory to investigate its conformal symmetry algebra. We demonstrate that this algebra includes higher-spin symmetries corresponding to the global subalgebra of the Kac-Moody algebra associated with $\mathfrak{sl}_3$. Employing a method inspired by recent research, we calculate the central charge and primary conformal weights, which align with known values for rational models. Furthermore, we establish that the symmetry algebra is infinite-dimensional and conjecture its specific structure. Finally, we present evidence supporting a proposal regarding the correspondence between rational and generic models. Our findings indicate that the spectrum of a rational model is isomorphic to that of a specific free fermion conformal field theory. Consequently, we propose that rational $\mathfrak{sl}_n$ Toda conformal field theories are equivalent to systems comprising $n-1$ free fermions. Additionally, we offer evidence suggesting that the symmetry algebra of this free fermion theory is a novel infinite-dimensional algebra termed $C^{sl}_n$. This algebra serves as a coset of the Kac-Moody algebra for $\mathfrak{sl}_n$ and was previously conjectured based on rigorous mathematical analysis. We conclude by outlining several promising directions for future research. This contrasts with the $\mathfrak{sl}_2$ Toda (sine-Liouville) model, which is equivalent to a free boson theory with only higher-spin symmetries. Twin-field quantum key distribution (TF-QKD) has become a promising solution for long-haul fiber-optic communication, yet its reliance on precise phase locking has traditionally hindered practical implementation. We introduce a practical variant of TF-QKD that eliminates the need for phase locking, thereby significantly reducing equipment costs and complexity. In this framework, a conventional coherent-state protocol functions as a classical channel to enable two remote users, Alice and Bob, to exchange secret keys. Our analysis demonstrates that this scheme offers security comparable to standard TF-QKD key rates. Furthermore, we validate the feasibility of this approach using commercial fibers, showing that it can achieve a secret key capacity of 1 bps over 10,000 km without phase locking. Additionally, we estimate that a fiber with an attenuation coefficient of 0.16 dB/km could support a secret key capacity of 10 bps at distances up to 4,000 km, all while maintaining phase locking-free operation. This results in an effective maximum transmission distance of approximately 15,000 km, achieving the ultimate limit of quantum key distribution. We anticipate that this practical TF-QKD scheme will facilitate the rapid deployment of global quantum communication networks. The PDRs are influenced by multiple stars within S1. Furthermore, we identified a correlation between the PDR and HI, suggesting that PDRs may be formed by the compression of HI by ionized gas. This model indicates that the PDRs are illuminated by ultraviolet radiation from the most massive star in S1, SMM1, and that the gas has a temperature of approximately 100 K. Ultimately, we conclude that the PDRs in S1 are the result of the combined radiation from multiple stars. This study is the first to provide a comprehensive survey of the distribution of ionized, atomic, and PDR gas around the S1 cluster. This paper aims to synthesize and categorize current transformer-based vision methods to highlight key trends and future directions. We begin by outlining the foundational transformer building blocks and their primary applications in vision, covering tasks such as image classification, object detection, segmentation, and others. Neural Architecture Search (NAS) utilizes reinforcement learning to automatically explore a vast architecture space in search of high-performance models. However, the target computational resource often suffers from resource contention within datacenter environments, leading to interference that degrades policy learning and compromises result quality. To address this, we introduce an interactive, interference-aware reinforcement learning framework. This approach dynamically adjusts the reward signal based on real-time resource contention to mitigate intermediate policy degradation. Additionally, a novel inter-epoch policy transfer technique is employed to speed up policy convergence. Extensive experiments across multiple workloads demonstrate that this framework significantly enhances policy convergence, yielding better results with up to a 10x speedup. Furthermore, the method generates superior models compared to standard reinforcement learning and outperforms state-of-the-art NAS approaches, such as ENAS, by up to 1.5% in Top-1 accuracy. Our code is available at https://github.com/ashwinbhat/Interference-Aware-NAS.

Pruning techniques have emerged as a promising avenue for both efficiency and interpretability within deep neural networks. By eliminating redundant components, researchers can derive insights into the internal workings of deep learning models. This study extends the features-through-pruning approach to convolutional networks, examining whether sparse feature selection can reveal their underlying structure. We investigate if convolutional networks can be interpreted as a collection of highly interconnected, sparse neurons and if their performance stems from the efficiency of their sparse subnetworks. Our findings indicate that while sparse feature selection is feasible, it does not necessarily lead to interpretable structures. Furthermore, subnetworks identified exclusively through pruning fail to generalize effectively. These results suggest that the sparsity achieved in highly efficient fully connected "winning lottery tickets" is not intrinsic to neural networks but rather emerges from the specific inductive biases of training algorithms. Consequently, we demonstrate that sparsification algorithms can produce sparse subnetworks that outperform their dense counterparts. This work underscores the potential of utilizing sparsity as a feature selection mechanism to enhance both the performance and interpretability of deep learning models. This study examines the optimal purchase of lottery tickets by introducing a novel, realistic scenario where a buyer lacks knowledge of upcoming draws and must acquire tickets over time. We introduce a new integer programming formulation to determine the optimal strategy for maximizing winning probabilities. Furthermore, we explore the associated computational challenges, demonstrating that even for small, practical integer values, the problem is likely NP-hard. Our numerical results indicate that our proposed approach can yield significant improvements in maximizing the expected value of purchased tickets. Additionally, we develop a new integer programming model designed to optimize the sale of expired lottery tickets, even after all draws have concluded. We suggest using this model for public sector planning to enhance the efficiency of expired ticket sales. Our computational testing confirms that this proposed model can achieve a public benefit of up to 10% in terms of expected value. Finally, we introduce a new clustering-based algorithm to solve this model for large-scale instances. We conclude by discussing how this algorithm can be applied in real-world contexts, such as managing a lottery booth. Our proposed methodology is supported by a real-world application where we optimized the sale of expired lottery tickets in Buenos Aires, Argentina. Our approach successfully increased the number of tickets sold by approximately 10% compared to previous methods. The valley concept is fundamental to understanding the electronic and optical properties of two-dimensional materials. This study investigates how two recently identified electron-phonon coupling mechanisms influence valley dynamics. The first mechanism involves phonons shifting the position of Fermi-valley states, which alters the valley Hall effect and valley Hall resistivity. The second mechanism features spin-phonon coupling, enabling phonon-mediated intervalley scattering that impacts valley relaxation times and electron mobility. These processes are analyzed in two specific systems: graphene and silicene, with a focus on the impact of different electron-phonon coupling models. Furthermore, the role of spin-orbit coupling in valley physics is examined within these systems. The findings are expected to enhance the understanding of electron-phonon interactions in two-dimensional materials and guide future experimental research. Additionally, the identified spin-phonon coupling mechanism is anticipated to influence the phonon-assisted spin Hall effect and magnetotransport phenomena in two-dimensional materials with strong spin-orbit coupling. The study concludes with a discussion on the potential applications of these results. The computational code used for this study is accessible at: https://github.com/abhishekdatta1992/Phonon-assisted-electron-phonon-coupling. The associated data can be found at: https://doi.org/10.1103/physrevresearch.4.023001.4. The source code is also available at: https://github.com/abhishekdatta1992/Phonon-assisted-electron-phonon-coupling/tree/master/valley_physics. The raw data supporting the results is available at: https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevResearch.4.023001.5. Abstract: The valley concept is fundamental to the valley Hall effect and electron mobility in two-dimensional materials. This work explores the effects of two new electron-phonon coupling mechanisms on these phenomena. The first mechanism involves phonons displacing the locations of Fermi-valley states, affecting the valley Hall effect and resistance. The second mechanism features spin-phonon coupling, leading to phonon-assisted intervalley scattering that impacts relaxation times and mobility. These effects are studied in graphene and silicene using different electron-phonon coupling models. The study also examines the impact of spin-orbit coupling on valley physics.

This paper introduces LEMDA, a novel cross-modal self-supervised domain adaptation algorithm, which secured first place in the "Visual Cross-Modal Domain Adaptation" track of the NeurIPS 2022 Visual Domain Adaptation Challenge. The challenge provided images from the source domain (VisA-L) and either text or speech for the target domain (VisA-S), requiring adaptation across this cross-modal gap. Leveraging the extensive text corpus, we employed a text self-supervised learning approach to adapt pre-trained image models to the target domain. Specifically, we utilized a combination of contrastive learning and masked language modeling to align images with modality-specific data, thereby significantly enhancing model performance on the target domain. Extensive experiments confirm the algorithm's efficacy in cross-modal adaptation, demonstrating substantial accuracy improvements over the baseline. Furthermore, our method achieves state-of-the-art results on the VisA-L dataset and establishes competitive performance on the VisA-S dataset. t-SNE is a widely adopted method for embedding high-dimensional data. It has demonstrated significant efficacy, particularly in visualizing small to medium-sized datasets. This study evaluates t-SNE performance on spherical data and introduces VMF-SNE, a novel variant that substitutes the Gaussian kernel with an VMF (Von-Mises-Fisher) kernel. We assess both approaches using synthetic and astronomical data. The results indicate that VMF-SNE outperforms standard t-SNE, offering superior data visualization and more accurate nearest-neighbor relationships. Additionally, we highlight the computational complexity of both algorithms and outline potential strategies for optimization. Finally, we compare the proposed method with existing VM-based techniques. The code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/abhishekkumar1998/vmf-sne. Our findings suggest that VMF-SNE is particularly well-suited for embedding spherical data, such as celestial objects. Furthermore, we note that recent advancements in machine learning have spurred extensive research into spherical data processing, including spherical CNNs, autoencoders, and clustering methods. However, research specifically addressing t-SNE for spherical data remains limited. We anticipate that VMF-SNE will prove valuable in this domain. Our future work will explore parameter optimization and scalability improvements for large datasets. We intend to compare VMF-SNE with other spherical data embedding algorithms in subsequent studies. The rapid and unattended evolution of quantum simulation has positioned it as a leading application for near-term quantum devices. However, the quantum advantage anticipated for this field is expected to be realized only in the mid-2020s under current experimental conditions. To accelerate this progress, it is essential to explore new algorithmic strategies that are both hardware-friendly and capable of simulating fermionic systems with high fidelity. In this work, we propose a hybrid digital-analog quantum computing algorithm designed to model fermionic systems. Our approach leverages the native connectivity of quantum hardware and utilizes fermion parity conservation to reduce the number of costly two-qubit gates. Additionally, we incorporate a variational component to mitigate errors arising from finite-time evolution. We demonstrate the application of our algorithm to the Kitaev chain and the Hubbard model, showing that the variational method can effectively capture system properties even under significant noise. Furthermore, we assess the quantum resource requirements of our proposed algorithm compared to existing digital and analog methods. These findings establish a pathway for the efficient quantum simulation of fermionic systems on hybrid digital-analog near-term quantum computers. Finally, we examine the potential applications of this algorithm within the broader quantum computing landscape. Our results are supported by extensive simulations and the open-source QASC framework, which is available at https://github.com/Quantum-AI-Simulation-Centre/QASC. This work provides an explicit formula for the pullback of the Hitchin connection defined on the universal Teichmüller space to a sixfold integral logarithmic hypergeometric function associated with Veech curves. As a result, we demonstrate that the monodromy group of this connection contains a copy of the braid group. Furthermore, we show that certain special values within the connection are equivalent to polyzeta values with multi-index (1, 1, ..., 1). In the instance of Loewner curves, this connection offers an explicit solution to the Bloch conjecture. Additionally, we establish that the pullback of the Chordial connection to the universal Teichmüller space yields a hypergeometric function known as the Dyck function. Finally, we derive a differential equation with finite rank that governs the pullback of the Hitchin connection to the moduli space of Veech curves for curves with small genus. Our methods also generate explicit solutions expressed through polyzeta values and provide an explanation for the recently conjectured relation between the pullback of the Hitchin connection and the Kaluza-Weyl connection proposed by Takahiro Nishikawa. In collaboration with Takahiro Nishikawa, we have extended these results to the Kaluza-Weyl connection. Over the past few years, remote work has become increasingly common in the IT sector, with many companies implementing fully remote schemes. This shift significantly affects project management, as distributed teams face challenges in communication and collaboration. Consequently, managing distributed Scrum software engineering projects is a complex endeavor. This study aims to quantify the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on the success of remote software engineering projects, specifically within the Scrum framework. Utilizing a multi-method approach, the research combines data from 100 online surveys with 10 in-depth case studies of projects launched during the pandemic. Findings indicate that while remote work presents difficulties for Scrum teams, it does not inherently hinder project success. Ultimately, the report offers practical recommendations to assist organizations in effectively managing their remote Scrum initiatives. The concept of non-singularity extends beyond square matrices to encompass higher-dimensional matrix functions. The Gau-Wu (GW) number, a specific function, serves this purpose and is particularly effective for assessing the non-singularity of Hermitian matrices. This paper selects arrowhead matrices, denoted as $AH_n(x)$, which appear in various mathematical fields, to calculate their GW numbers. We present a derivation for a specific closed-form expression of the GW number for these matrices and utilize this finding to compute the GW numbers for select matrices within the Arrows and $4\times 4$ class. Additionally, we examine the relationship between the determinants and GW numbers of $4\times 4$ arrowhead matrices. This research is grounded in the work of J. Liu, S. Liu, and C. Using the ALICE detector at the LHC, researchers measured the elliptic flow ($v_2$) of electrons originating from beauty hadron decays in Pb-Pb collisions at $\sqrt{s_{\rm NN}}$ = 5.02 TeV within the transverse momentum range of 1.5 to 6 GeV/$c$. This was achieved by analyzing the same-sign and opposite-sign correlations between electrons and charged hadrons. The study reports the first direct observation of $v_2$ for these high-$p_{\rm T}$ electrons, demonstrating that they exhibit non-zero collective flow behavior consistent with that of light hadrons. Additionally, the electron $v_2$ values are compared against predictions derived from a state-of-the-art hybrid model. These findings indicate that beauty quarks participate in the hydrodynamic evolution of the quark-gluon plasma and are sufficiently light to respond to its anisotropic expansion. Furthermore, the results suggest that the elliptic flow of electrons is primarily determined by the $p_{\rm T}$ distribution of the parent beauty hadrons. Finally, the combined $v_2$ measurements for electrons and light hadrons provide a novel method for investigating the in-medium properties of beauty quarks. The consistency between the electron $v_2$ data and model predictions, which rely on bottomron ellipticities derived from heavy-ion collisions, supports the hypothesis that the $v_2$ of beauty hadrons arises from the initial anisotropies in the beauty quark $p_{\rm T}$ distribution. Ultimately, the elliptic flow of electrons from beauty hadron decays in heavy-ion collisions serves as a valuable probe for understanding the interaction of heavy quarks with the quark-gluon plasma. These findings are based on Pb-Pb collision data from Run 1, collected using the ALICE detector at the Large Hadron Collider. The analysis utilized a dataset with an integrated luminosity of 250 $\mu$b$^{-1}$, corresponding to an average multiplicity of 120,000 events per unit rapidity. The results were presented at the 55th International Conference on High Energy Physics (ICHEP 2020) in Madrid, Spain. The full paper is available at arXiv:2101.00079. The underlying data can be accessed via https://alice-dataops.gitlab.io/ALICE_152_Electron2020/

Driven by the hypothesis that finite cell complexes capture intrinsic geometric information via their Betti numbers, we investigate the chromatic versions of these complexes. Our primary finding is that, unlike the standard case, the persistent homology of chromatic complexes does not yield a topological invariant. Furthermore, we demonstrate that even reconstructing geometric data at any scale remains unattainable. However, by utilizing chromatic simplicial volumes, we establish that it is possible to reconstruct a subset of geometric data, albeit with a significantly more complex and less intuitive persistence diagram. This (non-)invertibility stems partly from the fact that chromatic complexes associated with distinct triangulations of the same geometric shape can be chromatically homotopy equivalent. Consequently, we explore various methods to address this issue. Additionally, we present a novel approach to chromatic reconstruction that leverages finite point sets on geodesics, thereby enhancing both geometric intuition and algorithmic efficiency. Finally, we examine the relationship between chromatic reconstruction and the covering problem. Through numerical experiments, we analyze the trade-off between reconstruction error and runtime, revealing that chromatic reconstruction offers substantial advantages in both error metrics and computational speed. These results indicate that chromatic techniques are highly promising for real-world applications involving noisy point clouds. Furthermore, we propose a chromatic version of persistent homology that, while not strictly invertible, is at least partially so, and we establish an upper bound for its Betti numbers. The computational efficiency of our chromatic approach is also superior to other inverse triangulation methods. Our code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/alejandro-fernandez/chromatic-persistent-homology. This study examines the $K$-user linear interference network, comprising $K$ users, $M$ antennas per user, and a total of $T$ time slots. We evaluate the performance disparity between optimal precoding and binary precoding (where users employ independent, uniform binary phase shifts) across all possible configurations of $M$ and $T$. Our findings indicate that when $M$ and $T$ approach infinity such that their ratio $M/T$ remains constant, optimal precoding surpasses binary precoding by an extremal GDoF ($\text{GDoF}_{\text{ext}}$) of $\Theta(\sqrt{K})$. This result holds specifically when $M/T$ scales as $1/\sqrt{K}$ or faster. Conversely, if $M/T$ scales as $\sqrt{K}$ or faster, the $\text{GDoF}_{\text{ext}}$ of optimal precoding is limited to $\Theta(K^{1/4})$. Furthermore, we extend the concept of $\text{GDoF}_{\text{ext}}$ to scenarios with finite $M$ and $T$, demonstrating that the $\text{GDoF}_{\text{ext}}$ gain of optimal precoding over random precoding (where each user selects a random vector from the complex unit sphere) remains $\Theta(\sqrt{K})$. Additionally, we observe that optimal precoding yields the same $\text{GDoF}_{\text{ext}}$ gain as random precoding over a Gaussian codebook when $M$ is sufficiently large relative to $T$. These conclusions are supported by a detailed analysis of the necessary and sufficient conditions for the existence of solutions to the minimum mean square error (MMSE) estimation problem for users under optimal, random, and Gaussian precoding strategies. Finally, we explore the implications of these findings regarding the fundamental limits of $\text{GDoF}_{\text{ext}}$ in wireless communication networks. Specifically, we demonstrate that the $\text{GDoF}_{\text{ext}}$ gain of optimal precoding over any other precoding strategy is bounded by $\Theta(\sqrt{K})$. We further conjecture that this bound is tight for optimal precoding relative to random precoding, thereby confirming that random precoding is nearly optimal. The necessity to categorize activities within auditing standards has been established. This paper introduces a new framework for categorizing audit activities that integrates formal concept analysis and Dempster-Shafer theory. The process begins by modeling auditing knowledge through an ontology, which is subsequently translated into an instance-based knowledge base using a method proposed by the authors. Categorization is achieved by constructing an implication network derived from this knowledge base and applying belief rule-based rules to the network. The study validates the proposed framework through a case study of internal control, with results demonstrating that the generated categorization effectively supports the modeling of audit procedures. The paper concludes by outlining future research directions. Keywords: Audit procedure modeling, flexible categorization, formal concept analysis, Dempster-Shafer theory, ontology.

We present a straightforward approach for sampling from the Strauss process. This method adheres to the over-repulsion constraint by connecting points from two independent Poisson point processes using stitching. We provide an explicit formula for the resulting point process and demonstrate its feasibility when the decay parameter is small enough to permit significant stitching. Additionally, we provide simulated results. This technique builds upon and extends the stitched Poisson process introduced by Shafiei and Shiri (2019) and the pairing-coalescent point process described by Shiri (2019). Our method is notably simpler than the rejection sampling approach proposed by Diggle (1988). Furthermore, we show that the Strauss process can be derived as the limit of stitching when the Poisson rate approaches infinity, a result that also recovers pair interactions from pair-correlation functions, as noted by Shiri (2019). Ultimately, this offers a new perspective on constructing interacting particle systems. We also explore an extension of this method to generate the Gibbs process associated with Diggle's one-dimensional pair potential, $\log V(x) = -\nu \mathbb{I}_{(-r,r)}(x)$. This specific pair potential was previously addressed by other authors using rejection sampling, marking the first instance where Gibbs processes are generated via stitching. The main contribution is a constructive representation of pair interactions, which is valuable for understanding the internal structure of interacting particle systems. We believe this approach can also aid in developing new point processes. Specifically, we propose an extension to generate inhomogeneous interacting particle systems, where intensity and repulsion are defined by functions. We illustrate this proposal by applying it to generate a process with two such functions. This work represents a significant step toward achieving the long-standing goal of constructing particle systems with a specified pair-correlation function. Additionally, it provides a new interpretation for the pairing-coalescent point process introduced by Shiri (2019). Finally, we outline some potential research directions inspired by this study. Our hope is that this work will inspire others to explore generating interacting particle systems through stitching.

**Keywords:** Pair potential; Pair interaction; Pair potential process; Pairing-coalescent point process; Pair-correlation function; Strauss process; Strauss process with a gamma mixing distribution.

The Generalized Uncertainty Principle (GUP) is a universal framework that incorporates quantum gravity effects into standard quantum mechanics. Within the non-relativistic framework of Galilean relativity, these effects manifest as an infinite mass scale, $\Lambda_{\rm GUP}$, characterizing the associated deformation. However, this study demonstrates that when relativistic transformations are applied to GUP-deformed states, the GUP scale transforms in accordance with special relativity, thereby introducing a momentum scale, $\Lambda_{\rm GUP}\sqrt{g}$, where $g$ represents the Lorentz factor. This relativistic momentum scale is significantly lower than the Galurevian scale, making it more readily observable in high-energy processes. These findings suggest that precise measurements of the GUP scale, utilizing data from high-energy collisions, could potentially determine the nature of quantum gravity, specifically distinguishing between Galilean and Lorentz invariance. Such a determination would resolve a fundamental issue regarding the symmetry group of quantum spacetime, which remains independent of the Planck scale. Furthermore, this research underscores the necessity of a comprehensive understanding of Lorentz transformations within deformed quantum mechanics, a topic that has received insufficient attention in the literature. The paper concludes by outlining potential extensions of this work. Finally, the study examines the kinematics of a single particle under both Galilean and Lorentz transformations, deriving the corresponding inverse transformations and examining the associated inconsistencies. These issues are subsequently addressed through two distinct approaches: Lorentz transformations that fail to align with the covariant GUP action, and Lorentz transformations that preserve the form of the GUP uncertainty relation. The latter scenario yields a universal maximum speed, $\nu_{\rm max}$, which may differ from the speed of light, $c$. The authors argue that the specific value of this speed can be determined through precise time-of-flight experiments. Additionally, the paper derives the transformation laws for the GUP-deformed energy-momentum four-vector and the Lorentz force, while also deriving the transformation rules for the electromagnetic potential four-vector and the Lorentz gauge condition. Finally, the paper derives the field transformation laws for the GUP-deformed electromagnetic four-potential, which reduce to standard Lorentz transformations when $\nu_{\rm max}=c$. The text concludes with a discussion on the physical significance of these results. Multitasking scheduling encompasses scheduling systems where processing capabilities are divisible and can be shared among multiple jobs. This study explores the study of online algorithms in this context, specifically addressing scheduling on uniform machines and identical machines with reconfigurable computing power. We demonstrate that the sample complexity for determining the optimal rate for a specific scheduling problem scales logarithmically with the maximum error permitted. Furthermore, we apply this finding to the fully online budgeted ad selling problem, proving that the sample complexity for identifying a high-quality solution for this sale is also logarithmic with respect to the desired error margin. Finally, we examine a scenario involving a limited number of sample sales and introduce a novel sales strategy that effectively leverages this data. Our theoretical findings are complemented by computational results that validate this approach. This research is conducted within a multidisciplinary framework, integrating concepts from scheduling, online algorithms, and machine learning. Consequently, we establish a link between the sample complexity of data-driven decision-making and the complexity inherent in multitasking scheduling problems. The paper concludes by outlining several potential avenues for future research. This work is derived from the thesis of the second author. This paper introduces a reduced-order model for the dynamics of a monopod leg during the hopping phase of a two-legged robot, accounting for energy exchange with yielding terrain. Our primary finding is that energy exchange is governed by the robot's vertical velocity at the end of the ground contact phase. We initially develop this reduced-order model and validate it against full-order simulations across various yielding terrains, demonstrating close alignment with the actual dynamics. Subsequently, we create a simplified periodic gait for the robot and verify its stability under parameter perturbations. Finally, we implement model predictive control (MPC) to optimize performance, enabling the robot to adapt to diverse yielding terrains and achieve a record-breaking vertical leap of 1.5 meters. We believe these modeling and optimization methods will facilitate the design of effective gait strategies for legged robots facing challenging, yielding environments. The proposed model and MPC algorithm are also expected to be applicable to multi-legged robots. Internet of Things (IoT) systems are becoming increasingly prevalent in both residential and industrial settings, driving the need for robust security and dependable communication protocols. A critical security measure for these systems is the regular update of firmware to fix vulnerabilities and enhance resilience. However, deploying and executing these updates in IoT networks is complex due to diverse hardware architectures, heterogeneous communication protocols, and the inherent unreliability of wireless communications. This paper presents a comprehensive analysis of large-scale IoT network experiments conducted on 300 IoT nodes using LoRaWAN, a widely adopted protocol. Our findings indicate that attempting updates during high network load results in the loss of approximately 90% of nodes, whereas nodes operating as end devices experience minimal disruption. Consequently, we propose a straightforward algorithm that leverages the specific characteristics of each node to schedule updates, thereby mitigating risks and ensuring a reliable update process. Furthermore, we outline an implementation of this algorithm on LoRaWAN and discuss its potential applicability to other protocols. This approach can significantly improve the update reliability of the most extensively deployed IoT networks globally. Additionally, we provide an online demonstration of our method at https://demo.iot-fuwu.org/. Given that this work is open-source, researchers can easily replicate our results by accessing the corresponding GitHub repository at https://github.com/SmartCityResearchGroup/IoT-FUWU. This work was partially funded by the EU-funded project Smart City Research Group (SCiG), accessible at https://www.smartcityresearchgroup.eu/. Smart city initiatives are expected to be the primary adopters of IoT technology, with an anticipated 10 billion IoT devices by 2030, as noted in the 2018 White Paper on the Internet of Things (IoT). These deployments will likely rely on wireless communication, which is inherently unreliable, complicating the delivery of crucial updates. This challenge is particularly acute in large-scale networks where managing 100,000 nodes is not uncommon. The primary objective of this work is to enhance the reliability of IoT network updates. We aim to achieve a success rate of at least 90% for every node, ensuring that updates are delivered to every device. To achieve this, we must address two key challenges: (1) the performance of the update process itself, and (2) the ability to perform these updates without interrupting normal network operations. Interactive Graph Search (IGS) is a data-driven method designed to help users identify target objects within large datasets. This study introduces the first fully automated, fully data-driven Interactive Graph Search model capable of handling multiple targets while adhering to a budget limit on the maximum number of unvisited nodes. This constraint is crucial for multi-target scenarios, where visiting too many nodes could compromise the ability to retrieve all targets. We rigorously evaluate the proposed BIMUSAT model against baseline approaches using standard benchmark datasets and report the results. The experimental findings demonstrate that BIMUSUAT effectively balances performance and efficiency, successfully retrieving multiple targets within the specified visitation budget. Notably, BIMUSUAT achieves higher recall rates than baseline methods, improving target retrieval from 70% to 80% and from 60% to 70% respectively. Furthermore, a case study on a real-world multiple target identification problem in the power industry confirms the model's practical effectiveness. The results indicate that BIMUSUAT can recover 80% of multiple target objects in complex industrial networks. The source code is accessible at: https://github.com/Chenchenchenchen/BIMUSUAT. Quantum machine learning (QML) holds the promise of redefining the relationship between data and models. Adversarial attacks on QML represent a nascent field that has not yet been thoroughly researched. This study investigates the existence and characteristics of adversarial examples within quantum classifiers. We examine the adversarial robustness of both quantum neural networks and support vector machines by introducing adversarial examples and analyzing their impact on classification outcomes. Furthermore, by drawing a parallel between the von Neumann entropy of quantum states and the Shannon entropy of classical data, we demonstrate that adversarial examples in quantum classifiers possess a distinct nature compared to their classical counterparts. Our findings indicate that quantum adversarial examples are more potent and potentiate more broadly than those in classical settings. Finally, we explore the existence of universal adversarial examples and perturbations for quantum classifiers, a concept that is well-established in the classical domain. These results hold significant implications for the security and reliability of quantum machine learning systems. Our research underscores the urgent need for the development of universal adversarial training methods tailored specifically for quantum classifiers. Additionally, we provide open-source code to facilitate the advancement of this field. We establish that for sufficiently close spherical limits, the Steklov eigenvalues of smoothly bounded domains in $\mathbb{R}^n$ admit a polynomial moduli space description relative to the bounded harmonic Dirichlet energy over the domain. Our primary application demonstrates that the $k$-th Steklov eigenvalue of a nearly spherical domain in $\mathbb{R}^n$ is strictly greater than that of a ball sharing the same surface area, calculated as an explicit polynomial in the truncation order. This result holds provided the domain's deviations from sphericity have a total Fourier mode index exceeding $k$. Furthermore, our approach yields a new Steklov version of the Yau-Chen sphere theorem. In a complementary finding, we explicitly determine the Steklov eigenvalues of a nearly spherical domain when these values are defined via normal derivatives on the boundary. This explicit formula confirms a recent conjecture by Hardt and Tostad as well as a related conjecture by Li and Topping. Additionally, our methodology offers novel explicit constructions of harmonic functions with minimal Dirichlet energy on nearly spherical domains. Finally, we explore applications to highly symmetric domains, including ellipsoids, and illustrate our general results by explicitly computing the moduli space of Steklov eigenvalues for perturbed 3-balls. In this specific instance, we prove that the first nontrivial Steklov eigenvalue of a perturbed ball is strictly less than that of a ball with an equivalent surface area, a result that contrasts with the outcome for the Dirichlet eigenvalue. Our analysis also reveals new connections between Steklov spectral geometry and the geometry of harmonic functions, the theory of isoperimetric inequalities, and the mathematical theory of ellipsoids. Finally, we establish new explicit bounds for Steklov eigenvalues of ellipsoids, thereby confirming a conjecture by Li and Topping. In the process, we derive explicit formulas for the spectral gap of ellipsoids and their corresponding eigenfunctions. Moreover, we explicitly calculate the first nontrivial Steklov eigenvalue for ellipsoids with small axis ratios, contrasting it with the value for a sphere of equal surface area. This calculation provides a concrete example of the general result regarding the moduli space description of Steklov eigenvalues for nearly spherical domains. Our work includes the full derivation of the spectral gap for ellipsoids, along with a detailed examination of the spectral geometry of ellipsoids possessing small axis ratios. Conformance checking involves comparing the behavior of modeled processes against observed process behavior captured in event logs. Alignments represent a cutting-edge method for identifying, locating, and measuring deviations in process executions (traces) relative to reference process models. However, alignments are computationally expensive and typically require complete process executions that span from start to finish. In reality, we often deal with partial process executions represented by trace fragments, and in many scenarios, only post-completion activity sets are accessible. This paper introduces infix/postfix alignments, a novel alignment type for trace fragments that combines infix alignments (for pre-completion activities) with postfix alignments (for post-completion activity sets). Additionally, we investigate strategies for calculating infix/postfix alignments efficiently and assess the quality of these alignments in comparison to related alternatives. The proposed approach is implemented in the ProM process mining framework, and a case study on a business process from the automotive industry demonstrates the benefits of this methodology. The ProM framework offers a library for computing infix/postfix alignments, which is accessible at https://github.com/Ad-hoc-Research/infix-postfix-alignments. The example trace data utilized in this case study can be downloaded from https://github.com/Ad-hoc-Research/infix-postfix-alignments/tree/master/data. Our findings indicate that infix/postfix alignments yield high-quality results when applied to post-completion activity sets. Furthermore, they outperform alternative approaches in scenarios involving long event logs and complex process models. The resulting alignment scores are comparable to those achieved using full traces. The primary advantage of infix/postfix alignments lies in their application to short event logs, which significantly reduces the computational effort needed to determine alignments. Additionally, these methods are well-suited for trace fragments that may be incomplete due to data privacy concerns. The primary limitation is the necessity to perform separate calculations for infix and postfix alignments, though this limitation is not unique to the proposed approach. The study also identifies several avenues for future research, including the development of heuristics for efficient alignment computation, the creation of quality metrics for trace fragments, and the formulation of invariants for these alignments. Overall, this work represents a significant step toward achieving the ideal scenario of conformance checking with process models and partial observations. The findings open up new research opportunities, such as utilizing process models to select a subset of events from large event logs for analysis. Furthermore, the results suggest a potential shift in how we approach conformance checking in an increasingly privacy-conscious world.
