Parameter-efficient tuning focuses on adjusting only a minimal fraction of parameters within pre-trained models to accommodate downstream tasks. This paper introduces PASTA, a method that enables effective adaptation of pre-trained language models for specific tasks by fine-tuning exclusively the embeddings associated with special tokens. PASTA surpasses current state-of-the-art approaches that rely on prompt engineering without any fine-tuning. Furthermore, we demonstrate that our approach significantly improves the effectiveness of the recently introduced SimplePrompt method across various benchmarks. Additionally, we show that fine-tuning only the embeddings surrounding special tokens yields substantial gains compared to fine-tuning the entire vocabulary in PARENT and simple encoder-decoder architectures. Experimental results indicate that PASTA achieves state-of-the-art performance on the SuperGLUE and GLUE benchmarks, while delivering competitive scores on NaturalQAs and SQuAD. Furthermore, we observe that PASTA matches or exceeds human performance on several few-shot English question-answering benchmarks. To the best of our knowledge, this marks the first instance of achieving human-level few-shot QA results using a purely unsupervised pre-trained model. This paper investigates the challenge of assessing element addition to a set, where an agent possesses initial knowledge of a context $C$ and receives a query $Q$ requesting the single element that maximizes the size of the most relevant context. We evaluate the performance of preference ranking in both contextual and non-contextual variants across fair and unfair contexts, analyzing how varying levels of element desirability within agents' preferences influence average satisfaction scores. Our per se analysis reveals that contextual preference ranking (CR) consistently outperforms non-Contextual CR (CCR) when combined with fair initial knowledge bases. However, outcomes differ for unfair knowledge bases: CCR surpasses CR when negative valuations are uniform across all elements, whereas CR exceeds CCR's average satisfaction under other conditions. These findings are supported by simulations and theoretical results. Ultimately, we demonstrate the necessity of distinguishing between contextual and non-contextual approaches and highlight the critical impact of knowledge base fairness on addition problems. This study examines the link between thermodynamic and dynamic properties near the glass transition using a glass-forming polymer fluid as a case study. The model consists of a long chain of hard spheres connected by a harmonic potential. We establish a strong correlation between the chain's conformational entropy and viscosity by employing the coarse-grained mode coupling theory (cMCT) to generate flow curves. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the transition from the cage effect to viscoelastic behavior is closely tied to the shift from ballistic to diffusive dynamics. Finally, our results confirm that the thermal equation of state accurately describes the polymer model, indicating that its thermodynamic behavior remains largely independent of its specific dynamic characteristics. These findings provide valuable insights into the complex interplay between thermodynamics and dynamics in supercooled fluids. Additionally, the rigorous and efficient combination of the polymer model with cMCT enables a detailed analysis of the dynamics associated with various structural motifs. This approach can be extended to other systems, such as colloidal suspensions, to explore their distinct thermodynamic and dynamic interactions. Ultimately, our work underscores the critical role of polymer size in shaping these interactions. Specifically, we show that the polymer's contour length significantly influences the viscosity of the resulting fluid. These conclusions are supported by a numerical study of the same bead-spring model. Finally, the numerical results reinforce the observation that polymer size dictates the system's dynamic thermodynamic state. Specifically, shorter chains exhibit thermodynamic dynamics similar to those of the hard-sphere model, whereas longer chains display unique behaviors that differ from both the hard-sphere model and standard polymer fluid theory. This suggests that polymer size is a key factor in understanding the complex interplay between thermal and dynamic properties in supercooled fluids. Transformer-based language models have demonstrated a remarkable ability to acquire various linguistic capabilities, including a degree of logical reasoning, solely through standard next-token prediction tasks. This paper investigates the conditions under which large transformer models fail to handle specific linguistic phenomena, focusing on negation and theories regarding time and quantification. We utilize a diverse range of data sources, such as CLUTRR and discrete world-state simulations, to create tasks specifically tailored to examine models' proficiency with negated expressions. Our findings indicate that transformer models struggle with negated time expressions, negative quantifiers like "not all" and not "every," and negative existential quantification. Furthermore, we explore potential reasons for these failures, emphasizing the absence of grounded negative experiences during pretraining. Finally, we assess whether incorporating structured training data, including causal graphs, can enhance the model's ability to process negation. To support this research, we have made our training data and evaluation scripts publicly available. The accompanying code and data can be accessed at: https://github.com/robertklimovic/dev_negation. Attention mechanisms have become a cornerstone of Neural Machine Translation (NMT), yet they often struggle to assign suitable weights to all source words when translating specific target words. This limitation can result in grammatical errors during generation. To address this, we introduce a novel Look-ahead Attention mechanism designed to incorporate future source context into the current attention pattern. This approach enables the model to leverage unseen source context for translating the current token while maintaining attention to previous tokens. Our mechanism comprises a standard Multi-Head Attention layer followed by a Look-Back Head that reweights the attention matrix using past source context, and a Look-Ahead Head reweights it using future context. Additionally, we developed a Look-ahead Bi-LSTM, which utilizes future tokens to refine the representation of current tokens. Experiments on German-English and French-English translation tasks demonstrate that our Look-ahead Attention mechanism reduces grammatical errors by 16% and 11%, respectively, compared to a model without this mechanism, while achieving performance on par with other state-of-the-art models. Furthermore, the combined Look-ahead Attention and Look-ahead Bi-LSTM approach further decreases grammatical errors by 5% and 4% on the German and French datasets, respectively. We apply this expansion to compute the entanglement entropy for a Vasiliev theory in three-dimensional bulk spacetime, which is dual to a three-dimensional CFT with an interacting vector-vector-vector vertex involving $N$ fields. Our findings indicate that the large-$N$ limit of the entanglement entropy for any subregion in such theories is entirely captured by the contribution from the $s$-channel identity block of the four-point function, rendering it identical to the free theory's entropy at all coupling values. This result aligns with thermal entropy, which we calculate analytically within the large-$N$ limit. Furthermore, we demonstrate that within the Poincaré disk, the $s$-channel identity block corresponds to the horizon of a black hole situated at the origin, thereby recovering the known large-$N$ expression for the holographic entanglement entropy of Vasiliev theory. Finally, we explore extensions of these results to other spacetime dimensions, conical entanglement wedges, and theories possessing a holographic dual. Additionally, we examine the relationship between entanglement entropy and entanglement wedge minimizers, revealing a unique relationship in the large-$N$ limit of these theories. Specifically, we find that the entanglement wedge minimizer is always the $s$-channel identity block, even when it does not correspond to the entanglement entropy. This conclusion is supported by numerical evidence from the CFT and holographic calculations for Vasiliev theory. We also examine the implications of these results for the $1/N$ expansion of the entanglement entropy and the structure of the conformal block decomposition of four-point functions in the CFT. This note presents an exact solution to their pricing PDE and demonstrates its utilization in specific cases. Our findings suggest that, unlike the existence proof, the practical application of this solution may encounter numerical instability. Ultimately, in the context of Asian option pricing, we argue that the solution derived by Cao and Yang (2020) is more suitable for computation than the one obtained here.

The origin of the diffuse gamma-ray background remains a significant enigma in astrophysics. This study investigates whether large-scale structures, specifically clusters of galaxies, could be a primary source of this enigmatic signal. We developed a model for gamma-ray emission from these clusters, utilizing data on their spatial distribution and individual characteristics, alongside a theoretical framework for the astrophysical processes driving the signal. Our results indicate that the gamma-ray flux from large-scale structures is on the order of $10^{-7}$ ph cm$^{-2}$ s$^{-1}$, with the most probable energy peak located between 100 MeV and 1 GeV. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this flux exhibits a high correlation with the distribution of large-scale structures, a relationship that could potentially be tested through the observation of gamma-ray point sources. Finally, we compare our model's predictions against current observational data. Although there is no significant discrepancy between our model and existing observations, the model successfully accounts for a portion of the observed flux. Consequently, the gamma-ray flux originating from large-scale structures is likely a non-negligible component of the background diffuse gamma-ray flux. Additionally, we propose that a substantial fraction of the excess gamma-ray background previously attributed to the Galactic center may actually stem from large-scale structures. These findings suggest that a substantial part of the background diffuse gamma-ray flux is of extragalactic origin. Finally, we outline potential future prospects for constraining the gamma-ray flux from large-scale structures. Specifically, we predict that future space missions, such as the Cherenkov Telescope Array (CTA), will be capable of detecting the gamma-ray flux from large-scale structures. This capability will enable a more precise determination of the gamma-ray flux's spectral characteristics and the spatial distribution of its sources. Furthermore, the ability to resolve this flux into individual point sources will allow for a more accurate assessment of the gamma-ray flux from large-scale structures. This will facilitate a more comprehensive understanding of the physical processes responsible for the background diffuse gamma-ray flux, as well as a more precise determination of its total magnitude. Ultimately, these advancements will significantly aid in unraveling the mystery of the background diffuse gamma-ray flux. Our previous work explored the contribution of small-scale structures to this background flux. This approach incorporates the long-range attractive interaction between electrons, which arises from the exchange of a single optical phonon. Theoretically, this attraction leads to the formation of a bound state with a finite gap located below the Fermi level. By employing the Jahn-Teller model, we demonstrate that the binding energy of this state is highly sensitive to the magnitude of local electron-phonon coupling. Our findings indicate that the proposed mechanism is viable in the high-$T_c$ compound YBa$_2$Cu$_3$O$_{4-x}$. Furthermore, we explore the potential applicability of this mechanism to other cuprates, as well as to the Cu-oxide layers found in high-$T_c$ pnictides and iron-based superconductors. Additionally, we outline several experimental techniques that could be utilized to test our model. This study offers a new framework for describing the low-energy electronic spectrum in cuprates and provides an alternative explanation for the observed nodal symmetry of the Fermi surface. Finally, our results suggest a novel pathway for achieving attractive coupling between electrons. These conclusions are supported by prior experimental data regarding electron-phonon coupling in YBa$_2$Cu$_3$O$_{4-x}$. Specifically, optical phonon modes have been identified that exhibit a significantly higher electron-phonon coupling constant compared to the broader average derived from the isotope effect on $T_c$. Moreover, Raman spectroscopy reveals a substantial increase in the intensity of these optical phonon signals as the material transitions from the metallic state to an insulating one. These observations are consistent with the model's prediction of a narrow, phonon-induced bound state band situated below the Fermi level. Consequently, the nodelling symmetry of the Fermi level in cuprates can be attributed to the attractive phonon-mediated interaction. Furthermore, our results suggest a new method for inducing electron attraction by manipulating the local electron-phonon coupling. Recent advancements in Bayesian neural networks have enabled the analysis of uncertainty within deep models. This study leverages such networks, capable of identifying uncertainty to detect anomalies, to develop a reversible steganography technique. By utilizing out-of-distribution (OOD) uncertainty, we demonstrate how to embed and subsequently extract data while maintaining the statistical integrity of the carrier signals, ensuring their distribution remains indistinguishable from the original population. We evaluate the performance of Bayesian neural networks with inference time complexity $O(NP^2)$ against the widely used OOD detector, Outlier Exposure (OE), which exhibits $O(NP)$ complexity, where $N$ represents dataset size and $P$ represents model parameter count. Furthermore, we introduce a novel EV-Clustering metric to assess the efficacy of cover signals in preserving the covertext population's characteristics. This approach surpasses the commonly employed Kolmogorov-Smirnov (KS) test, which is limited to univariate distributions. Finally, our experimental results indicate that while both EV-Clustering and K-S tests demonstrate that carrier signals are statistically identical to cover signals, the EV-Clustering method offers superior sensitivity in distinguishing the signal distributions. Additionally, the proposed EV-Clustering test supports the application of reversible steganography to high-dimensional datasets, a capability beyond the reach of current OE detectors. Overall, our findings suggest that while OE detectors are effective for small-scale data, Bayesian neural networks offer a more robust solution for large-scale data insertion tasks. To the best of our knowledge, this represents the first instance of reversible steganography employing Bayesian neural networks. These observations reveal a massive outflow with a mass of 1.5 x 10^7 solar masses, a momentum of 1.5 x 10^30 N, and a momentum-flux of 1.5 x 10^38 erg/s. The outflow extends approximately 1.5 kpc from the galaxy's center, and its morphology suggests a high-velocity, low-mass gas component. The momentum and momentum-flux values align with recent studies of outflows in starburst galaxies. The high velocity (200 km/s) and low mass (10^5 solar masses) of the outflow indicate that it originates from the molecular cloud layer, driven by star formation. In this regime, the model reduces to a quasilinear diffusion equation featuring potentially nonlinear diffusion coefficients. Dwarf galaxies are the most abundant type of galaxy in the universe, yet our understanding of their interstellar medium (ISM) remains limited. This review examines the current state of knowledge regarding the ISM in these dwarfs, focusing on observational data from the last decade. It addresses key ISM properties, including their total quantity, thermal structure, and turbulent dynamics. The review also addresses the relationship between galactic mass and ISM characteristics, as well as the specific roles of stellar feedback and cosmic rays in regulating ISM conditions. Finally, it highlights several critical open questions that require further investigation. Overall, the ISM in dwarf galaxies appears to be hot, turbulent, and metal-poor, with significant variations in thermal structure and the presence of extensive molecular gas. The strong correlation between galactic mass and ISM properties suggests that galactic mass is a fundamental factor in ISM regulation. Furthermore, stellar feedback appears to be highly inefficient in these systems, whereas cosmic rays may play a more significant role. Future research should prioritize observations of previously undetected dwarfs, alongside continued and more detailed studies of known objects. Additionally, developing a more realistic theoretical framework for ISM regulation in dwarfs is essential, one that incorporates the effects of cosmic rays and the specific characteristics of their low-mass, low-metallicity systems. Finally, ISM studies in dwarfs must be integrated with broader investigations of galactic evolution. This can be achieved through dedicated observational programs and by incorporating dwarf galaxy properties into numerical simulations. Ultimately, the ISM in dwarfs serves as a critical link between high-redshift galaxies and the local dwarf population. A comprehensive understanding of their ISM is essential for elucidating the processes that govern galactic evolution. This research investigates the structural characteristics of directed networks generated by combining the preferential attachment (PA) and uniform attachment (U) mechanisms. A network labeled $\mathcal{N}_{\alpha, \beta, p, q}$ is created through four steps: (i) initiating with a seed containing one bidirectional link; (ii) adding $\alpha$ nodes with in-degree 1 and $\beta$ nodes with out-degree 1 at each step; (iii) with probability $p$, selecting an existing node $i$ to attach a new out-link to node $i$'s out-neighbors based on their in-degree; and (iv) with probability $q$, selecting an existing node $j$ to attach a new in-link to node $j$'s in-neighbors based on their out-degree. The model parameters are defined as $\alpha, \beta, p, q \in [0, \infty)$ and $N_{\alpha, \beta, p, q} = \lfloor \gamma t \rfloor$, where $\gamma = \alpha + \beta$, $t$ represents the total time steps, and $N_{\alpha, \beta, p, q}$ denotes the count of newly added nodes. We demonstrate that this hybrid model exhibits a double threshold phenomenon governed by the $p$ and $q$ values. Furthermore, our findings indicate that when $p$ and $q$ are both sufficiently small, the resulting network displays a more uniform degree distribution. Additionally, we establish that this model possesses a small-world property. Finally, we analyze the relationships among node in-degrees, out-degrees, and network size, revealing that these relationships are influenced by the parameters $\alpha$, $\beta$, $p$, and $q$. Our theoretical predictions align with the experimental results. To our knowledge, this study presents the inaugural application of the PA and U models to directed networks. To our knowledge, this represents the first systematic analysis of the structural properties of directed hybrid random networks. These insights can inform the construction of various types of directed random networks. This study examines the dynamics of both charged and neutral Klein-Gordon particles within the Som-Raychaudhuri spacetime, which describes a mixture of cosmic strings and cosmic rings alongside space-like dislocation. The cosmic string exerts a gravitational influence that drives the cosmic ring to generate vorticity. The paper derives the Klein-Gordon equation for charged scalar particles in this spacetime and determines the corresponding wave function solutions. Subsequently, the charged Klein-Gordon equation is transformed into a set of coupled first-order equations, which are then solved to obtain the wave functions for charged particles. To analyze these dynamics, the study calculates vorticity-energy and charge-energy correlations. Finally, the authors discuss the implications of these findings regarding the nature of the cosmic string, cosmic ring, and dislocation. The cosmic string creates a conical geometry characterized by a deficit angle, while the cosmic ring and dislocation contribute to the spacetime's vorticity and twist, respectively. The analysis reveals that the charged scalar particle's dynamics are shaped by the combined gravitational and electromagnetic effects of these structures. Countable locally standard measure algebras are defined as those possessing a sequence of pairwise disjoint elements whose closed subalgebra consists exclusively of locally standard elements. The research presented in this work examines the structural characteristics of this specific class of measure algebras. Additionally, the authors address the problem of characterizing locally standard measure algebras through the lens of operator theory by constructing a suitable Banach space within the framework of a general symmetric F-normed space. Furthermore, it is demonstrated that every locally standard measure algebra can be embedded into a $\sigma$-finite countably generated locally standard measure algebra, and a complete system of necessary and sufficient conditions for the existence of such an embedding is established. Finally, the paper highlights the utility of this embedding by deriving several significant results regarding function representations. Specifically, it is shown that the space of all $\sigma$-weakly continuous functions from a countably generated locally standard measure algebra to a Banach space admits an abstract representation as $L^\infty\left(\bigoplus_{i=1}^\infty M_i,T\right)$, where each $M_i$ is a $\sigma$-finite countably generated atomic algebra and $T$ is a positive operator on a Banach space. Consequently, partial isometries between locally standard measure algebras are fully characterized, and the structure of functions mapping countably generated locally standard measure algebras into a Banach space is derived. As an application, a substantial extension of the classical Gleason's theorem is obtained, which characterizes $\sigma$-finite countably generated locally standard measure algebras based on the properties of their functions.
Keywords: measure algebra, locally standard measure algebra, function on a locally standard measure algebra, function space over a locally standard measure algebra, function representation, generalized Gleason's theorem.

A wide range of kernels can be derived from specific mathematical expressions. By understanding an expression's meaning, one can create kernels with inherent characteristics, such as an upper bound on kernel values indicating a bounded input domain or a peak in the y-direction for regression tasks. This paper introduces a Bayesian optimization framework to search for suitable kernels by optimizing mathematical expressions within a defined search space. The primary goal is to identify expressions that maximize GP regression performance on a target dataset while staying close to an initial reference kernel. Bayesian optimization is utilized to explore the input search space, which comprises elementary mathematical functions like polynomials, trigonometric functions, and others. To manage this search space effectively, the representations of expressions are simplified, and non-redundant search spaces are generated for various scenarios. Furthermore, the proposed method supports both classification and regression tasks. Experimental results on both synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate that the resulting kernels achieve competitive performance compared to state-of-the-art kernels selected from existing literature. The main advantage of this approach is the ability to discover new kernels tailored to specific problem requirements, such as the unique characteristics of the task or dataset, whereas traditional literature-based selection lacks this specificity. A primary challenge in the design of future muon collider facilities is beam-induced background generated by beam losses and beam dumps. This issue is particularly acute during commissioning and testing phases, where reduced machine reliability leads to more frequent losses. Consequently, mitigating these backgrounds is essential to protect off-beam detector components and minimize interference with beam-line instrumentation. This paper outlines beam-loss-driven background characteristics and presents various beam loss mitigation strategies to address this challenge. Specifically, we examine methods for reducing losses from the final beam loss system, including fast beam dump operations, localized loss dumps, and beam loss masking. Furthermore, we address the reduction of off-axis losses, which are a significant source of background at the detector site, by proposing techniques such as beam switching and fast kicker systems. Finally, we examine beam loss reduction within the final beam loss system, highlighting solutions like improved loss localization and advanced beam loss monitoring. Finally, we present a comprehensive strategy for background reduction at the beam loss front-end, emphasizing the necessity of real-time, fast beam loss monitoring and control systems. These proposed mitigation techniques are applicable to both continuous-wave and pulsed collider designs. Furthermore, we demonstrate their potential to lower integrated beam-induced background by approximately two orders of magnitude compared to scenarios without any mitigation measures. This substantial reduction significantly alleviates constraints on detector background rejection capabilities. Finally, we illustrate how these mitigation strategies can be integrated into existing background reduction approaches, such as detector timing and advanced readout readout technologies. This integration further diminishes background-induced limitations on the collider's physics discovery potential. Overall, these mitigation methods are especially critical for continuous-wave colliders and those operating with small on-time pulses. Additionally, we address the challenges associated with implementing these strategies and their impact on the overall collider design process. Specifically, we discuss how these factors influence the development of final accelerator and detector designs. Finally, we examine how these considerations affect the creation of intermediate accelerator and detector prototypes. In conclusion, we demonstrate that incorporating beam loss mitigation strategies into background reduction efforts is essential for achieving the background levels necessary to fully exploit the discovery potential of a muon collider. Furthermore, we argue that these strategies should be integrated into the initial design and R&D phases of the collider to ensure their successful implementation. This approach is particularly crucial for ensuring that background levels remain sufficiently low to avoid compromising the collider's discovery potential. Finally, we emphasize the importance of a comprehensive and systematic approach to background reduction, as this ensures that all aspects of the background problem are adequately addressed throughout the entire design and development process. The phenomenon of Pauli blocking, where fermions occupy low-energy states and thereby inhibit other fermions from transitioning to lower energy levels, is a fundamental concept that enables superfluidity in ultra-cold spin-orbit coupled gases. In this work, we demonstrate a surprising finding: Pauli blocking can emerge in Bose gases, which typically lack this effect, when they interact via $s$-wave scattering. This occurrence is driven by the formation of large, weakly bound dimers within the gas. Utilizing the Bogoliubov-de Gennes formalism, we show that the lowest-energy quasiparticle modes in such a gas possess the necessary structure to block further transitions, resulting in superfluidity. Furthermore, we establish a quantitative link between the binding energy of the dimers and the energy gap of the quasiparticle modes. Our theoretical predictions are corroborated by exact diagonalization calculations for small finite systems. These findings are crucial for understanding the quantum phases of weakly interacting Bose gases with spin-orbit coupling, which are currently being investigated in cold-atom experiments. Additionally, this mechanism is anticipated to be operative in other fundamental quantum systems, such as polar molecules. Finally, we explore the implications of these results for the broader field of quantum chemistry. Specifically, we note that the emergence of Pauli blocking in a bosonic system is closely tied to the concept of correlation holes, which describe the reduced probability of finding like particles at short distances. This correlation-induced Pauli blocking is widely recognized in chemistry as a key element in the chemical bonding of weakly bound molecules. Consequently, our findings underscore the vital role of bosonic Pauli blocking in chemical bonding. To our knowledge, this represents the first time that the connection between these two concepts has been explicitly established. Our findings are expected to be highly relevant for advancing our understanding of the quantum phases of Bose gases and for the development of new quantum technologies. For instance, the existence of a gap in the quasiparticle spectrum is essential for achieving long coherence times in quantum computing schemes that utilize Bose gases. Thus, our findings are anticipated to be pivotal for the development of emerging quantum computing platforms based on ultracold atoms. Finally, we introduce a conceptual model that illustrates the universality of the correlation-induced Pauli blocking mechanism across various quantum systems, including those involving fermions, bosons, and mixed systems. This model is expected to be highly relevant for the design of new quantum technologies, such as quantum sensors and quantum simulators. Test code is frequently overlooked during software development, often resulting in the creation of test doubles that are difficult to maintain and tests that are brittle and error-prone. These issues stem from "test smells," which are well-documented in software engineering literature. However, the severity of these smells varies depending on the specific smell and the software system's context. While previous studies have suggested that developers tend to ignore or accept these smells, there is a lack of consensus. Consequently, this study aims to investigate developers' perceptions regarding the severity of different test smells. Data was collected through an online survey administered to 100 software developers, with 70 valid responses received. The analysis employed a Friedman test followed by Nemenyi post-hoc testing. Results indicate that test code duplication, excessive abstraction, and tests overly sensitive to black-box changes are generally perceived as the most severe. In contrast, tests overly sensitive to white-black changes and tests overly sensitive to side effects were viewed as the least severe. These findings suggest that when test smells are identified, developers are likely to prioritize addressing the most severe ones first. This research contributes to the body of knowledge by providing the first empirical evidence on developer perceptions of test smell severity, offering valuable insights for guiding developers in deciding which smells to tackle first. Furthermore, it informs tool developers by suggesting that tools designed to detect and refactor test code should prioritize generating messages for the most severe smells. Finally, by facilitating better-informed decisions, this work supports the broader goal of enhancing the quality of test systems. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first study to examine developer perceptions of test smell severity. Additional details, including the survey instrument and raw data, are available at: https://github.com/fernanda-garcia/test-smell-severity-survey. This study introduces the Tiramisu model, a method for estimating inter-beat intervals (IBI) that demonstrates superior accuracy compared to state-of-the-art models. In Tiramisu, each network module is trained to estimate IBI at every specific time step, effectively simulating a multi-layer architecture. We evaluated this model using two distinct datasets: the MIT-BIH Arrhythmia dataset and the PPG dataset from the PhysioNet/Computational Cardiology Challenge 2020. Calculating a tensor singular value decomposition (t-SVD) via the power method involves iteratively multiplying a tensor $A$ by itself and then normalizing the result. This study introduces a randomized algorithm for t-SVD that utilizes any number of multiplication steps, controlled by a parameter $k$. The approach demonstrates $k$-pass acceleration, achieving substantial reductions in runtime. We establish a high-probability bound for the algorithm's accuracy and empirically validate both the significant acceleration and tightness of this theoretical bound. Additionally, we outline extensions of both the theoretical analysis and algorithmic framework to other matrix factorization tasks, such as matrix low-rank approximation and principal component analysis (PCA). Our theoretical guarantees for these extended methods rely on the assumption that tensor entries are drawn from a Gaussian distribution. However, numerical experiments indicate that these theoretical bounds remain valid for tensors with non-Gaussian entries. The implementation is publicly accessible at https://github.com/ashwinbharathikar/Randomized-tSVD. Furthermore, we demonstrate that for large-scale tensors, these theoretical guarantees do not hold for standard t-SVD power methods that employ standard initialization. We also explore alternative initialization strategies for power methods that yield tighter theoretical guarantees. Embedding static graphs has garnered significant attention due to its robust performance and versatility, effectively translating complex graph structures into simpler vector representations. This success has spurred extensive research into developing techniques for dynamic graphs. Dynamic graphs are characterized by time-stamped events that evolve over the lifetime of the graph. Dynamic graph embedding aims to extend the benefits of static graph embedding to enable machine learning applications in dynamic environments. This survey examines recent advancements in dynamic graph embedding, beginning with an analysis of the dynamic graph extension problem and its associated challenges. Subsequently, we categorize existing solutions into three primary families: (1) incremental embedding, (2) trajectory inference, and (3) trajectory prediction. We then explore various machine learning tasks utilizing dynamic embeddings, including link prediction, community detection, and anomaly detection. This study investigates the properties of the $^7$H nucleus by modeling it as a four-neutron resonance bound to a $^3$H core. It is assumed that the nuclear force between the extra neutrons is negligible, allowing their dynamics to be described by the $n-n$ scattering length. By employing the hyperspherical adiabatic method, we calculate the energy spectrum and wave functions for the non-adiabatic Schrödinger equation within the $\alpha + \alpha + 4n$ model. Utilizing these wave functions, we determine the resonance energy, width, and radius for the $^7$H state composed of a $^3$H core and four neutrons. The resulting values for the resonance energy and width align with predictions from the adiabatic limit, whereas the radius is found to be approximately 1 fm larger. Furthermore, we compute the form factors for the $^3$H$\rightarrow$ $^7$H transition, analyzing both their magnitude and $l$-dependence. These findings are subsequently applied to study the one-body transfer reaction $^7$He$(d,p)^8$He. We find that, compared to the adiabatic approximation, the non-adiabatic approach yields a modest increase in the magnitude of the astrophysical cross section, $\sigma_{c\ell}$, while producing only a slight shift in the position of the giant resonance. Additionally, the calculations reveal a significant change in the $\pm 1/2$ versus $3/2$ spin assignment for this resonance. Finally, we examine the influence of the four-body nature of the target nucleus on the reaction cross sections. Specifically, we compare the $^7$He$(d,p)^8$He results with those of the $^7$Li$(d,p)^8$Li reaction, which utilizes a $^3\alpha$ core. In this scenario, the non-adiabatic method results in a more than two-fold increase in the cross-section magnitude. This work provides a foundation for future theoretical investigations into neutron-rich nuclei. All computational details are available in a supplementary file. This paper investigates a Nirenberg-type problem on the standard half-sphere $(\mathbb{S}^n_+, g_0)$, focusing on the existence of conformal metrics with prescribed scalar curvature. We demonstrate that for dimensions $n \geq 10$, and under the condition that $\sigma \in L^{\frac{n}{n-8}-\epsilon}$ where $\epsilon > 0$, there exists a $\delta > 0$ such as a conformal metric with the desired scalar curvature. Furthermore, utilizing a gluing construction, we establish that the resulting metric possesses a singularity of order $\delta^{-2}$. Additionally, we present a non-existence result when $\sigma$ belongs to $L^{\frac{n}{n-8}}$. Our work also features non-existence results grounded in positive mass theorems. Finally, we provide an alternative, self-contained proof of the non-existence theorem originally established by Chen and Lin. Finally, we address a question posed by Chou and Zhang regarding conformal metrics with constant mean curvature. Specifically, for $n \geq 10$, given $\tau \in L^{\frac{n+1}{n-7}-\epsilon}$ with $\epsilon > 0$, we show the existence of a conformal metric achieving the prescribed constant. The resulting metric exhibits a singularity of order $\delta^{-\frac{n+1}{2}}$. We also examine non-existence and multiplicity scenarios, alongside the case of $\tau \in C^0(\mathbb{S}^n_+)$. Our findings include a non-existence theorem for $\tau \in L^{\frac{n+1}{n-7}-\epsilon}$ alongside an $\epsilon$-regularity theorem, as well as the existence of a constant scalar curvature metric with constant mean curvature. In the sub-critical regime, we prove that if $\tau$ is a smooth function satisfying $\tau \geq 0$ and $\tau \not\equiv 0$, no such metric exists. In the critical case, we demonstrate that if $\tau$ is a smooth function satisfying $\tau \geq 0$ and $\tau \not\equiv 0$, then a conformal metric with constant scalar curvature exists. The metric exhibits a singularity of order $\delta^{-\frac{n+1}{4}}$. We also present non-existence results based on positive mass theorems. The paper concludes with an alternative

Deep Optimal Embedding with Sinkhorn Divergences (DOES) represents a new approach integrating two prevalent techniques: deep autoencoders and optimal transport. Optimal transport theory is renowned for its utility in various machine learning domains, particularly for unsupervised clustering and semi-supervised learning. This study introduces a novel autoencoder framework that employs Sinkhorn divergences as reconstruction losses. These losses exhibit desirable mathematical characteristics, including non-negativity, data fidelity, and asymptotic equivalence to standard Lp distances. The proposed model is computationally efficient, supports parallel processing across GPUs, and is readily adaptable for handling categorical data. Empirical evaluations on diverse clustering tasks demonstrate that this method surpasses traditional L2 autoencoders and matches the performance of state-of-the-art approaches. Furthermore, additional experiments confirm the model's superior robustness in semi-supervised learning contexts. The source code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/leopoldz/does. These findings suggest that DOES holds significant promise for a broad spectrum of machine learning applications. Additionally, the methodology is readily extensible for supervised learning, enabling its deployment in various downstream tasks. The authors intend to release a new repository containing source code for supervised learning implementations in the near future. To achieve herd immunity, COVID-19 contact tracing must rapidly identify and isolate infected individuals, alert their contacts, and encourage them to self-isolate. This paper assesses how different levels of participation in Local Trace Partnerships (LTPs) influence the performance of England's National Test and Trace (NTT) system. We evaluate LTP impacts on detection rates, the duration infected individuals remain undetected, and the generation of false alarms. Our methodology involves adapting an existing mathematical model of contact tracing to incorporate LTPs, which we then numerically simulate. Results indicate that including LTPs in the model significantly improves detection rates and reduces the time to detect infections, with performance varying based on the number of regions involved. Furthermore, we analyzed the stability of these numerical results regarding the rate of false alarm investigation. Our findings suggest that LTPs substantially decrease false alarm investigations, thereby enhancing efficiency. Ultimately, the evidence points to LTPs having a significant positive impact on NTT's effectiveness. Additionally, we discuss potential future extensions to the model, such as the role of digital contact tracing applications. This study contributes to the broader understanding of how modeling contact tracing interventions can inform policy decisions. Ultimately, this work supports the goal of using contact tracing to control the pandemic and mitigate its effects on society. By demonstrating how LTPs influence detection rates and the stability of key model parameters, we provide valuable insights for policymakers and decision-makers involved in the NHS NTT program. Furthermore, this research aids in planning future interventions, including the eventual relaxation of lockdown restrictions. We conclude by outlining how this model can be extended to assess the impact of tracing interventions in other countries. Our approach underscores the value of mathematical modeling in providing a scientific basis for policy decisions, while also highlighting the challenges in translating such models into actionable outcomes. We have utilized a variety of data sources to inform the model, and we have begun to address uncertainties in parameter values. Moving forward, we aim to refine the model by incorporating more accurate data and refining parameter estimates. This will involve collaborating with NHS officials to refine the model structure and refine parameter values. We believe this model can be further refined to provide a more accurate representation of the impact of LTPs on NT T performance. This study examines the characteristics of Melotte 72, an open cluster located in the Galactic anti-center direction, utilizing data from the second Gaia Data Release alongside ground-based observations. The analysis focuses on determining the cluster's fundamental parameters, identifying its member stars, and investigating its dynamical state through an investigation of the velocity dispersion. Furthermore, we present the cluster's Color-Magnitude Diagram (CMD) and analyze its physical properties based on the released Gaia data. Finally, we discuss the potential future applications of this open cluster within the context of the Gaia survey. The data utilized include Gaia DR2, the 2MASS All-Sky Survey, and the Sloan Digital Sky Survey. The study's findings are anticipated to contribute to a deeper understanding of the cluster's nature and its evolution. The analysis was conducted using the TOPCAT software package. This study examines the behavior of certain Gaussian excursion sets, specifically focusing on the variability of their expected Betti numbers as a function of a threshold parameter. The analysis targets a broad class of stationary, homogeneous, anisotropic Gaussian fields that satisfy mild regularity constraints. We establish that within the "sparse" regime—characterized by low correlations and minimal smoothness—the Betti numbers either remain constant or fluctuate at a first-order scale across most of the threshold spectrum. The nature of this fluctuation is dictated by the underlying field's characteristics, particularly its anisotropy and the decay rates of its spectral moments. These insights are achieved through an approximation of the field via band-limited versions, leveraging recent breakthroughs in approximating general Gaussian excursion sets using such limited spectra. The resulting findings regarding the band-limited fields are subsequently applied to derive analogous conclusions for the original field. Our work thus offers a comprehensive description of how various geometric properties of stationary Gaussian excursions depend on correlation strength and smoothness, extending beyond the traditional "regime" of strong correlation and high regularity. Furthermore, we elucidate the interplay between asymptotic behavior and heuristic observations regarding finite samples and specific parameter values. While the primary focus is stationary and homogeneous fields, we also extend these findings to stationary, inhomogeneous settings and non-stationary cases under mild additional assumptions. Additionally, the methodology used to examine anisotropy provides a framework for analyzing how excursions respond to coordinate rotations in both stationary and non-stationary contexts. Finally, the paper includes a simulation study to empirically validate several of these theoretical results. This work serves as a sequel to our earlier publication in *Advances in Applied Probability* (2021), which addressed the corresponding "rich" regime. Collectively, these two papers provide a thorough characterization of how stationary Gaussian excursions respond to changes in correlation and regularity, spanning the entire spectrum from sparse to rich regimes. The specific anisotropy examined here is functional in nature, arising from differing levels of smoothness across various coordinate directions. The paper concludes with several intriguing open questions and conjectures. Notably, one conjecture addresses conjectures established in the "rich" regime paper, while another proposes an intriguing relationship between the sparsity of a field and the magnitude of its Betti numbers. Eye-in-hand camera calibration remains a critical challenge in robotics. While numerous learning-based approaches have emerged recently, they predominantly depend on video recordings featuring multiple frames with significant camera movement. Our approach, however, utilizes only a single image depicting an object viewed by the eye-in-hand camera. This method eliminates the requirement for object 3D models or precise prior knowledge of the object's position within the robot's end-effector coordinate system. We employ a novel strategy leveraging the object pose identified through dense visual feature matching. Our method demonstrates superior performance compared to existing solutions when precise 3D object knowledge is unavailable. Furthermore, in simulations featuring noisy single images, our approach achieves up to 1.5 times greater accuracy in 3D point localization relative to competing methods. Additionally, experimental results indicate that learning-based techniques, including ours, can reduce calibration time by as much as 99.5% relative to traditional techniques. Finally, we release an extensive new benchmark dataset comprising 100,000 images captured by an eye-in-hand camera across 20,000 poses for seven objects. To our knowledge, this is the largest learning-based eye-in-hand camera calibration dataset available. The code and dataset can be accessed at https://github.com/aleksandar-korica/learning-based-calibration. Recent advancements in machine learning have enabled the creation of neural networks capable of generating images from textual descriptions. In contrast, this paper addresses a less explored challenge: determining the inverse problem of learning text from images. Specifically, we focus on inverse constrained reinforcement learning, where the objective is to identify a natural language description corresponding to a given image that a policy can utilize to replicate the image. To achieve this, we introduce Inverse Constrained Policy Learning (ICPL), a novel algorithm designed to jointly train an effective text-to-pixel policy and a precise pixel-to-text value function. Our results demonstrate that ICPL surpasses current state-of-the-art methods in both success rates and the fidelity of generated outputs. Furthermore, we show that our approach can learn inverse constraints that appear non-Markovian and exhibit high data efficiency. Finally, we provide empirical evidence indicating that ICPL produces generated text with higher quality compared to competitors. To facilitate this, we also release a large-scale, high-quality dataset comprising paired images and their associated captions. The dataset comprises over 1.5 million images annotated with more than 1 million captions, covering a diverse array of visual objects and scenarios. We anticipate that ICPL and the accompanying dataset will serve as a robust foundation for future research in constrained reinforcement learning. The code and data are accessible at https://github.com/1000x1000/ICPL. Additionally, video demonstrations of our achievements can be viewed here: https://1000x1000.github.io/ICPL/. Gaia, the European Space Agency's astrometric satellite launched in 2013, is currently generating the most extensive and precise celestial map ever created. This data will be compiled into a multi-terabyte catalogue and database, serving as a foundational reference for all future astronomical research. By extending the celestial sphere's coordinate system into three dimensions, this map includes parallax measurements for over one billion stars and astrometric time-series data for 10 billion objects. Additionally, the survey provides photometric and radial velocity data for 1.2 billion stars, while the Gaia Data Release 2 (GAIA DR2) has expanded these capabilities to include near-infrared wavelengths. This article reviews the GAIA mission's objectives and methods, and details the multi-dimensional maps and catalogues contained within the Data Releases 2 and 3. The GAIA mission is designed to operate for a decade, with plans to release Data Release 3 in 2023. Future observations aim to refine GAIA DR2's astrometric precision by a factor of ten, thereby significantly enhancing our understanding of the Galaxy and its stellar populations. Ultimately, GAIA's unprecedented accuracy and sensitivity are expected to uncover numerous new exoplanets, black holes, and other elusive celestial objects. (A full English version is available at https://arxiv.org/abs/2008.00259). (These proceedings were prepared for the GAIA Symposium, held in Madrid, Spain, from May 22 to 26, 2017).

We introduce a new, straightforward algorithm that provides vertex separators for $n$-vertex graphs $G$ with treewidth $k$ using $O(k^2\log^2{kn})$ bits of space, operating under the RAM model. This algorithm is deterministic and operates within $O(\log{kn})$ words of external memory. Our method is significantly more space-efficient than prior vertex separator algorithms, which typically required $O(n)$ space. By integrating our space-efficient algorithm with existing time-efficient solutions, we enable deterministic $O(n)$-time algorithms for various graph problems that utilize vertex separators. Furthermore, our approach resolves an open question posed by Brodal et al. (Extended Abstract, ESA 2017) and builds upon their framework. Additionally, our findings complement the work of Chuzhoy and Chen (FOCS 2018), who developed a vertex separator algorithm with $O(n)$ time complexity but $O(n)$ space complexity and a complexity constant of $O(k^2\log^2{kn})$. We demonstrate that their high-level methodology can be adapted to our space-efficient algorithm. Moreover, our algorithm can be integrated into their method to yield an $O(n)$-time algorithm for vertex separators with $O(k^2\log^2{kn})$ bits of space and a complexity constant of $O(\log{kn})$. Finally, we highlight that our algorithm can be embedded into their method to produce a randomized $O(n)$-time algorithm for vertex separators with a complexity constant of $O(k)$ and $\Omega(k)$ space usage. This represents a substantial improvement over all prior randomized methods, which had $O(k^2\log{kn})$ space complexity. Our work also complements their randomized method, which offers $O(k)$ space usage but $O(n\log^2{kn})$ time complexity and a $O(k\log{kn})$ complexity constant. We show that their method can be adapted to our algorithm to achieve $O(k^2\log{kn})$ space complexity, $O(n\log{kn})$ time complexity, and $O(\log{kn})$ complexity constant in the randomized setting. The analysis of high-dimensional heterogeneous networks has become increasingly vital across diverse fields. While current methods typically rely on ad-hoc, case-specific decisions for handling non-existent or inferred links, as well as variable user-defined weights, we propose a formal framework for the directed clustering of weighted, heterogeneous networks. This work examines multiple proposed metrics, analyzes their properties, and investigates the impacts of different decision-making approaches on network analysis. We stress-test these methods using both synthetic and real-world networks, demonstrating that the specific context and objectives significantly influence the optimal approach. Furthermore, we address a fundamental issue regarding the clustering of non-existent and inferred links, arguing that the standard practice of treating them as unweighted is often inappropriate. We outline specific scenarios where this convention fails and suggest alternative strategies. Finally, we present a series of questions regarding the requirements for clustering inferred networks, aiming to stimulate further research and discussion in this emerging domain. Our findings offer valuable insights and guidance for researchers and practitioners engaged in analyzing high-dimensional directed networks. Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) represent a machine learning framework designed to resolve partial differential equations (PDEs) with integrated physical laws expressed as residual constraints. This study presents a novel, rigorous, and adaptive a posteriori error estimation framework for PINNs. The proposed method is versatile, capable of addressing both linear and nonlinear elliptic PDEs. By integrating a high-order finite element solution into the error analysis, the framework establishes a posteriori bounds for the PINN error across $L^2$, Hölder, and Sobolev spaces. Furthermore, error sensitivity with respect to data points is examined, demonstrating that the magnitude of the PDE residual depends on the count of certified data points. Finally, the framework's ability to provide certified solutions for nonconvex and high-dimensional PDEs is illustrated. Numerical experiments further validate the method's performance in handling singularities and ill-posedness. Additionally, the approach is applied to uncertainty quantification within a convection-diffusion PDE, where it facilitates a highly accurate comparison between PINN and finite element results. Finally, the framework is extended to a hyperbolic PDE, where it enables a rigorous analysis of the stability and convergence properties inherent to PINNs. Throughout this work, all solutions are rigorously certified, and parameter selection is optimized using the proposed error estimation technique. Notably, the method is computationally efficient, requiring minimal additional time beyond that of the PINN solution itself. To facilitate reproducibility, a Python package implementing this framework is made available. A key advantage of our approach is its capacity to deliver a convergence rate analysis for PINNs, thereby advancing the understanding of their behavior. Overall, this work significantly enhances the practical utility and reliability of PINNs. In summary, we offer a new, practical, and robust tool for applying PINNs to real-world problems. Air pollution epidemiology relies on statistical models that integrate data from various sources, including long-term cohort studies, time-series analyses, and hospital-based research. These approaches depend on heterogeneous data streams, such as measurements from ground-level air quality monitoring networks, satellite observations, and ground-based remote sensing. To address the scarcity of air quality data, particularly for long-term epidemiologic studies, there is an increasing need to generate high-resolution spatiotemporal air pollution datasets. This study evaluates and compares three machine learning techniques—generalized additive models, kriging, and random forests—for spatio-temporal interpolation of air pollution data. The analysis utilizes a three-year dataset (2017–2019) of hourly air pollution readings from a network of ground-based sensors in Santiago, Chile. The proposed methodology offers a straightforward framework for deriving high-resolution spatio-temporal pollutant maps, which can support diverse epidemiologic investigations. Furthermore, the method demonstrates the ability to produce accurate spatiotemporal pollutant estimates even under conditions of high data sparsity. The implementation is available as an open-source package on GitHub.

Keywords: air pollution, random forests, kriging, spatiotemporal interpolation, air pollution models, air quality data, air quality data generation, air pollution data.

Gapped graphene exhibits an orbital Hall effect that differs fundamentally from the spin, charge, and valley Hall effects found in other materials. This phenomenon arises from a non-zero Berry curvature defined in the momentum space of the Berry phase. Unlike valley-dependent effects, the orbital Hall effect persists even in a disordered lattice where grain boundaries are present. At a specific magnetic field, the orbital Hall effect is expected to be substantial, potentially enabling the detection of Berry curvature in the solid state. Furthermore, the orbital Hall effect in gapped graphene is not merely a theoretical construct but a manifestation of a broader class of topological effects. This is evidenced by the presence of a Hall conductivity peak at the charge neutrality point and a non-zero Hall resistivity near zero current. These findings underscore the significance of the orbital Hall effect in graphene and suggest that the Berry curvature of the electronic wave function is a prevalent physical property found in many other materials. This property is essential for the development of orbital electronics. Additionally, the orbital Hall effect in gapped graphene demonstrates a unique characteristic: it can be interpreted as a valley Hall effect occurring in the presence of a Berry curvature dipole, a concept previously introduced for non-centrosymmetric systems. This interpretation offers a novel perspective on the valley Hall effect. Consequently, the valley Hall effect may be more prevalent than previously believed, as it can be observed in both centrosymmetric and non-centrosymmetric materials. This insight could facilitate the discovery of new materials for the design of orbital transistors. Finally, the valley Hall effect in graphene is closely linked to the Berry curvature induced by a magnetic field, a phenomenon that has been the subject of extensive debate. The current study provides a comprehensive analysis of the orbital Hall effect in gapped graphene, addressing various aspects of this debated phenomenon. By doing so, it clarifies the relationship between orbital and valley Hall effects, thereby simplifying the understanding of the valley Hall effect in graphene. This clarification is crucial for the practical application of the valley Hall effect in this system. Ultimately, the valley Hall effect in graphene may soon be confirmed experimentally, a milestone that could usher in the era of orbital electronics. In this context, graphene could serve as a pivotal material for advancing this new technological field. Specifically, the valley Hall effect in graphene could be interpreted as a manifestation of the spin Hall effect, a discovery that would significantly contribute to the development of spintronics. Neural network models are frequently deployed in the wild for numerous applications, prompting attackers to introduce backdoors to compromise their integrity. While graph data is prevalent in real-world scenarios, traditional linear models often fail to capture its complex structures effectively. Consequently, researchers have turned to graph neural networks (GNNs) to process this type of data. However, GNNs are susceptible to data poisoning attacks, where adversaries inject backdoors to corrupt the model's behavior. This paper introduces a novel method for training GNNs using reinforcement learning to resist data poisoning. Our approach demonstrates that reinforcement learning can successfully defend against such attacks, achieving superior defense performance compared to other methods. Furthermore, we find that the Adam optimizer is particularly effective for reinforcement learning defense against data poisoning, surpassing other common optimizers. Finally, we propose a new defense technique called "Adam+," which integrates reinforcement learning with the Adam optimizer. This method is computationally efficient and yields state-of-the-art results. Extensive experiments across three benchmark datasets confirm that our method outperforms existing adversarial training approaches in both clean and test-time poisoned scenarios. Additionally, we observe that reinforcement learning-based defenses are more effective when attacks are applied during training, whereas adversarially trained models perform better when attacks occur during inference. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first study to explore reinforcement learning as a defense mechanism against data poisoning in GNNs. Catalogue matching serves as a critical method for identifying objects in astronomical data, yet it remains a highly labor-intensive task. This difficulty is exacerbated by the lack of supplementary data in traditional astrometric catalogues, which typically include only position and position angle. This paper introduces a novel catalogue matching approach that leverages rich information from recent multi-epoch surveys, such as PanSTARRS1, by generating catalogue models that incorporate both position and magnitude. These models are enhanced through the application of a new unsupervised learning technique designed to capture the complex behavior of source variability. The proposed method is rigorously evaluated using simulated data, demonstrating a significant improvement in matching completeness compared to traditional techniques. Furthermore, the study includes an analysis of a real-world sample of sources identified in PanSTARRS1 but absent from existing astrometric catalogues, revealing that the majority are variable sources. These findings suggest that leveraging photometric data offers a promising avenue for enhancing catalogue matching accuracy. The code required to replicate this work is publicly accessible at https://github.com/astro-ml/catalogue-matching. This paper identifies a hypergraph's infinite vertex cover number as the least upper bound of the finite vertex cover numbers across all its finite sub-hypergraphs. We demonstrate that this infinite vertex cover number represents the supremum of the cardinalities of the smallest vertex covers in the graph's induced 2-factors. The study highlights significant combinatorial applications for this definition. Additionally, we prove that every hypergraph with an edge number $\aleph_n$ possesses a vertex cover number no greater than $\aleph_{n-1}$ for any natural number $n$. Finally, the paper examines the maximum possible size of a minimal vertex cover within infinite hypergraphs. Specifically, it constructs a hypergraph featuring a vertex cover of cardinality $\aleph_c$ where every subset of cardinality $\alpha < c$ fails to cover any edges, and it constructs another with a vertex cover number of $\aleph_c$ containing a subset of cardinality $\alpha$ that covers all edges, provided $\alpha < c$. In both scenarios, the vertex cover number is precisely $\aleph_c$. Furthermore, we establish that the existence of such a hypergraph with a small yet maximal minimal vertex cover number is contingent upon the failure of the Generalized Continuum Hypothesis. The paper concludes with several open questions. Notably, we address whether a hypergraph with $\aleph_c$ edges can be defined such that every vertex cover has a cardinality of at least $\alpha > c$. This problem is closely linked to the existence of a partition of $\mathbb{N}$ into finitely many subsets, each containing a square-free number. Additionally, we explore the infinite hypergraph chromatic number, demonstrating that it does not necessarily equal the supremum of the chromatic numbers of all finite sub-hypergraphs. We construct a specific example of such a hypergraph and propose that this phenomenon may be universal. Finally, we investigate the existence of hypergraphs with a finite chromatic number that possess vertex covers of arbitrarily large cardinality. Ontologies serve as formal models of concepts and their interrelations, typically represented through Knowledge Graphs. While various visualisation tools exist for browsing these graphs, they often struggle with overviews of large structures due to visual clutter and the inability to distinguish between different relation types. This paper introduces OntoPlot, a new visualisation method that supports multiple relation types and employs a non-geometric layout algorithm to avoid clutters. The result is a concise overview that effectively highlights large ontology "communities" while preserving information about specific relations. We validate this approach using a visual regression test and demonstrate its utility with three ontology use cases. Our evaluation indicates that OntoPlot surpasses existing solutions in visual clarity, particularly when applied to large ontologies. The implementation is publicly accessible at https://onto.plotly.com. (Demo video: https://youtu.be/2142222222)

This study addresses semi-supervised End-to-End Automatic Speech Recognition (EEASR) by enhancing its robustness through the integration of CycleGAN and loss functions designed to strengthen cycle consistency. CycleGAN enables unsupervised translation between two datasets without paired training examples. We investigate the impact of CycleGAN on EEASR and introduce two inter-domain loss functions applied within the adversarial network to learn more accurate domain mappings. Our findings indicate that both CycleGAN and these loss functions significantly boost EEASR performance. Furthermore, we propose an improved cycle consistency loss that yields better results than the original formulation. Finally, experimental evidence confirms that the Inter-domain Loss functions effectively reinforce cycle consistency and facilitate more precise domain mapping. On the Librispeech-10% dataset, the proposed approach surpasses the baseline EEASR by 1.4 WER points. Additionally, when combined with other unsupervised techniques, this method achieves a 2.1 WER improvement over the baseline EEASR. Active inference serves as the theoretical framework for perception, cognition, and action within embodied artificial intelligence. This study explores its application in two primary domains: predicting future sensor observations and inferring the intentions of other agents. While the theoretical underpinnings for these applications are established, the original free energy minimization principle relies on model-based prediction, which demands an explicit generative model. In contrast, deep recurrent neural networks facilitate model-free active inference. We address two critical challenges in this framework: ensuring the stability of recurrent neural networks and enhancing the accuracy of future observation predictions. First, we introduce a method to stabilize recurrent networks by mitigating internal energy descent through weight regularization and recurrent dropout. Second, we implement a variational attention mechanism to boost prediction performance. Our approach for deep active inference utilizes a goal-directed recurrent attention network to forecast future observations, thereby guiding the robot's behavior to reduce reconstruction error under varying conditions. Experimental results demonstrate that this method achieves superior robustness and prediction accuracy in both simulated and real-world autonomous robot navigation scenarios. Furthermore, the proposed method effectively predicts future observations while simultaneously conserving energy and maximizing mutual information. These findings offer a promising pathway for developing energy-efficient, real-time autonomous navigation systems. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/ChenchenLi1993/DAINet.

Keywords: Deep active inference, autonomous robot navigation, future observation prediction, intention inference, goal-driven recurrent attention network.

This study theoretically examines the Contribution of Internal Freedom to the Soret effect (CIFST) arising from the internal degrees of freedom (IDF) of molecular solutes in soft molecular mixtures. By incorporating solute IDFs and utilizing partition functions to characterize temperature-dependent entropic variations upon adding IDFs, we derived the CIFST coefficient for a trinary system comprising a solvent, a solvent-like solute, and a solute-solute bound complex. To validate our theoretical approach, we applied it to model systems representing solvent, alcohol, and salt, as well as alcohol, salt, and water. Our findings indicate that solute IDFs significantly influence the CIFST coefficient, resulting in a non-monotonic relationship between solute concentration and CIFST. Furthermore, we observed that bound complexes can induce a sign reversal in the CIFST coefficient, producing counterintuitive concentration-dependent behaviors. These results align with experimental data regarding the non-monotonic and reversible concentration effects of CIFST. Additionally, the impact of IDF on CIFST is more pronounced in mixtures involving charged solutes, suggesting that accounting for solute IDFs is essential for accurately predicting the Soret effect. Finally, our analysis demonstrates that a single sign of the partition function ratio is insufficient to explain CIFST; instead, entropic changes associated with IDFs must be considered. These insights provide a comprehensive understanding of solute IDF contributions to the Soret effect, which is critical for applications such as thermal separation, heat management, and thermal energy harvesting. Our framework is also extendable to systems with adsorption-desorption IDFs, as well as to phenomena like the isotope Soret effect and thermal fractionation. Furthermore, the model is applicable to various soft matter systems, including colloidal mixtures, biological cells, and synthetic polymers. Overall, this research advances the fundamental understanding of the Soret effect and establishes a foundation for developing advanced separation technologies. Additionally, the findings may offer new perspectives for thermal energy harvesting, as heat fluxes induced by the Soret effect are a primary focus in this field. By elucidating the role of solute IDFs in CIFST, our work may facilitate the design of advanced thermal energy harvesting devices. Our theoretical framework can be extended to investigate other internal degrees of freedom, such as adsorption-desorption IDFs, thereby enhancing the fundamental understanding of thermal transport in soft matter systems. Automated Essay Scoring (AES) represents a critical area within natural language processing (NLP) and speech assessment. The primary objective of AES is to assign a single score to input essays, reflecting their language quality and grammatical correctness. This study investigates the performance of pre-trained transformer-based language models on this task. We evaluate popular transformers, including BERT, RoBERTa, and XLNet, which are typically fine-tuned on NLP challenges. Through extensive experiments, we demonstrate that these pre-trained models can effectively and automatically correlate input essay data with the assigned scores. Furthermore, we analyze the AES dataset to identify patterns in student writing that correspond to the grades they receive. Our findings indicate that pre-trained models are highly effective for automatically grading language proficiency. Additionally, we introduce a new pre-trained language model specifically trained to predict AES scores, achieving state-of-the-art results on the PewterScale dataset. This new model surpasses all other approaches on three out of four evaluation metrics, while also showing strong performance in generating human-like comments for student essays. False positives remain a critical challenge in domain-adaptive pedestrian detection, where models trained on image patches often struggle to generalize to full images, generating an excessive number of spurious detections. This paper introduces Box Re-Ranking, a method designed to efficiently suppress these false positives without compromising detection performance. The approach leverages a box re-ranker built upon the popular detection transformer to refine candidate boxes from low-reliability domains. By employing feature calibration and adaptive refinement, the re-ranker suppresses false positives while maintaining performance. Extensive experiments on real-world datasets demonstrate that our method significantly reduces unsupervised false positives in real-world applications while keeping performance unchanged. Low-quality music recordings, often captured by consumer devices like smartphones, frequently suffer from distortions such as background noise, reverberation, and microphone-induced equalization. This study investigates a deep learning approach to music enhancement by framing it as a continuous image translation task focused on spectral masking. We introduce Period-GAN, a novel architecture designed to generate long-term spectrums for enhancement. Additionally, we develop Vocoder-GAN, which utilizes a generator paired with auxiliary discriminators to effectively convert spectrums into waveforms. Comprehensive evaluations demonstrate that the proposed network outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods. Furthermore, our approach achieves superior quality in both the enhanced music and the underlying vocal track, highlighting its significant potential for music separation tasks. The code is accessible at https://github.com/ailab-tku/Vosep. To facilitate further research, we have also established a new dataset for music enhancement, available at https://github.com/ailab-tku/Vosep/tree/master/data. This collection includes various types of music recordings, such as vocals, instruments, and mixed tracks. Our contributions lie in two key areas: first, the development of Period-GAN and Vocoder-GAN, which advance periodic signal generation and audio synthesis, respectively; second, the provision of a versatile dataset covering diverse music scenarios, offering a comprehensive resource for researchers. The associated experiments and evaluations are detailed in our paper. We hope this work will inspire future advancements in the field of music enhancement. This paper introduces three Motional Deformation Networks designed to simulate a person releasing an object at a specified location. Release action simulation is crucial for creating realistic animated sequences, yet existing techniques often fail to capture the realism of the protagonist's movement. We identify that a key factor in authenticity is the point of release, which prior methods typically ignore. To address this, we developed FauxThrow, a novel network capable of deforming motion based on custom release points. Additionally, we present a new dataset, the Throw dataset, featuring annotated 3D trajectories for over 1,000 release points. This dataset enables the evaluation of self-consistency in generated motions. Our findings indicate that FauxThrow achieves the most realistic motion deformations, surpassing state-of-the-art methods. Furthermore, we demonstrate that FauxThrow can be adapted to other datasets to perform motion deformation in diverse contexts, such as kicking a ball or opening a door. A user study involving 20 participants confirms that FauxThrow outperforms existing approaches. The dataset and code are accessible at https://github.com/SeongWooJeon/Motional_Deformation.
