Although Neural Machine Translation (NMT) models are capable of generating syntactically plausible sentences, they frequently fail to maintain overall sentence coherence. To address this, we introduce a top-down tree-structured beam search algorithm that ensures syntactically consistent decoding across entire sentences. This method leverages the parse tree of the most recently completed word to capture structural context, which is then used as additional feature input for predicting the next token. Furthermore, to enhance efficiency, we implement a connection mechanism between the encoder and decoder based on part-of-speech (POS) tags. This synergy between top-down tree-structured beam search and POS-based syntactic connections leads to superior sentence-level coherence in NMT. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach improves automatic metrics like BLEU, ROUGE, and METEOR by 1.0–2.5 points on standard English-to-English and English-to-Chinese translation benchmarks. Additionally, our model achieves an average F1 score improvement of 0.5 to over 1.0 point in English dependency parsing tasks. Our source code is publicly available at: https://github.com/ChenYi2020/Tree-search-and-Syntactic-Connections. This study concludes that top-down tree-structured beam search, when combined with syntactic connections, yields a significant boost in sentence-level coherence. The proposed method is also applicable to various sequence generation tasks, such as speech recognition and machine summarization. Our future work will focus on extending this approach to Chinese, Japanese, and Korean languages. Finally, we plan to explore its utility in few-shot learning scenarios. Our contributions are as follows: (1) We developed a novel and efficient algorithm that ensures syntactic consistency during NMT decoding; (2) We demonstrated that the algorithm's effectiveness stems from its ability to preserve syntactic information throughout the decoding process; (3) We validated the algorithm's capacity to enhance sentence-level coherence through comprehensive empirical analysis. (4) We applied the algorithm to NLP tasks, achieving significant performance gains. (5) The algorithm is source-code open and has been successfully tested on multiple languages. (6) The application demonstrates the algorithm's potential for few-shot learning. (7) We offer a comprehensive analysis of the algorithm's contributions. The binding energy (BE) of molecules on icy grains is a critical parameter for modeling astrochemical reactions. This value significantly influences the mobility of reactants and radicals, determining whether they can locate reaction partners, and it also impacts the activation energy required to overcome reaction barriers. Due to the complex nature of icy grain surfaces, experimental determination of BE distributions is currently unfeasible. Consequently, researchers rely on computationally intensive quantum chemical calculations to derive these distributions. This study introduces the Binding Energy Evaluation Platform (BEEP), a database containing over 100,000 such calculations. In BEEP, molecular species adsorb onto icy surfaces via hydrogen bonds, forming configurations that minimize the DFT-calculated total energy. The database includes comprehensive details on the computational processes, such as the specific software used, levels of theory, and atomic coordinates for both complexes and isolated species. Additionally, the platform offers a web-based interface to visualize complexes and retrieve individual BE values. The study examines a multiplicative stochastic process constrained by a lognormal lower bound. A model for this process is developed using a stochastic differential equation featuring a non-constant diffusion coefficient that follows a specific functional form. Key parameters are estimated via a two-stage approach: first, a least-squares method is applied to time-interval data to determine the distribution of the diffusion coefficient's values; subsequently, these values and their distribution are utilized within a least-squares least-curvature framework to fit the diffusion coefficient's functional form to the time series. Finally, the analysis investigates the conditions under which a stable least-squares fit exists, alongside scenarios where only a limited number of data points allow for diffusion coefficient values to be derived from a finite least-curvature fit. Additionally, the upper bound of the least-curvature solution space is defined, marking the transition to an infinite curvature regime where no stable least-curvature solution exists. The study presents a theory of "criticality" regarding this upper bound, demonstrating that a system approaching this criticality undergoes a qualitative shift in behavior, where the influence of the entire data set extends beyond the immediate vicinity of any single data point. A simulation of a synthetic data set illustrates these properties. Furthermore, the analysis explores how the choice of weight function affects the criticality of the least-curvature solution space. Finally, the time series of a real-world stock, Starbucks, is examined to test the validity of the model's assumptions. The results indicate that while the model is appropriate for periods of low market volatility, it is not suitable for periods of high volatility. Overall, the findings suggest that multiplicative stochastic processes with time-varying diffusion coefficients can be effectively used to analyze and simulate the temporal evolution of systems exhibiting diffusive behavior. However, the analysis also identifies limitations regarding the model's validity when market volatility is high. The 2008 financial crisis serves as a prime example of such a period of high volatility. We introduce a new approach for estimating expectations of Pauli operators within quantum states without direct access. Given black-box state preparation, our method achieves an absolute error of $\epsilon/m$ for $m$ operators while requiring only $O(n^2/\epsilon/m)$ query time, where $n$ denotes the number of qubits. This technique leverages random Clifford circuits of low depth, demonstrating that substantial information can be gained by sampling outside the preparation circuit. Our findings advance the fields of shadow tomography and randomized benchmarking. Specifically, we enhance the scalability of shadow tomography protocols and offer a practical solution to a longstanding challenge in randomized benchmarking: accurately determining the decay rate of multi-qubit operators under noise. Furthermore, we present a protocol that scales linearly with $m$, thereby resolving a major open problem previously identified by Huang, Kueng, and Preskill. Additionally, we generalize this result from stabilizer states to broader classes of quantum states. We contend that, in the context of shadow tomography, low-depth random circuits serve as a vital resource that should be integrated into future protocols. Finally, our work yields the first provably efficient randomized benchmarking protocol that is scalable in all dimensions, including the number of errors. Notably, our methods are scalable with respect to both the number of operators and the number of errors. Our results are derived from a novel technique that utilizes the randomization of observables rather than the randomization of circuits. The study examines the reflection coefficient $r(k)$ for Davey-Stewartson II equations, deriving an explicit formula for its large $|k|$ asymptotic behavior when the potential corresponds to a solution with constant coefficients. This approach involves analyzing the reflection coefficient's analytic continuation across the complex $k $-plane via a nonlocal integro-differential equation. The analysis covers two distinct scenarios: first, when the function is in the Berg class, yielding the asymptotic form $r(k)\sim\frac{1}{k}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}q(x)dx$ as $|k|\to\infty$ within the upper half-plane; and second, for functions possessing a finite number of poles in the upper half-plane, where $r(k)$ exhibits asymptotic behavior $r(k)\sim Ck^{\alpha}$ with $\alpha\in\{0,1\}$ and a constant $C$ dependent on the residues at the poles. Furthermore, it is demonstrated that the potential $q(x)$ is identically zero if any of the following conditions hold: (i) $\lim_{|k|\to\infty}kr(k)$ exists and is finite in the upper half-plane; (ii) $\lim_{|k|\to\infty}kr(k)=0$ in the upper half-plane; (iii) $kr(k)$ is bounded in the upper half-plane. These findings extend previous results regarding the inverse scattering transform for the Schrödinger equation. Additionally, the paper presents several applications of these results to the dKdV and mKdV equations. Situational Adversarial Training (SAT) is a recently introduced framework designed to enhance the robustness of text classification models. It functions by employing transformations that mimic context-switching, such as word insertions, deletions, and reordering. However, current SAT implementations are limited because they rely on random transformations, which can result in noisy data that obscures the original labeling context. This paper presents Sibyl, a novel framework for generating Sibylvariant Transformations (SBT). Unlike traditional SAT, Sibyl operates as a self-supervised learning framework. We demonstrate that Sibyl significantly boosts robustness, achieving a 10.5% improvement over random transformations on the TextBlob dataset. Furthermore, utilizing SBT for pre-training yields additional gains, elevating the robust accuracy of models trained on clean data from 71.5% to 75.0%. Finally, we show that Sibyl enhances robustness across various other tasks, including entity linking, named entity recognition, and part-of-speech tagging. Meta-learning aims to create algorithms capable of rapidly acquiring new skills from limited data. This paper focuses on linear meta-learning, which seeks to learn a generic feature representation that facilitates quick adaptation to various downstream tasks. Although recent empirical studies have yielded promising results, theoretical guarantees for this approach remain absent. We address this gap by introducing an information-theoretic lower bound that demonstrates the necessity of specific dimensions within the linearly transformed features for successful meta-learning. Furthermore, we present a provable algorithm that matches this lower bound up to a constant factor, effectively bridging the divide between empirical methods and rigorous theoretical analysis. Our experiments confirm that this algorithm performs competitively in this setting. Finally, we extend our main findings to scenarios involving high-dimensional feature spaces. Overall, this work establishes a foundational framework for further research into meta-learning representation. For code and experiments, see: https://github.com/ashkanf/LinearMetaLearning. Although Massively Multilingual Models (MMLMs) have demonstrated promising results in both understanding and translating low-resource languages, their substantial size hinders deployment. While recent studies have attempted to adapt these MMLMs for translation tasks, our analysis reveals that current approaches lack robustness. Specifically, methods utilizing MMLMs as teacher models exhibit significant performance fluctuations when distilled into smaller student models across various student configurations. To address this, we introduce a novel multi-stage distillation strategy featuring multiple teachers and students, alongside an unsupervised pre-training phase. This approach enhances stability and yields consistent performance gains. Furthermore, we demonstrate that these techniques maintain high effectiveness under extreme conditions, such as distilling into an 8MB multilingual model supporting 100 languages. The implementation is accessible at https://github.com/DeepMind/parametric-student. The code and model card will be released shortly. Additionally, we provide a Python package, parametric-student, featuring a new API for easily distilling multiple sequential backbones. The package is available on PyPI at https://pypi.org/project/parametric-student/. The model card can be found at https://huggingface.co/parametric-student. Finally, we highlight a stable implementation for Machine Translation using Parametric Student Models.

Deep learning-based segmentation models typically require large amounts of labeled data, a significant challenge given the scarcity of labeled medical images. This study investigates the impact of image augmentation on training data requirements for a standard segmentation model. We evaluated a conventional U-Net across six augmentation strategies on a dataset of 1,000 chest X-rays annotated for lung fields and consolidation regions. Our findings indicate that a combination of horizontal flip, vertical flip, and rotation by 90 degrees is the most effective approach, enabling accurate training with only 100 images. This result is particularly significant given the high annotation costs associated with medical imaging. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/abhishekgupta123456789/pneumonia_segmentation. To our knowledge, no prior research has examined the specific effects of image augmentation on the data needs of standard segmentation models. We anticipate this work will inspire further exploration of data augmentation strategies in medical image analysis. Although image captioning has advanced significantly, generating diverse descriptions for the same image remains an unresolved issue. Existing approaches often fail to fully leverage pre-trained models for this purpose. To address this, we introduce a simple yet effective framework that regulates text diversity through prompt-based learning. Our method involves feeding identical images into a Vision-Language Transformer (VLT) with various textual prompts to produce multiple descriptions. To enhance both quality and diversity, we implement two strategies: first, we design a self-distillation framework that utilizes prompts with broader search spaces to learn supplementary diverse captions; second, we apply a contrastive objective to maximize the semantic similarity between different captions while increasing their diversity. Extensive experiments on the MS-COCO dataset demonstrate that our approach effectively balances these two objectives. Furthermore, as shown in additional experiments, the method generalizes well to other domains, including COVID-19 X-rays, Dermatology, and X-Ray imaging. The code is accessible at \url{https://github.com/1000x1000x1000/Controllable-Image-Captioning}.

We introduce a novel analytical framework for harm that incorporates causal structures, offering a unified explanation for numerous well-established phenomena. This work establishes core properties, including independence, monotonicity, and the separation of concerns, and demonstrates their interdependencies. Additionally, we extend these properties to analyze correlated harm and provide proof for an instance of compositional harm, specifically the merge property. Our study also proves and demonstrates the loss function property, highlighting the distinction between harm and utility. Furthermore, we present an algorithm to determine if a specific causal harm structure exists within a defined probabilistic program. We validate this method by demonstrating the existence of harm in various probabilistic programs, such as those modeling security vulnerabilities and data breaches. The proposed algorithm and proof techniques are expected to be applicable in a wide range of other contexts. Finally, we discuss the relationship between our findings and existing literature, demonstrating that our framework can offer fresh perspectives on numerous related problems. Speech translation involves converting spoken audio from one language into written text in another. This paper introduces an unsupervised method for speech translation, enabling translation between languages for which no parallel training data exists. We present two key innovations: (1) an acoustically-informed neural architecture that utilizes a contrastive loss function to learn language-invariant acoustic representations, and (2) a bootstrapping technique that automatically generates synthetic parallel data across two languages without human involvement. Our proposed method achieves competitive performance on the English-French SpeechTrans benchmark and demonstrates promising results on the EMT SpeechTranslationService benchmark. Additionally, we provide a comprehensive implementation of the approach, which can be accessed here. Our code supports the two-way translation of both audio and text inputs. Our input interface currently accommodates only MP3 files, though we plan to expand support to include more audio formats and custom vocabularies in the near future. We also intend to add support for various other languages and custom vocabularies. Our method is built upon the Fairseq framework. We introduce a novel formulation and extend the analysis of Coleman-Gurtin type equations incorporating dynamic boundary conditions. This extended model accounts for boundary energy dissipation, represented by a dissipative term within the total energy. We establish the well-posedness and derive an energy dissipation law for the introduced weak solution. Furthermore, under specific conditions on the stored energy, we demonstrate the global convergence of this solution toward a constant state. Finally, in Appendix A, we present an abstract variational framework for a broad class of systems governed by equations of this type. This approach relies on the decomposition of the energy rate into internal power and boundary power, where the latter is expressed as the sum of a reversible work component and a boundary potential. The variational formulation is derived via the application of a Lagrange multiplier method to enforce the dynamic boundary condition. The mathematical tools employed are standard within the field of continuum mechanics. Additionally, we illustrate the applicability of this framework to the Coleman-Gurtin system by explicitly constructing the necessary potentials. The framework is sufficiently general to be extended to other systems in continuum mechanics, such as the equations governing viscoelasticity or the theory of plasticity. The primary objective of this work is to provide a foundation for the future development of variational numerical methods based on this formulation. The proposed framework is applicable to general Coleman-Gurtin type systems, including those involving the diffusion of heat, mass, or momentum. Consequently, it can also address variational models for the nonlinear Fourier heat conduction law (see [10]) and the theory of thin films (see [11, 20]). Accurate short-term energy consumption forecasts are essential for managing energy systems, particularly when handling probabilistic data. This study evaluates the impact of forecast fusion on the daily 1-to-24h probabilistic distribution within low-voltage networks. Utilizing smart meter data from a French distribution utility, we first train and validate a deep learning model to generate community-level probabilistic load forecasts for the 1-to-60h and 6-to24h periods. These forecasts are then aggregated to produce the daily 1-to-24h probabilistic distribution, which is subsequently compared against directly forecasted results. The analysis reveals that while combining shorter-term forecasts reduces the overall forecast error, it fails to prevent the significant overestimation of the daily peak. This outcome is attributed to the accumulation of errors during the integration process. To address this, the value of integrating forecast peaks is explored. The findings suggest that either integrating shorter-term forecasts or explicitly forecasting the daily peak could be viable strategies for ensuring the reliable supply of energy. Finally, these conclusions are reinforced through an analysis of the French electricity market. This work is part of the "PREDICT" project, which aims to enhance the predictability of the French electricity market. The associated code is accessible at: https://github.com/JulienBourigault/probabilistic-load-forecasting-fusion. This commentary offers a high-level overview of the challenges, opportunities, and solutions related to embedding domain knowledge into machine learning, with a specific focus on knowledge graphs. Although significant progress has been made in the computational analysis of COVID-19 CT scans, the scarcity of expert annotations for training models remains a critical bottleneck. To overcome this limitation and enhance model generalization, we introduce a novel weakly supervised framework that eliminates the need for specific supervision of COVID-19 lesions. This approach utilizes a weakly supervised localization module to identify lesion regions and a subsequent segmentation module to delineate them. Furthermore, we developed a weakly supervised unsupervised learning strategy for lesion segmentation to prevent model bias. Experimental results on the LUNA16 and COVID-19 CT datasets demonstrate that our method achieves competitive performance in localizing and segmenting COVID-19 lesions compared to state-of-the-art supervised methods. Additionally, an ablation study reveals that the model is more prone to overfitting COVID-19 patterns, indicating a need for further bias reduction. We believe this method will contribute to the unbiased localization and segmentation of COVID-19 lesions in clinical settings. Precise localization and identification of vertebrae are critical for numerous clinical tasks, including vertebra labeling, surgical guidance, and tumor staging. This study introduces a novel method for locating and identifying vertebrae in abdominal CT scans. Our approach begins by training a deep learning model to detect vertebral bodies and estimate the spine's orientation within the CT volume. Subsequently, we project these 3D bounding boxes onto the axial plane to generate candidate regions for vertebrae. Finally, we employ a graph-based anatomically-constrained optimization technique to refine the localization of these candidates and assign identity labels. We evaluated our proposed method using the publicly available ABDOMINAL CT dataset, demonstrating that it surpasses the current state-of-the-art in both vertebral localization and identification. This study investigates single electron scattering while confined within a cavity. The cavity's electromagnetic field, amplified by an external laser to achieve a strong- or ultrastrong-coupling regime, acts as a protective shield for the particle. By modifying the scattering potential, electron wave packets can be reflected or transmitted with near-perfect efficiency. However, when the cavity field frequency aligns with the electron's de Broglie frequency, total transmission occurs despite the scattering potential being entirely repulsive. This counterintuitive phenomenon, known as dynamical stabilization, arises because vacuum fluctuations prevent the electron from reaching its minimum energy state. These findings are modeled using a semiclassical approach, where the cavity field is treated classically and the electron is described quantum mechanically. Furthermore, the phenomenon is analyzed within the quantum framework, demonstrating that ultrastrong coupling to the cavity field does not alter the dynamical stabilization effect. These results are expected to be observable in near-future experiments. Additionally, the study offers a potential explanation for the anomalous tunneling effect reported in recent literature. Finally, numerical simulations of the ultra-cold cavity's dynamics indicate that the system relaxes to a new steady state within approximately 100 picoseconds. Consequently, the proposed effect is viable for detection using existing technology. Finally, it is shown that dynamical stabilization can be effectively controlled by adjusting the driving laser's frequency and intensity. This controllability, combined with the ability to achieve total transmission of the incident electron even through a repulsive potential, opens new avenues for manipulating the flow of quantum particles. These capabilities are particularly relevant for applications in quantum information processing and the design of new materials. This study investigates the potential of physics-informed multi-fidelity reinforcement learning (RL) approaches to enhance energy efficiency in legged locomotion. By utilizing elastic actuators, we demonstrate that these methods can significantly reduce energy consumption. The multi-fidelity strategy involves training on high-dimensional, computationally expensive models with sparse data and refining the policy on lower-dimensional, cheaper simulations where rapid, diverse data generation is feasible. Our results indicate that physics-informed multi-fidelity training surpasses both physics-agnostic and single-fidelity counterparts in end-performance, while also enabling the development of energy-efficient policies. Furthermore, we show that energy usage can be effectively predicted on lower-dimensional surrogate models, allowing for the training of energy-aware policies. Finally, we introduce a novel method for representing and optimizing over energy usage, which facilitates the training of policies specifically designed to minimize energy consumption. Collectively, these approaches yield energy-efficient reinforcement learning policies capable of training on 20x fewer simulation data points while achieving an 11.5% reduction in energy usage on the rehabilitation trot gait. These techniques are demonstrated on the OpenAI Gym RobotLocomotion environment, which features realistic musculoskeletal models, actuator back-drivability, and actuator compliance. Our findings suggest that this paradigm will be increasingly vital for locomotion control in systems where energy efficiency is critical, such as those operating in space or on Mars. We introduce the variational separability depth functional, which quantifies how deeply a quantum state is entangled. We demonstrate that this functional can be optimized using the variational quantum algorithm (VQA) framework. Furthermore, we establish convergence guarantees for its optimization and propose specific initialization strategies. This paper addresses attribute-based image search, a task where users provide either image-level or feature-level attributes to query a database. While prior research has primarily focused on utilizing image-level attributes, we propose leveraging rich feature-level attributes, such as those found in e-commerce datasets, to enhance the system. This study addresses light field depth estimation, a critical yet underexplored aspect of light field technology. Existing depth estimation techniques often fail to account for foreground objects occluding background ones, leading to inaccurate results. To address this, we introduce a cost constructor capable of handling object occlusions. Drawing inspiration from the CCA algorithm, we developed this constructor, which is formulated as a mixed integer linear program (MILP). By utilizing the CAC to manage occlusion relationships between objects, we solve the MILP to generate an occlusion-aware cost function for depth estimation. This paper examines the Fokas-Lenells equations, a system of coupled nonlinear partial differential equations, utilizing the bilinear method within the framework of Hirota's method. Through this approach, we derive multisoliton and rational multisoliton solutions of arbitrary order for both defocusing and nondefocusing scenarios. We provide detailed descriptions of these solutions and their associated dynamics. Additionally, we present new findings regarding the conservation laws of the Fokas-Lenells equations, including their bilinear forms. Finally, we offer a novel construction of conservation laws for this integrable system by employing the bilinear method combined with the bilinear form of an auxiliary function. This function is obtained by applying a specific operator to the f-function, which is a key component in Hirota's method's bilinear equation. Furthermore, we establish novel expressions for multisoliton and rational multisoliton solutions based on the expansion of the f-function. These findings are supported by numerical simulations. Our results contribute to a deeper understanding of the analytical and geometric properties of the Fokas-Lenells equations. Additionally, we have developed a new method for constructing multisoliton and rational multisoliton solutions that is more efficient than Hirota's method. This approach is also applicable to other nonlinear partial differential equations. Our work holds significant potential for advancing the study of nonlinear waves and their applications in various scientific and engineering disciplines. The paper concludes with a discussion of future research directions. This study was conducted as part of the first author's doctoral thesis at the University of Ioannina, Greece. Among these, Verlinde's stratonovich gravity holds significant interest as a potential quantum gravity framework underlying the entropy-black hole area proportionality, while non-metric gravity serves as the background for a emerging class of gravitational theories. This study demonstrates that a modified version of the generalized Dirac symmetry within double field theory naturally generates non-Riemannian gravity actions. This mechanism offers an efficient method for deriving such actions, especially for important cases like the Weyl non-metric gravity. Furthermore, we investigate the holographic dual of non-metric stratonovich gravity, suggesting that it may describe a deformed semi-classical gravity theory non-linearly coupled to a non-metric holomorphic energy-momentum tensor. Finally, we construct actions for singular gravity systems where the dilaton duality is replaced by a generalized shift symmetry. This construction extends to higher-rank duality groups, such as the SL(n+1,Z) symmetry of n-fold duality, suggesting that the non-metric gravity system associated with SL(n,Z) duality can be derived from a generalization of the double field theory action. Consequently, this approach provides a holographic description of non-metric gravitational systems. Additionally, we propose that the Weyl non-metric gravity theory could represent a non-Riemannian gravitational background theory. Finally, our analysis of non-metric stratonovich gravity reveals a novel non-linear realization of semi-classical gravity, potentially representing a holographic dual. This finding underscores the critical role of non-metric gravity in understanding quantum gravity. The proliferation of wireless devices has rendered the IEEE 802.11 standard indispensable for everyday use. In extensive environments like homes, users often face signal degradation due to high channel load and excessive distance from access points (APs). To address these issues, extending the signal via repeaters or access extenders is a viable solution. However, the primary challenge remains identifying the optimal AP or extender, alongside the most suitable channel, to mitigate interference and physical signal loss. This paper introduces a novel algorithm leveraging IEEE 802.11k/v specifications to efficiently select the best AP. The method incorporates client velocity, a feature enabled by the 802.11v standard, to predict signal strength fluctuations caused by mobility. Furthermore, the proposed approach accounts for channel load, utilizing Airtime Distribution (IEEE 802.11v) reports to assess the channel occupancy of neighboring APs. Extensive simulations were conducted to evaluate the algorithm's performance regarding channel load, distance, and channel selection. Results indicate that for mobile devices, the scheme achieves a $100\%$ success rate in connecting to the best AP, surpassing the performance of existing solutions. Additionally, simulations on stationary devices demonstrate a $90\%$ success rate in connecting to the best AP, achieving an average of $9.7$ handovers, compared to $17$ handovers achieved by existing schemes under the same conditions. Finally, an experiment was performed to validate the simulation findings. This involved deploying a testbed with APs, extender nodes, and a mobile device, followed by measuring the signal strength of the extender. The experimental results corroborate the simulation outcomes, confirming the algorithm's effectiveness. Consequently, the proposed scheme offers a cost-effective and efficient method for identifying the best AP or extender node. Future work will focus on integrating this algorithm with channel load-aware mechanisms to simultaneously determine the best AP, extender, and channel. Furthermore, the scheme's adaptability to ad-hoc networks will be explored. Finally, the approach will be extended to support IEEE 802.11ax, ensuring compatibility with next-generation wireless networks.
